dialogue.text: Thank you. A sensible amount of snacks is a concept I understand, if not one I always practice.

details_in_summary: Hannah wants to leave room in the trunk for a small cooler.
Riley offers to bring snacks for the drive.
key_facts: Hannah will drive her car and collect Riley in Ballard.
Riley plans to fly back to Seattle on Sunday, January 11.
Hannah will stay with Walter until Monday.
minor_details: Hannah wants to leave room in the trunk for a small cooler.
Riley offers to bring snacks for the drive.

summary: Riley discussed driving to Spokane for the January visit, planning to meet Hannah in Ballard Friday, January 9. They will drive in the morning to avoid dark driving; Riley needs to return to work Monday, while Hannah stays with Walter until Monday. Riley will fly back Sunday, January 11. They will bring snacks, leave space in the trunk for a small cooler, and Riley will keep snacks compact.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so I finally tested the green bike in my apartment building's courtyard.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How'd it feel with the new tire?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: The tire seemed fine. The rear brake, though, was sluggish when I squeezed the lever.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Sluggish as in it took a while to slow you down?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. I squeezed and it didn't respond as quickly as I expected. I wasn't going fast, thankfully.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good call keeping it in the courtyard.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: It was drizzling lightly, too, so I wasn't keen on getting ambitious.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A very Seattle test ride.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Very glamorous. A delivery van briefly blocked the courtyard entrance, so I had an audience of 1, maybe.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you stop right after the brake felt weird?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, I got off. With those cables already frayed, I don't want to pretend it's fine.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Definitely not something to find out about in traffic.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Exactly. The brakes need attention before I take it into traffic.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And you've still only spent $38 on the tire and tube, right?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Right. I'm still trying to keep the total under $250. My favorite hobby: comparing the cost of a bicycle to the cost of a bicycle.

key_facts: Daniel tested the bike in his apartment building's courtyard.
The rear brake responded sluggishly when he squeezed the lever.
minor_details: He rode in light drizzle.
A delivery van briefly blocked the courtyard entrance.

summary: Riley discussed Daniel's courtyard test of the green bike. The rear brake was sluggish and cables appeared frayed, leading to the decision to address braking before riding in traffic. Weather and a temporary audience were noted, but not critical. Riley confirmed the test occurred with conservative speed due to safety concerns. Cost tracking remained a focus, with total expenses kept under $250. Action items include inspecting/replacing brake cables and re-testing braking performance in a safe area before any traffic exposure.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: We should figure out when to do laundry next. That late Wednesday wasn't quite the victory I'd hoped for.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It was nice walking down there and not finding both machines taken, though.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah, on December 10 both washers were available. But we didn't finish the laundry until 10:45 p.m.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I was ready for bed way before the dryer was done.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: You did have chamomile tea while you were waiting for the dryer.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Which probably didn't help me stay awake. It was good tea, though.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but if the reward for finding 2 empty washers is staying up until 10:45, I'm not sure we won.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: We could try Sunday morning again. At least we got it done that time.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: We did wait 20 minutes for the second washer.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: True. Still, I'd rather wait in the morning than finish that late.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: How about Sunday, December 21? Could we go downstairs before lunch?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, before lunch works for me.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Good. Oh, I folded this pillowcase inside out.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I don't think the pillow will mind.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Probably not. Okay, Sunday before lunch it is.

key_facts: On December 10, both washers are available, but the laundry is not finished until 10:45 p.m.
They plan to go downstairs before lunch on Sunday, December 21.
minor_details: Maya folds a pillowcase inside out.
Riley has chamomile tea while waiting for the dryer.

summary: Riley discussed laundry planning with Maya, noting past delays and a 20-minute wait for the second washer. They preferred finishing by morning and tentatively scheduled Sunday, December 21, before lunch as the next window. Action item: go downstairs before lunch on December 21 to complete laundry.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How are things looking for you before you head out?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Pretty good. I'm just starting to think about a spring visit to my aunt Ada in Victoria.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. What got you thinking about it?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: We were on the phone after dinner, and it came up. I'd really like some unhurried time with her.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Have you started planning anything yet?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Barely. I've got a paper list on the back of an envelope, which is a very sophisticated system.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, it's a start. What's on it?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Mostly things I need to think through. One is meals. I don't want Ada to feel like she has to host me for every one.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, you could sort out some meals yourself and still have plenty of time together.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. What if I keep that in mind from the beginning, instead of turning up and making it her problem?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Seems like a good thing to put on the envelope.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: It is now. Well, the short version: arrange some meals independently.

details_in_summary: Sam has started a paper list on the back of an envelope.
key_facts: Sam is beginning to plan a spring visit to Ada in Victoria.
Sam wants to arrange some meals independently rather than have Ada host them all.
minor_details: The idea came up during a phone call after dinner.
Sam has started a paper list on the back of an envelope.

summary: Riley discussed Sam Okafor's spring visit to aunt Ada in Victoria. They considered an unhurried visit. Sam uses a paper list on the back of an envelope for planning and identified meals as a key item. Decision: Sam will arrange some meals independently to avoid burdening Ada and to allow more relaxed time together.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. Okay, so, how's your evening going?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Pretty good. I'm waiting for the kettle to boil, which is apparently taking all evening.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I'll keep you company. I just realized the first episode of The Quiet Beacon is scheduled for December 20.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, that's Saturday. I would've forgotten.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, I figured a reminder might help us get to it before we accidentally see any spoilers. I'll text you the series page now.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Got it. Your text just came through, and I'm still waiting for this kettle to boil.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Excellent. I've managed to be useful before a kettle, which is a new personal best.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Low bar, but congratulations. We're still listening separately, right?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yep, and comparing notes afterward. And no reviews until we're done.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right. I'll stick to the series page, then.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, good. I was about to compare 3 different ways of sending you the reminder, so this was surprisingly efficient.

key_facts: The first episode is scheduled for December 20.
Daniel sends Riley the series page through a text message.
minor_details: The message arrives while Riley is waiting for a kettle to boil.

summary: Riley and Daniel coordinated a reminder for The Quiet Beacon premiere on December 20 to avoid spoilers. They decided to listen separately and compare notes afterward, with no reviews until completion. Daniel texted Riley the series page as the reminder, and they discussed efficiency, noting they were exploring multiple reminder methods. Action items: Riley to review the series page; Daniel to continue sending reminders and compare methods.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Oh, Ada just got back to me about 2 of those photo dates.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. The ones you weren't sure about?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. The picture on the Victoria pier, the one with the white border, is from 1988.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's satisfying. What was the other one?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: A family picnic photo. Someone's holding a striped umbrella in it. Ada dated that one to 1996.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did she remember the year?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: She had a note on her own copy, actually. That's how she dated it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, even better. You don't have to just take a guess.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. I added Ada's explanation to the picnic photo's notes, so the reason for 1996 is there too.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That seems useful. Otherwise it's just a year in a filename with no clue where it came from.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Right. What if I look at it later and wonder whether I made it up? Past Sam is not always a reliable source.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Well, this morning Past Sam has receipts.

key_facts: Ada identified a picture on a Victoria pier as being from 1988.
Ada dated a family picnic photo to 1996 using a note on her own copy.
Sam added Ada's explanation to the picnic photo's notes.
minor_details: The pier picture has a white border.
Someone in the picnic photo is holding a striped umbrella.

summary: Riley discussed Ada’s dated photos: the Victoria pier image is 1988 and the striped umbrella picnic photo is 1996. Ada’s note on her copy explains the picnic date, and Sam added this explanation to the photo notes. They emphasized the value of documented notes over filenames and noted the need to verify later whether Past Sam’s recalls are reliable, planning to review the receipts and notes.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: And did you end up booking the flight back?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, I booked it. It leaves Spokane at 4:30 p.m. on Sunday, January 11.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Oh, good. That gives us a bit of Sunday before you have to go.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, and I'll be back in Seattle for work on Monday.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I checked with Dad about where we'll sleep, too. I'll use Walter's guest room, and you can sleep on the living-room couch.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The couch is fine. Did he have enough bedding?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: He says he has an extra quilt in the hall cupboard.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Perfect. I'm making a note to pack slippers, too.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: That's sensible. I always think I'll remember things like that, and then, well, I don't.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So you're still staying with him until Monday?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes. And I'll pick you up in Ballard on Friday, January 9, in my car.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay. Flight's booked, couch is sorted. I think that's everything on my end.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Mine too. I can finally stop comparing routes. Driving gives me the flexibility I wanted, and in theory I can leave it at that.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm going to hold you to 'in theory.'

details_in_summary: Walter says he has an extra quilt in the hall cupboard.
Riley makes a note to pack slippers.
key_facts: Riley's return flight leaves Spokane at 4:30 p.m.
Hannah will use Walter's guest room, and Riley will sleep on the living-room couch.
minor_details: Walter says he has an extra quilt in the hall cupboard.
Riley makes a note to pack slippers.

summary: Riley confirmed the Spokane flight for Sunday, January 11, and lodging with Walter: couch with an extra quilt; packing slippers noted. Hannah will pick Riley up in Ballard on Friday, January 9, and Riley remains with Walter until Monday for stay. Action items: Riley packs slippers; both finalize travel plans and housing arrangements; comparison of routes discussed.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I'm still picking dust off my sweater from Mom's place.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, did the demolition finally happen?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. It began on December 15 and finished on December 16. It looks very different in there.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How's Teresa managing without a kitchen?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, she set up a temporary meal station in the dining room. The toaster's sitting on a folded bath towel.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A bath towel? Is that to protect the table?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, that's the idea. And there's a blue tarp covering the doorway to the kitchen, so at least she's not looking straight into it every time she eats.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds like a pretty strange dinner setup.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: It does. She's making it work, though.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And the cabinets are still due January 22, right?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Right. We still need to decide what kind of lighting will actually make the new workspace useful. I've already spent too long comparing options, which I'm sure surprises you.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Not even a little. Just make sure Teresa can see what she's chopping.

details_in_summary: A blue tarp is covering the doorway to the kitchen.
The toaster sits on a folded bath towel.
key_facts: Demolition began on December 15 and finished on December 16.
Teresa has set up a temporary meal station in the dining room.
minor_details: A blue tarp is covering the doorway to the kitchen.
The toaster sits on a folded bath towel.

summary: Riley noted that the demolition occurred on December 15–16 and that Teresa is managing with a temporary dining setup, including a toaster on a folded towel and a blue tarp over the kitchen doorway. Cabinets are due January 22, and the group needs to decide lighting for the new workspace. Riley emphasized the need for lighting that lets Teresa see what she’s chopping, and to keep progress on cabinet options moving forward.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Hey. Is it just me, or does it feel later than it is tonight?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It does. It's been dark forever. Here, I put a coaster under your drink.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Thanks. I took a look at that loop today.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The one reaching NW 57th Street and 24th Avenue NW? How was it?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: There was uneven pavement near the 24th Avenue NW portion. Enough that I'd want people to know about it before setting out.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Was it just one patch, or did it go on for a while?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: More than one patch. And there's a crossing on the loop I want to reconsider, too.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What about the crossing?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I'm not confident I've checked it well enough to describe it. I don't want to assume it works just because it's on the map.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. Especially since the library asked you to check crossings and places to rest.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Exactly. Oh, my notebook got damp in a light shower, so some of my notes are a little wavy.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The map got a field test, and so did the notebook.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: The notebook passed with reservations. Okay, but instead of trying to make that whole loop work, what if I test something shorter?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That makes sense. Do you have a route in mind?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: An out-and-back along 22nd Avenue NW. I'd still need to walk it and check the conditions.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And where people could stop and rest. Shorter doesn't necessarily mean easier for everyone.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Right. I can describe what I find rather than just call it accessible. And an out-and-back would give people the option to turn around sooner.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Let's try that instead of squeezing the whole loop into the trial. You can see what the shorter route is actually like first.

details_in_summary: Her notebook got damp in a light shower.
key_facts: Maya found uneven pavement near the 24th Avenue NW portion of the loop.
She plans to test an out-and-back route along 22nd Avenue NW.
minor_details: Her notebook got damp in a light shower.
Riley puts a coaster under her glass.

summary: Riley and Maya discussed testing a loop along NW 57th Street to 24th Avenue NW, noting uneven pavement and multiple patches, plus a crossing to reconsider. The notebook was damp, and there were reservations about the map’s crossings. They agreed to test a shorter route: an out-and-back along 22nd Avenue NW, with notes on rests and accessibility, and the option to turn back early.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. Is it already this dark, or did Friday just give up early?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It's nearly 6. I was about to pack up.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Same. I've got this mug of mint tea beside my laptop, and it's basically cold now.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Before we go, did you want to look at that queue example?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. What if a delivery is late and it's also headed to the wrong place? It could qualify for both 'Delayed' and 'Wrong destination'.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right. We put both labels in the prototype, but we haven't said what happens when both apply.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: And stacking two equal labels on the row might make the queue harder to scan.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Especially if you're looking down the list by destination.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. I'd put 'Wrong destination' first. That's the problem with where it's going, not just when it'll get there.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So the destination problem is the main status on the row, even when the delivery's late too?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yes. Then the late condition can be a secondary note on that same row. We shouldn't make people open the delivery to find it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I like that. Destination and expected arrival time can still stay on the row too.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Right. Different jobs for those bits of information. The note says it's late; the time gives them something specific.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm circling this example with my green pen so I remember which case we're talking about.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Very high-tech. I'll write an example of the combined case for the test script.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Great. We can see if people understand the main status and still notice the late note.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah, without a legend doing the explaining for us.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: All right. Let's leave it there for tonight.

details_in_summary: Riley circles the example with a green pen.
key_facts: For a delivery that is both late and headed to the wrong place, the row will show the destination problem first.
The late condition will appear as a secondary note on that row.
Sam will write an example of the combined case for the test script.
minor_details: Riley circles the example with a green pen.
Sam has a mug of mint tea beside the laptop.

summary: Riley and Sam discussed how to label a delivery that is both late and at the wrong destination. They agreed the main status should be the destination, with lateness as a secondary note on the same row, so users don’t need to open the delivery. They’ll keep destination and ETA visible on the row. Actions: create a combined case example for the test script; use a green-pen marker to highlight the example; verify user understanding without a legend.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. How's your Saturday morning going so far?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Pretty good, just easing into it. How about you?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Not bad. Oh, I meant to tell you, Nadiya did come look at the living-room window.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good. Did she find the spot where the tissue was moving?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes. She brought a small flashlight to the inspection, which was sensible. I'd cleared a stack of magazines off the windowsill, so she could actually get to it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And what was going on with it?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: The existing weatherstripping was flattened. So there wasn't much left to fill the gap along the bottom of the sash.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That would explain the cold patch Owen noticed, too.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yeah. Nadiya plans to replace it with compressible foam weatherstripping. It should have a bit more give than what's there now.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you settle on when she'll do it?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: We did. The repair is scheduled for January 6. I considered trying to sort it myself, but, well, I still didn't want to stick anything on the painted frame without permission.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Makes sense. At least you know what the problem is now.

details_in_summary: Nadiya brought a small flashlight to the inspection.
key_facts: Nadiya found that the existing weatherstripping was flattened.
Nadiya plans to replace it with compressible foam weatherstripping.
The repair is scheduled for January 6.
minor_details: Nadiya brought a small flashlight to the inspection.
Hannah cleared a stack of magazines off the windowsill.

summary: Riley and Hannah discussed the living-room window. Nadiya inspected the area, found flattened weatherstripping and a cold patch (noted by Owen). The plan is to replace with compressible foam weatherstripping. Repair is scheduled for January 6. Riley considered DIY but decided not to modify the painted frame without permission.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How's the Italian coming along?

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: Pretty well, actually. I was pleased after our walk last Saturday, December 13.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, we practiced greetings while we were walking that afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: I tried 'buongiorno' and 'come stai?' And I remembered both without checking my notes.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You did! Did they feel any easier to say out loud than they did in your head?

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: A little. I still had to pause before 'come stai?' but at least I didn't have to dig through my bag.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Your scarf was giving you enough trouble as it was.

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: Oh, it kept slipping off one shoulder. I spent half the walk putting it back.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And then there was that dog carrying a stick wider than the path.

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: Yes. Very ambitious dog. We were lucky it didn't take the scarf with it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I think you managed to say 'buongiorno' while we were getting out of its way.

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: I did, didn't I? It wasn't the most... orderly practice, but the words came back.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a nice feeling, not having to check.

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: It is. They're small things, but I want to be able to use Italian with Francesca instead of always defaulting to English. It's a start.

key_facts: They practiced greetings during a daytime walk on December 13.
Amara tried both “buongiorno” and “come stai?”
minor_details: A dog had been carrying a stick wider than the path.
Amara's scarf kept slipping off one shoulder.

summary: Riley and Amara reviewed Italian progress from the December 13 walk. Amara recalled 'buongiorno' and 'come stai?' without notes, with partial fluency improvements but still pausing. They experienced distractions (scarf adjustment, a large dog) during practice. The goal is to use Italian with Francesca instead of English, and they plan to continue practicing to build conversational comfort.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So, where do we stand on the dog question?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Still interested. But I was looking at our work schedules, and Wednesdays are pretty long.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. With our usual schedules, a dog would be alone from about 8:30 a.m. until 4:30 p.m.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but could a walker come in the middle of that? I found a local one who lists $30 for a half-hour visit.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That seems possible. We'd probably want help on more than just Wednesday, though.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Maybe 3 weekday walks? Let me do the arithmetic on this yellow notepad.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: While you're doing that, do you want a clementine? I've got a bowl of clementines on the coffee table.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah, thanks. So, 3 walks at $30 is about $90 a week.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh. That adds up pretty fast, doesn't it?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: It does. And that's every week, not just the $325 adoption fee we saw.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right. The walker could solve the long-day problem, but we'd have to be comfortable paying for it regularly.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: And we'd still need written approval from the landlord. The dog cannot sign its own lease, unfortunately.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Let's keep looking at the numbers. I still like the idea, but $90 a week gives me pause.

key_facts: On Wednesdays, their usual schedules would leave a dog alone from about 8:30 a.m. until 4:30 p.m.
A local walker’s listed rate is $30 for a half-hour visit.
They estimate that three weekday walks would cost about $90 a week.
minor_details: Maya does the arithmetic on a yellow notepad.
Riley has a bowl of clementines on the coffee table.

summary: Riley discussed the dog question with Maya. Wednesdays have long schedules; a dog would be alone 8:30–4:30. A dog walker could cover mid-day visits; 3 weekday walks at $30 each totals about $90/week, plus a $325 adoption fee previously noted. Written landlord approval is required. They considered ongoing costs and whether to proceed. Next steps: Maya to finalize walking schedule arithmetic, assess ongoing costs, and confirm landlord approval.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I'm sitting here with the Crystal Mountain ticket page open and my lunch getting cold.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good timing. Did you get a total for January 17?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes. For 2 lift tickets, it's $278 total. I wanted to check with you before I bought them.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, I'm good with that. I'll reimburse you for half, so $139.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Okay. Let me just make sure I've got Saturday, January 17, 2026 selected. Yes. All right, I'm buying them online now.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How's the website treating you?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Well, it keeps asking me to review things. Which is sensible, but I have reviewed them approximately 6 times.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A very thorough ski trip.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: There. I bought the 2 lift tickets. $278 total, just like it said.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Great. I'll get you the $139.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Thanks. Oh, the confirmation email's here. I'm putting it in a folder labeled ‘Trips,’ so I can actually find it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Look at you, with a system.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: In theory. And the rental packages are still for pickup on January 16 and return on January 18, so that's covered.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Nice. We should still check the road and weather forecast the evening before, though, before deciding whether to drive.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Absolutely. Friday evening, January 16. Having the bookings doesn't mean we have to drive if it looks unsafe.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Agreed. We'll make the call then.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Good. And I'm planning to pack extra socks, which is the one part of skiing I feel fully qualified to prepare for.

details_in_summary: Hannah puts the confirmation email in a folder labeled “Trips.”
She plans to pack extra socks.
key_facts: Hannah buys two lift tickets online for a total of $278.
Riley will reimburse Hannah for half of the ticket cost.
They will check the road and weather forecast the evening before and decide whether to make the drive.
minor_details: Hannah puts the confirmation email in a folder labeled “Trips.”
She plans to pack extra socks.

summary: Riley discussed purchasing 2 lift tickets for January 17 with Hannah; total $278, with Riley reimbursing half ($139). Hannah filed the confirmation email in a Trips folder. Rental packages are booked for pickup January 16 and return January 18. They agreed to review road and weather forecasts Friday evening January 16 to decide whether to drive. Hannah plans to pack extra socks and keep preparing for the trip.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, I'm having lunch and trying not to check my phone for theories.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good. We said no reviews, remember?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I remember. Have you listened to both episodes of The Quiet Beacon?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. I listened to the second one while shelling peas.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: That's a very calm way to listen to a missing logbook mystery.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The peas didn't seem worried. Episode 2 came out today, December 22, so I put it on as soon as I could.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I paused mine to answer the delivery buzzer, and then had to get back into it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you catch the envelope in the empty drawer?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I did. Addressed to the visiting inspector, right?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right. I think he hid the logbook. Why else would an envelope addressed to him be in there?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, I'm not sure it points to him. Someone else may have placed the envelope there.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: To make him look responsible?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Maybe. Or they put it there for some other reason. An envelope with his name on it doesn't prove he put it in the drawer.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: True, but it's still a pretty direct link. I'm sticking with the inspector for now.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Fair. I'm apparently going to compare every possible explanation until I forget what the question was.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Classic you. Do you still think the logbook was moved before the storm?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I do, but I don't know by whom. I'm not ready to give the envelope that much weight.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And I'm still betting there's an ordinary explanation for the haunting. The inspector hiding the logbook fits that well enough for me.

key_facts: Episode two was released on December 22.
Riley thinks the visiting inspector hid the logbook because an envelope addressed to him was found in the empty drawer.
Daniel thinks someone else may have placed the envelope there.
minor_details: Riley listens to the second episode while shelling peas.
Daniel pauses his playback to answer a delivery buzzer.

summary: Riley and Daniel discussed The Quiet Beacon episodes and the ongoing logbook mystery. They noted an envelope addressed to the visiting inspector found in an empty drawer and debated whether the inspector hid the logbook or someone else planted it. Riley remains inclined to link the envelope to the inspector for now; Daniel cautions against over-relying on the envelope. They considered both a pre-storm logbook move and a ordinary explanation for the haunting.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I'm having peppermint tea at my desk before I head out. It's doing a reasonable impression of warmth.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good evening for it. How's the train-and-bike commute going now?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: It's settled down, actually. The fender helps, and I can get into the bike room with my badge. I'm planning to keep doing it after the holidays.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Nice. Does it take much more planning now?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: A little. I charge the bike lights on Sunday and Wednesday evenings, so I don't have to wonder if they're going to give up halfway there.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a good system. What about getting the bike on the train?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I allow an extra 10 minutes for a train with room for the bike. Not every train has a convenient spot when I need it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And if the weather's really awful?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: On particularly windy days, I leave the bike at home, take the train and walk the last stretch instead.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, the wind can make that short ride feel a lot longer.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. What if I just don't fight it? That's been my very sophisticated solution.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Sounds like you've got the whole thing sorted.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Mostly. I even keep a folded tea towel by the apartment door. Useful for the wet bits, and it means I'm not hunting for one when I get home.

details_in_summary: Sam keeps a folded tea towel by the apartment door.
key_facts: Sam now charges the bike lights on Sunday and Wednesday evenings.
They allow an extra ten minutes for a train with room for the bike.
On particularly windy days, Sam takes the train and walks the last stretch instead.
minor_details: Sam keeps a folded tea towel by the apartment door.
They were drinking peppermint tea when they talked with Riley.

summary: Riley discussed Sam’s bike-and-train commute, including recent improvements (fender, bike-room badge) and a charging routine on Sundays and Wednesdays. Sam plans extra 10 minutes for trains with a bike and avoids the bike on very windy days, preferring to walk portions. Riley noted the practical setup and a folding tea towel kept by the door for wet bits. Action items: continue post-holiday commute plan and maintain charging routine.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: Hello, Riley. It's a chilly evening, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It is. I'm glad to be inside.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: I've been looking at that bare bit of hallway wall. I thought a photograph of a ferry might be nice there.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds good. Do you have one in mind?

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: A few, I think. My family photographs are in a box in the hallway closet, but I'd like another pair of eyes. Would you help me choose one?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Of course. We can look through them together.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: Good. I don't want to turn it into an expensive project, though. And I'd rather not damage the photograph.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Makes sense. We can start by seeing what you've got, and take it from there.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: There's an empty frame in a kitchen drawer, too. It might be useful, or it might just be taking a very long holiday.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: We can have a look at that too. Are you free during the day on December 27?

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: Yes, Saturday works. Come over in the afternoon, and we'll choose a photograph. What do you think?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That works for me. I'll come by in the afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: Lovely. And mind the closet door when we get to it. I've been using a folded grocery bag to keep it from swinging shut.

details_in_summary: Lian has been using a folded grocery bag to keep the closet door from swinging shut.
She mentions that she has an empty frame in a kitchen drawer.
key_facts: Riley will visit Lian on December 27 to choose a photograph.
Lian keeps her family photographs in a box in the hallway closet.
minor_details: Lian has been using a folded grocery bag to keep the closet door from swinging shut.
She mentions that she has an empty frame in a kitchen drawer.

summary: Riley discussed helping Lian choose a photograph for the hallway wall. They will review family photos from the closet and consider using an empty frame. They agreed it should be inexpensive and not damage photos. Action: Riley will visit on Saturday afternoon, December 27, to help select a photo. Note: the closet door is currently held shut with a folded grocery bag.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Oh, come on. I just compared those 2 listings, and I don't think either one's worth pursuing.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What happened?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, I opened both listings in separate browser windows. Very advanced comparison system. One's a basement apartment in Wallingford, listed at $1,695 a month.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's comfortably under your limit. What's the catch?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Very little daylight. The photos made it look like the sun had been politely asked to leave.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Is that a deal breaker, or just not ideal?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I think it's a deal breaker. I could live with a smaller place, but I don't want to feel like I'm underground all day.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Fair. What was the other one?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: A top-floor apartment in Greenwood, listed at $1,975 a month.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So $75 over the $1,900 ceiling, before utilities.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. I started trying to convince myself the ceiling was more of a suggestion.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You set it before you got attached for a reason. Is there anything about the place that really changes that?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: No. I've decided not to stretch my budget for it. I can live without the top floor; I can't really live with pretending $1,975 is $1,900.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's pretty clear, then. Daylight and budget are the deal breakers, not whether the listing has perfect furniture.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Right. Though the basement photos did have this narrow blue sofa. I spent an embarrassing amount of time looking at it instead of the windows.

key_facts: A basement apartment in Wallingford was listed at $1,695 a month but had very little daylight.
A top-floor apartment in Greenwood was listed at $1,975 a month.
Daniel decides not to stretch his budget for the Greenwood place.
minor_details: The basement listing showed a narrow blue sofa in its photos.
Daniel had opened both listings in separate browser windows.

summary: Daniel evaluated two listings with Riley Morgan: a Wallingford basement at $1,695 with poor daylight—a deal breaker; a Greenwood top-floor at $1,975—over the $1,900 ceiling. Daniel decides not to stretch the budget. Riley notes that daylight and budget are the deal breakers, not furniture. Outcome: neither listing will be pursued; no further action items identified.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: This blue 2020 Bolt in Shoreline has about 42,000 miles on it.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but what are they asking for it? Does it leave room for taxes and fees?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The asking price looks like it might, but I'd want the full numbers before we get excited. We're still capped at $20,000 out of pocket after the trade-in.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Right. And what does the listing say about the battery?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It says the high-voltage battery was replaced under Chevrolet's recall.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: That's good to see, though I'd want to verify it. Are there photos of the inside?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. Rubber floor mats, even.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: And those dealership photos make the parking lot look like a tourist attraction.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I know. They got a very flattering angle on the pavement.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but compared with the Leaf we looked at, I think the Bolt makes more sense for us.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Me too. The extra range would give us more room for longer drives, if we can find one in good condition.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: And we'd still need to sort out that outlet. We know it's on the building's common electrical system, but not whether we can use it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. The fast charger near 15th Avenue Northwest can be a backup, but I don't want every charge to be an expedition.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Especially for about 70 miles of driving a week. Anyway, do they have test-drive appointments on the listing?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: They do. There's one tomorrow, but that's Christmas Eve.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Let's not rush up there over Christmas. What about after the holidays?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: January 3 is showing as available. Does that work for you?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: It does. Can you book it for both of us?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. Okay, it's confirmed for January 3.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Good. We can see how it drives without deciding anything tonight.

key_facts: A blue 2020 Bolt listed in Shoreline has about 42,000 miles on it.
The listing says its high-voltage battery was replaced under Chevrolet's recall.
They arrange to test-drive it on January 3.
minor_details: The listing photos show rubber floor mats.
Maya jokes that the dealership photos make the parking lot look like a tourist attraction.
meta.storyline_title: A plug in the parking space

summary: Riley discussed a blue 2020 Bolt for sale, noting ~42,000 miles and an asking price with potential taxes/fees; they plan for up to $20k out-of-pocket after trade-in. Battery was replaced under recall; they’ll verify and review interior photos. Compared to the Leaf, Bolt offers more range but charging access is uncertain. Test-drive booked for January 3 for both; aim to assess drive quality before deciding.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The delayed one can show up in the queue before there's a driver assigned.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, right. So there's nobody to contact on the driver side yet.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. I noticed that edge case before the break, and I didn't want it to get lost.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good catch. Did you have wording in mind?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I drafted 'Driver not assigned' as a note for that case.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That seems clear. It doesn't make the delay sound like the driver's fault.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Right. The status would still be 'Delayed'; the note just explains what's missing.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And we wouldn't make someone open the delivery to find that out.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: That's what I was thinking. What if we put the note right on the row?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, let's include the unassigned example in the next round of review. I'll add it to the prototype after the holiday.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Great. I jotted the note in a small spiral notebook, which is apparently my very sophisticated tracking system.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It's working so far.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Well, it made it to this call, so that's 1 successful test.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm sitting by the apartment window, trying to get enough light to read my notes. Yours sound more organized.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I wouldn't go that far. It's just the one phrase, really.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's enough. We can see how it sits alongside the destination and arrival time.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: And check that it reads as a note, not another status. Or, sorry, not a replacement for the status.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yep. I'll put the example in, and we can look at that in review.

key_facts: A delayed delivery can appear in the queue before a driver has been assigned.
Sam drafts the note “Driver not assigned” for that case.
Riley will add the unassigned example to the prototype after the holiday.
minor_details: Sam had jotted the note in a small spiral notebook.
Riley is sitting by the apartment window during the call.

summary: Riley and Sam discussed the edge case when a delayed item has no driver assigned. They agreed to add a note 'Driver not assigned' to explain the missing driver while keeping the status as 'Delayed'. The note should appear on the row, not replace the status. They planned to include the example in the next prototype round and review after the holiday, noting the tracking note as a simple test.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You're still looking at that mark on your recorder case. What happened to it?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, it picked up a smear of blue ink. I have no idea where from.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A little souvenir. How did the Bremerton trip go?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Really well, actually. I recorded 4 more commuters on that trip.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. Did you get the different set of memories you were hoping for?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I think so. One passenger talked about using the crossing to decompress after a hospital shift.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That makes sense. Just having that stretch of time where nobody needs anything from you.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. And it felt pretty different from the person who recognized the same passengers every morning but didn't know their names.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Do you have enough interviews now?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I do. Enough to start selecting material, anyway. Now I get to spend an unreasonable amount of time deciding what to keep.

details_in_summary: Daniel's recorder case picked up a smear of blue ink.
key_facts: On the Bremerton trip, Daniel recorded four more commuters.
One passenger spoke about using the crossing to decompress after a hospital shift.
minor_details: Daniel's recorder case picked up a smear of blue ink.

summary: Riley noted a blue ink smear on Daniel's recorder case. Daniel described a successful Bremerton trip, recording four more commuters. One interviewee spoke about using the crossing to decompress after a hospital shift, highlighting difference between with and without name recognition. Riley asked about interview volume; Daniel confirmed there are enough interviews to begin selecting material, with the next step being decisions on what to keep.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Oh, honestly. The trial labels are much easier to read, but 2 of them have come loose already.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh no. What happened?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: We mounted them on the shelf edges, and coats and bags brushed them loose. Apparently readable isn't quite the same as safely attached.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you find both of them?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes. I found 1 loose card under a chair. I had a clementine on my break, so at least something held together.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Could you move the labels a little farther back, so they don't stick out into the path?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Maybe. We could still keep them near the shelf edges, just tuck them back a bit. In theory, people could see them without catching them on a coat.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And you wouldn't have to make the letters any smaller.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Right. I can talk it through with Marisol before we move anything. I'd rather not solve the brushing problem by making the ranges hard to read again.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, that feels like a small enough thing to try.

details_in_summary: Hannah found one loose card under a chair.
key_facts: The trial labels were mounted on the shelf edges.
Coats and bags brushed two labels loose.
minor_details: Hannah found one loose card under a chair.
She had a clementine on her break.

summary: Riley and Hannah discussed trial labels: two labels loosened after being mounted on shelf edges, with coats brushing them. A loose card was found under a chair. They considered moving labels slightly farther back to reduce snagging while keeping readability, and agreed not to shrink the text. Riley suggested finalizing the change after talking it through with Marisol.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: You're staring at the laundry basket like it's going to sort itself.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I was hoping it might. How much did we actually get done last Sunday?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: On December 21? We finished 1 load. There was only 1 washer available when we went down.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right. At least we didn't have to stay up until 10:45 again.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah, that late Wednesday experiment was a little too successful at avoiding people.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you see the notice downstairs?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: The one held up with blue painter's tape? Yes. The left-hand washer has been out of service since December 23.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did it say when they're fixing it?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: No, there's no repair date on the notice.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So we can't really count on having 2 machines next time.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but even before that, we only had 1 available on Sunday. Maybe we should just bring a smaller load.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Small enough for 1 machine, you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Exactly. Then if there's only 1 free, we're not hanging around waiting for another.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: When do you want to try?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: How about Tuesday, January 6?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Sure, 1 smaller load on Tuesday, January 6.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I'll sort this striped dish towel into the pile for that wash.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And we'll keep the rest of the pile from taking over the basket.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: A modest goal for a building with 1 working washer.

details_in_summary: Maya sorts out a striped dish towel for the next wash.
key_facts: On December 21, they complete one load using the only washer available.
A notice says the left-hand washer has been out of service since December 23, with no repair date given.
They plan to try one smaller load on Tuesday, January 6.
minor_details: The notice is held up with blue painter’s tape.
Maya sorts out a striped dish towel for the next wash.

summary: Riley and Maya discussed laundry capacity with one washer out of service since Dec 23 and no repair date listed. They agreed to schedule a smaller load for Tuesday, January 6, to avoid waiting for a second machine. Action items: sort the striped dish towel into the Jan 6 load; keep the rest of the pile manageable.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I'm having my bowl of oatmeal, and I just remembered to tell you: Omid gave us a date for the window repair. It's January 2.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good. So we should make sure he can get to the window.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah. The dresser's still away from the wall, but there are a few things left around there.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: There's a paperback lying on the bedroom floor. I can pick that up.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but let's clear the whole window area, not just the book. We can do it on January 1, the night before.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Works for me. We can move anything else that's in the way, too.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Do you think the dresser's far enough out already?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It's about a foot from the wall. We can have a look when we clear everything and move it farther if we need to.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Sounds good. No point making the window accessible by building a little obstacle course in front of it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right. I'll grab the paperback now, though, before I forget.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Thanks. Then we'll do the rest on January 1.

key_facts: The window repair is scheduled for January 2.
Maya and Riley plan to clear the window area on January 1.
minor_details: A paperback is lying on the bedroom floor.
Maya makes the plan over a bowl of oatmeal.

summary: Riley discussed preparing for a window repair with Omid on January 2. They plan to clear the window area on January 1, moving the dresser away and removing obstacles. Riley offered to pick up a paperback and both agreed to clear everything around the window to ensure access by repair day.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, my mom's thinking about where she wants the kitchen lights controlled.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The lights under the cabinets?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. An electrician is booked for January 8 to inspect the wiring for the under-cabinet lighting.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Does Teresa know where she wants the switch?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: She prefers it near the kitchen doorway. So she can turn the lights on as she comes in, instead of reaching across the counter.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That makes sense. Is she still using the dining room as her meal station?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. She labeled a box of plates with masking tape, which is more organization than I usually manage.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And now you can spend the next week comparing the exact positions for that switch.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I've already considered several. It's good to have a hobby.

details_in_summary: She has labeled a box of plates with masking tape.
key_facts: An electrician is booked for January 8 to inspect the wiring for under-cabinet lighting.
Teresa prefers the light switch near the kitchen doorway.
minor_details: She has labeled a box of plates with masking tape.

summary: Riley discussed a kitchen lighting project with Daniel Reyes: an electrician is booked for January 8 to inspect under-cabinet wiring. Teresa prefers a switch near the kitchen doorway to avoid reaching across the counter. They noted Teresa uses the dining room as a meal station and Daniel has labeled a box of plates. Action items include comparing switch positions next week and finalizing the placement. Daniel noted having considered several options.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.text: Hi, Riley. Have you managed to stay warm this evening?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, Ingrid. Yeah, I'm inside folding laundry, so it's a pretty exciting Saturday.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.text: A thrilling social calendar. I was thinking about what we were talking about over lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The case study for your consulting website?

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.text: Yeah. The old Routewise transit-app project. I want to keep it concise, but I'm not sure what to leave out.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What's taking up the most space in your head?

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.text: The early visual explorations. I'm deciding whether to leave them out, and I keep arguing both sides.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What would someone learn from seeing them?

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.text: That's the pointed question, isn't it? They might show how I was thinking, but they could also just look like a pile of options.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Maybe you don't have to show all of them. Is there one that helps explain a decision?

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.text: Possibly. I suppose I could include one only if it earns its place.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. And if you can't explain why it's there in a sentence, maybe cut it.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.text: That's a useful test. Show me the part that's bothering you, and then ask it to justify its existence.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A very calm interrogation. Oh, I still have the pen you lent me at lunch, by the way.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.text: Keep it for now. It's not an heirloom.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Thanks. And with Routewise, you could start by writing the main point without any of the explorations, then see if one actually adds something.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.text: I like that. Start with the point, not the pile. I'll give it a try.

key_facts: The case study is about an old transit-app project called Routewise.
Ingrid is deciding whether to leave out the project's early visual explorations.
minor_details: Ingrid had lent Riley a pen at lunch.
Riley is folding laundry during their evening call.

summary: Riley and Ingrid discussed refining the Routewise transit-app case study. The key decision: start with the main point, not the exploratory visuals. Ingrid will consider including one early visual exploration only if it clearly justifies its place and can be explained in a sentence. Riley suggested testing each element’s necessity by justification; Ingrid will try starting with the point and trimming the rest.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: They're in 2 different boxes, which is probably why I didn't notice how many there were.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What kind of boxes?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: A shoebox and a blue biscuit tin. Both full of family photographs.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, wow. I didn't know you had those.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Neither did I, apparently. There's a strip of masking tape on the tin's lid, but it doesn't say anything useful.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The tape is just there for moral support.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: In theory it was a label. Anyway, I'm sitting here with my peppermint tea looking at these and wondering what would actually be useful to you.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'd love digital copies, especially if I could find what I was looking for and share them easily.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Right. I was going to offer you the boxes, but then we'd just be passing them back and forth, wouldn't we?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, and I'd probably spend half the time trying to remember which box I'd looked in. I think sorting them would be worth it.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I do too. At least then we'd have something more useful than 2 mystery containers.

key_facts: Hannah has the photographs in a shoebox and a blue biscuit tin.
Riley would like digital copies they can find and share.
minor_details: There is a strip of masking tape on the tin's lid.
Hannah is drinking peppermint tea.

summary: Riley’s counterpart Hannah explains two containers hold family photographs (a shoebox and a blue tin). They discuss creating digital copies and sharing them, aiming to avoid back-and-forth passing of the boxes. They agree that sorting the photos would be more useful, producing a clearer, shareable collection rather than two mystery containers.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Oh, huh. I just noticed we're calling the same picking action 3 different things.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: In the warehouse screens?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. It shows up as 'pick,' 'collect,' and 'pull' in different places.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh. Those sound like they could be 3 separate steps.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. Or 3 very enthusiastic ways to describe 1 step.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Have you got somewhere to keep track of them?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I do now. I opened a working sheet called Warehouse Words today, December 29. I'm starting a terminology guide.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Nice. Do you want help finding more examples?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yes, please. What if we put the actual screen and the wording in the sheet, so we know where each one came from?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I can add examples from the warehouse flow designs. I'd rather look at those than try to settle the vocabulary from memory.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Same. My memory is a terrible source of screen copy.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Mine would confidently invent a 4th word.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Which, to be fair, would make the sheet more interesting. Not more useful, though.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Also, you've got a pencil tucked behind 1 ear.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Oh. I was wondering where that went. And is it already after 5?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Not quite. The meeting room clock is 3 minutes fast.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Good to know. I'll share Warehouse Words with you, and we can start with what's actually on the screens.

key_facts: Sam opened a working sheet called Warehouse Words on December 29.
One picking action appears as “pick,” “collect,” and “pull” in different places.
Riley will add examples from the warehouse flow designs.
minor_details: Sam has a pencil tucked behind one ear.
The meeting room clock is three minutes fast.

summary: Riley and Sam discussed inconsistent labeling of the pick action ('pick', 'collect', 'pull') across screens. Sam has started a working sheet called Warehouse Words to create a terminology guide. They agreed to compile examples from actual screens and warehouse flow designs, then share the guide. Action items: share Warehouse Words, begin with screen copy, and add design-derived examples.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I walked the shorter route along 22nd Avenue NW today. I've got a distance estimate for us to sort out.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good. Where did you turn around?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: At NW 57th Street. I think that makes more sense than trying to salvage the whole loop.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, especially after that uneven pavement near 24th Avenue NW. How far was it?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: My phone estimates the out-and-back at about 0.3 miles. That's the whole trip, not just the way out.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'll write about 0.3 miles on this yellow sticky note, then. Out and back.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Thanks. Okay, but let's keep 'about' in there. My phone isn't a surveyor.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A very small surveyor with a lot of other responsibilities.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Exactly. I was carrying my orange umbrella, too, so I was mostly concerned with keeping the phone dry.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did NW 57th Street feel like an easy turnaround to describe?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I think so. From the library, follow the route along 22nd Avenue NW to NW 57th Street, then turn back. It's a named street instead of some arbitrary spot.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And we can put the turnaround on the map and say the distance covers both directions.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yes. I still want to be clear about crossings and places to rest, though. The distance alone doesn't tell someone whether the walk works for them.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right. We could keep those as separate notes next to the route description, rather than squeezing everything into the map.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: That would help. And I don't want to call it accessible as if that means the same thing for everyone.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay. For tonight we've got the turnaround and the approximate distance, and room to add the practical details.

details_in_summary: Riley writes the distance on a yellow sticky note.
key_facts: The revised route turns around at NW 57th Street.
Maya's phone estimates the out-and-back distance at about 0.3 miles.
minor_details: She carries an orange umbrella on the scouting walk.
Riley writes the distance on a yellow sticky note.

summary: Riley and Maya discussed a short route: out-and-back distance about 0.3 miles along 22nd Ave NW, with a turnaround at NW 57th Street. They will note the distance as about 0.3 miles on a yellow sticky note. They plan to place the turnaround on the map and keep crossings and rest spots as separate notes. They caution that the route is not universally accessible. Tonight’s tasks: finalize distance and add practical details.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I floated that spring visit to Aunt Ada, and she's receptive to me coming to Victoria in May.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good. Are you thinking you'll go on your own?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah, just me. I'm starting to compare ways to get across the water.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What are you looking at?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: A direct passenger ferry, or a route through Port Angeles. I haven't settled on either.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'd check the whole journey, not just the ferry time. Getting to the terminal and waiting for connections could make a difference.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Right. The crossing is only the part where you get to sit down and feel like you've made progress.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And the rest is all the bits you can accidentally leave out of the comparison.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. My first comparison is scribbled in a pocket notebook, and it's mostly just ferry times so far.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Still a start. You could add the trips to and from the terminals.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: What if I put those next to each crossing, plus any waiting time? Then I can compare the actual days, not just the boats.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. And see what the connections look like before picking one because it seems faster.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I've got 6 browser tabs open for the trip already, so clearly I'm conducting a very controlled study.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Only 6? You're showing remarkable restraint.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Give me a minute. I should at least get the journey times into the notebook before I open another one.

details_in_summary: They have six browser tabs open for the trip.
key_facts: Ada is receptive to a visit in May.
Sam plans to make the trip on their own.
Sam is comparing a direct passenger ferry with a route through Port Angeles.
minor_details: Sam's first comparison is scribbled in a pocket notebook.
They have six browser tabs open for the trip.

summary: Riley summarized Sam's plan to visit Aunt Ada in Victoria in May, considering a direct ferry versus a Port Angeles route. Sam and Riley discussed evaluating the entire journey, including terminal access and waiting times, not just ferry durations. Sam began updating a notebook with journey times and suggested placing those alongside each crossing for a days-based comparison. Action items: add terminal legs and wait times to the notebook, compare overall trip days, and review connections before choosing a route; Sam has six tabs open.

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: Hi, Riley. Good to see you. How's your December 31 going so far?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Pretty good. It feels a little strange to be out at lunch today, though.

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: It does. Half the city seems to have decided the year is already over.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm not quite there yet. Oh, I'll have a bowl of tomato soup, please.

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: That sounds good. And sorry, is my folded paper shopping bag in your way beside my chair?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: No, you're fine. So how's work been?

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: Busy enough. Actually, there's an opening I thought might suit you.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh? What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: The short version is, it's a product designer opening at Bluewake. They're a Seattle shipping-software company.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Interesting. What do you know about the design work?

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: Not enough to give you a useful answer yet. I heard about the opening, but I haven't gotten the details.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay. I'd be interested in hearing more before I decide whether it's something I want to explore.

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: Of course. I can ask a few questions and see what I find out.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, would you? I'd appreciate it.

key_facts: The opening is for a product designer at Bluewake.
Bluewake is a Seattle shipping-software company.
Naomi raises the opening at lunch on December 31.
minor_details: Riley orders a bowl of tomato soup.
Naomi has a folded paper shopping bag beside her chair.

summary: Riley discussed lunch plans and noted the year-end mood. Naomi mentioned a potential opportunity: a product designer opening at Bluewake, a Seattle shipping-software company, but lacked details. Riley expressed interest in learning more before deciding. Naomi offered to ask questions and gather information to share; action item: Naomi will obtain specifics about the opening for Riley to review.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I'm sitting on the sofa, and it's actually not too bad in here tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, is the window behaving itself?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Well, sort of. I rolled up an old blue bath towel and put it along the lower edge of the window. It's helping with the cold until the repair.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The very sophisticated towel solution.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes. In theory, bath towels have other uses, but this one has a new career.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Can you still open the window with it there?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I can. I just lift the towel away first, and the window opens.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good. And Nadiya's still coming on January 6?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes. Owen moved the side table, so she can reach the window easily when she comes.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you find anything interesting behind it?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: A stray pen. Not quite the treasure I'd hoped for.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Well, at least you're a little warmer, and the window's ready.

details_in_summary: Hannah found a stray pen behind the table.
key_facts: Hannah has placed a rolled towel along the window's lower edge as a temporary measure.
Owen moved the side table so the window can be reached easily.
Hannah can still open the window after lifting away the towel.
minor_details: The towel is an old blue bath towel.
Hannah found a stray pen behind the table.

summary: Riley and Hannah discussed window insulation and repair status. Hannah improvised with a towel to seal the lower edge, allowing the window to open when needed. Owen moved a side table to improve Nadiya’s access for her January 6 visit. Hannah found a stray pen behind the window. Overall, they noted better warmth and the window is ready.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, I listened through the ferry interviews, and I think I've finally got a structure for the piece.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good. Where'd you land?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I've chosen excerpts from 3 commuters for the track. I want it to move from a morning departure to an evening return.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And still no narrator?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Right, no narrator. I'd rather let the commuters carry people through it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That could work. Does somebody actually say it's morning, though? A visitor might come in halfway through.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: That's the part I'm wrestling with. I don't want to make someone sound like they're announcing the time just to orient the room.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: No, but you could look for a little bit of ordinary context. Someone mentioning their morning routine, maybe.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. Something that belongs in the memory anyway, rather than an explanation stapled to it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Exactly. And for the evening, maybe the passenger talking about decompressing after the hospital shift?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: That's one I'm considering for the return. I'd need to listen for whether the excerpt makes the time clear on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How long have you got to make all that happen?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: The target is 3 minutes and 30 seconds. Which seemed generous until I started choosing between sentences.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Our old study-session problem. You'd spend 20 minutes deciding which pen to use.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: And the pen was always exhausted by the end. I've marked promising passages with orange sticky tabs, so at least those are easy to find.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Is that what all the notes are for, too?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, my editing notes are in that spiral notebook with the bent cover. It's less organized than the tabs make it look.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You might not need to tell visitors everything. If they know they're hearing ferry commuters, the shift from morning to evening could just emerge.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I like that. Give them enough to get their bearings, but leave the voices room to be a little messy.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. They don't need a timetable, just a way into the stories.

details_in_summary: He marked promising passages with orange sticky tabs.
His editing notes are in a spiral notebook with a bent cover.
key_facts: Daniel has chosen excerpts from three commuters for the track.
His target length is three minutes and thirty seconds.
He wants to move from a morning departure to an evening return without adding a narrator.
minor_details: He marked promising passages with orange sticky tabs.
His editing notes are in a spiral notebook with a bent cover.

summary: Riley and Daniel discussed shaping a 3:30 piece from three ferry commuters, with no narrator. They will move from morning departure to evening return and avoid explicit time cues, using ordinary context to orient listeners. Daniel will check excerpts for time clarity and consider a hospital shift decompressing moment for the evening. He’s organized with orange sticky tabs and a notebook of editing notes. Action items: select passages, ensure bearings without a timetable, and preserve voice variety.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I scanned another batch from the family photo box over the holiday.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. How many did you get through?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: 36 photos in the second batch. I copied the scans to an external drive as a backup before doing any more labeling.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good call. After all that scanning, I'd be nervous having just the 1 copy.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. The scanner and I spent enough time together already.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you use the same naming system as the first batch?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I'm sticking with a year when I know it and a short subject description. If I'm not sure of the date, I'm still leaving it open.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That makes sense. Ada was able to help with those 2 dates, at least.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Right. And I kept a mug of tea on a separate counter from the photos this time. Seemed like a reasonable precaution.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A very sensible distance between the tea and the archive.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. The photos have survived long enough without my tea getting involved.

details_in_summary: Sam kept a mug of tea on a separate counter from the photos.
