key_facts: The second scanning batch contained 36 photos.
Sam copied the scans to an external drive as a backup.
minor_details: Sam kept a mug of tea on a separate counter from the photos.

summary: Riley and Sam discussed scanning progress: Sam completed 36 photos in the second batch and backed up scans to an external drive before labeling. They will use a naming system based on year and a short subject, leaving unknown dates open. Ada helped identify two dates. Sam kept tea away from the archive as a precaution. Action items include continuing labeling with backups and maintaining separation between beverages and the archive.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I've been thinking about how we'd make the apartment quiet for a new dog. I found a rescue guide that suggests limiting visitors during the dog's first week.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That makes sense. I guess we shouldn't expect a dog to come in and feel at home right away.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah. Okay, but where would it go if it wanted to get away from us, too?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: We could put a dog bed in the corner beside the living-room bookcase. It's a little out of the way.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Would there be enough room for it to stretch out there?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I think so, depending on the dog and the bed. We could measure it before we get anything.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I'm folding this blanket now, and it just occurred to me we could put a blanket on the bed, too.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, something soft it can curl up on. And we'd let it come over to us when it's ready.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: And keep the first few evenings pretty quiet. No welcoming committee.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A very exclusive committee. Just us, sitting on the couch trying not to stare at the dog.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I can manage that. Probably.

details_in_summary: Maya folds a blanket while they talk.
key_facts: Maya found a rescue guide that suggests limiting visitors during a dog’s first week.
Riley suggests putting a dog bed in the corner beside the living-room bookcase.
minor_details: Maya folds a blanket while they talk.

summary: Riley and Maya discussed preparing the apartment for a new dog with a quiet first week—limiting visitors and creating a low-stimulus environment. They considered a dog bed in the corner beside the living-room bookcase and decided to measure the space before purchasing. They planned to add a soft blanket on the bed and allow the dog to approach when ready. They agreed on a quiet first few evenings with no welcoming committee and an exclusive, low-key welcome by the two of them. Action items: measure space, select bed, place blanket, enforce quiet period.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Oh, that's less wall than I thought.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: For the photo display?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yeah. I just measured it, and the usable wall space is 6 feet wide.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, that is small. How'd you measure it?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: With a retractable tape measure I borrowed from the circulation desk. There's a thermostat interrupting 1 end of the wall, too.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So you can't quite treat it like a clean rectangle.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Right. And Daphne has set a $70 budget, so I don't have a lot of room to experiment.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Do you know how many photos you want?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I'm considering 8 photographs. I keep going back and forth between that and fewer.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: 8 could work. You could do 2 rows of 4, with the same amount of space between them.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: That sounds tidy. I worry it'll look a little crowded, though.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Depends on the size. I'd leave some space around the outside, too, so it looks intentional.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes, rather than 8 pictures trying to escape the thermostat.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Exactly. Or you could use fewer, but make them bigger.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: In theory, that's simpler. But I want a little variety in the everyday life they show.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Then I'd start with 8 and see how the spacing feels. You don't have to fill every inch.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I could measure out a couple of sizes on paper. That'd be cheaper than guessing.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And if it feels too tight, you can take 1 or 2 out.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: All right. 8 as a starting point, not a sacred number. I can live with that.

details_in_summary: A thermostat interrupts one end of the wall.
key_facts: The usable wall space is six feet wide.
Daphne has set a $70 budget.
Hannah is considering eight photographs.
minor_details: A thermostat interrupts one end of the wall.
Hannah used a retractable tape measure borrowed from the circulation desk.

summary: Riley discussed displaying eight photographs on a 6-foot wall with a thermostat interrupting one end and a $70 budget. Options considered: two rows of four with equal spacing, outer margins, or larger single images. Action items: measure sizes on paper to approximate spacing; start with eight and adjust if the layout feels tight; be prepared to drop to fewer photos if needed. Decision: 8 is a starting point, not a fixed number.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, now that the 6th and final episode is out, are you satisfied? It came out on January 1, and I've been turning it over since.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Mostly, yeah. I can accept the caretaker hiding the logbook to cover up a misread storm warning. I was pretty sure it was the inspector, though.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: The envelope really did make him look guilty. I kept wondering if someone else had put it in the drawer.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You were less sold on it than I was. And I was right about the haunting having an ordinary explanation, at least.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: You were. But the splice in that earlier bit of audio was the clue for me. It hinted that the caretaker had altered the evidence.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: See, I missed the splice the first time. I wish it had been a little easier to hear.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, on the replay I thought it was clear enough. Not obvious, but clear enough that I didn't feel cheated.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I heard it once I knew to listen for it. I'm just not sure that counts as fair.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: That's fair. Sorry, I'm tapping my spoon against my empty mug. Apparently I need percussion to consider this properly.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I don't mind. I liked the ending, even if I needed it to point me back at the clue.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. And we managed to get through it without reading reviews. For us, that's almost as impressive as solving it.

key_facts: The sixth and final episode came out on January 1.
The station caretaker hid the logbook to cover up a misread storm warning; an earlier recording's splice hinted that the caretaker had altered the evidence.
minor_details: Daniel taps his spoon against an empty mug.

summary: Riley discussed the final episode, released January 1, and expressed conditional satisfaction with the reveals: the caretaker hiding the logbook to cover a misread storm warning, and the inspector possibly framed by the envelope. The pair debated the haunting’s ordinary explanation, and whether the audio splice signaled evidence alteration. Riley noted accessibility of the clue; they both preferred solving without reviews.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Oh, good, the window repair was completed yesterday, January 2.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, the worker replaced the exterior sealant around the window.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but how does the wall look from in here? I'm opening the curtains so we can get more light.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The patch looks dry to me. There's a bit of dust on the windowsill, though.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I can wipe that up. Does the wall feel dry too?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, it does. But it was dry during that light rain before, too.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Right. It was the wind-driven rain that seemed to make it damp.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So I wouldn't push the dresser back yet.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Agreed. Let's leave it where it is until we've seen how the wall holds up in a substantial rain.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And check the patch again afterward?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah. The dresser can enjoy its extended vacation from the wall.

key_facts: The repair was completed on January 2.
The worker replaced the exterior sealant around the window.
minor_details: Riley finds a bit of dust on the windowsill.
Maya opens the curtains to let in more light.

summary: Riley and Maya discussed window repair completed Jan 2, with exterior sealant replaced. Riley noted the wall patch is dry with some dust on the sill. They agreed the wall stayed dry during light rain but damp from wind-driven rain, so the dresser should not be moved back yet. They will monitor the wall during a substantial rain and recheck the patch afterward; the dresser remains away from the wall.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Oh, nice, I'm in. I just heard back about a neighborhood photography project.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, cool. What kind of project?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: It's run by South End Photo Walks. They're documenting neighborhood shopfronts, and I joined.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How'd you find out about it?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: There was a notice pinned beside a coffee-shop door. Very effective advertising, apparently.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: When does it start?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The first meeting is January 17. I'm curious whether I can make a coherent series instead of just collecting individual pictures.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, like what makes them feel like they belong together?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. What if I end up with 10 pictures I like and none of them have anything to say to each other? I mean, other than 'here's a shop.'

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I guess figuring that out is part of the fun, though.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I hope so. It'll be a good excuse to pay a little more attention when I'm out walking, at least.

key_facts: The project is run by South End Photo Walks.
Its first meeting is on January 17.
minor_details: Sam found the project through a notice pinned beside a coffee-shop door.

summary: Riley discussed Sam joining the South End Photo Walks neighborhood storefront project. The first meeting is January 17. Sam wonders how to create a coherent photo series rather than a set of unrelated shots. They noted the promotional notice was effective. Riley suggested figuring out coherence is part of the process and should be interesting. Action item: consider attending or following up about the January 17 meeting.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. Okay, so, how's your evening going?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Pretty good. How are you?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Good. I'm trying to get my apartment requirements down before I arrange any more viewings.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Probably a good idea after the restaurant fan and the dark basement.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. I wrote the list on the back of a grocery receipt, so it's a very official document.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What's on it?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I want a separate bedroom so I can shut the door on my work equipment. I don't need to look at it all evening.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Fair. What about laundry?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I'm willing to use shared laundry if it's in the building. And I want to listen for street noise with the windows closed.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You could bring a tape measure, too. And maybe check the building at different times of day, instead of spending hours scrutinizing listing photos.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, that'd tell me more. I can compare 2 pictures of a wall for an alarming amount of time.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: College-era Daniel would have made a spreadsheet for each wall.

details_in_summary: Riley suggests bringing a tape measure.
key_facts: Daniel wants a separate bedroom so he can shut the door on his work equipment.
He is willing to use shared laundry if it is in the building.
He plans to listen for street noise with the windows closed.
minor_details: He writes his requirements on the back of a grocery receipt.
Riley suggests bringing a tape measure.

summary: Riley discussed Daniel's apartment search, noting his objective list written on a grocery receipt. Daniel prioritized a separate bedroom for work equipment, acceptable in-building shared laundry, and listening for street noise with windows closed. Riley advised bringing a tape measure and checking the building at different times of day rather than relying on listing photos. Daniel acknowledged the idea of using photos for comparison. Riley referenced Daniel's college-era habit of making spreadsheets, highlighting a methodical approach to evaluating walls and listings.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Hi, Riley. How's your evening going?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, Hannah. Pretty quiet, which I'm enjoying. How about yours?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Quiet here too. Oh, I tried moving those holds signs we talked about.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The ones that kept getting brushed loose?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yeah. The revised signs sit above their respective rows now, instead of on the shelf edges. Marisol attached them with removable adhesive strips.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds promising. Can you still read the ranges easily?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I think so. They're higher up, obviously. I had to borrow a step stool from the workroom to reach.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And hopefully they're out of the way of coats and bags now.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: In theory, yes. I'm cautiously encouraged, but I'd like to see how they work when the shelf is busy.

details_in_summary: Hannah had to borrow a step stool from the workroom.
key_facts: The revised signs sit above their respective rows.
Marisol attached them with removable adhesive strips.
minor_details: Hannah had to borrow a step stool from the workroom.

summary: Riley discussed with Hannah the relocation of hold signs to above their rows, attached by Marisol with removable adhesive. Readability remains acceptable, though signs are higher and require a step stool. Potential interference from coats/bags noted; plan to observe effectiveness during busy shelf periods before confirming success.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I keep thinking about how easy the blue Bolt was to park when we test-drove it on January 3.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, and the driver's seat was comfortable for me. I wasn't sure it would be, just looking at it.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but did you feel like you could see well enough? Apart from when the windshield fogged up for a minute.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I did. Once the fog cleared, anyway. I could picture driving it regularly.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Same. And the coffee on the way home was good, even if it didn't help us decide anything about the car.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It helped me stay awake long enough to talk about it.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: So I think it's comfortable enough to pursue. But I don't want to make an offer until we know what we can actually do about charging here.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Agreed. That outlet's on the building's common electrical system, so having it next to our space doesn't mean we can just plug in.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Right. We need to find out whether we're allowed to use it, and what the arrangement would be. The parking space came with a mystery appliance.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And if that works out, we still need to make sure the numbers fit under $20,000 out of pocket after the trade-in, including taxes and fees.

details_in_summary: The windshield fogged briefly during the drive.
key_facts: They test-drove the blue Bolt on January 3.
Riley found the driver's seat comfortable, and Maya liked how easy it was to park.
minor_details: The windshield fogged briefly during the drive.
They stopped for coffee on the way home.
meta.storyline_title: A plug in the parking space

summary: Riley Morgan and Maya Chen discussed a test drive of the blue Bolt on Jan 3. They found it comfortable and acceptable visibility, noting windshield fog briefly. They agreed to pursue the car but need to confirm charging options: whether the building’s common outlet can be used and under what arrangement. They also must ensure the total out-of-pocket stays under $20,000 after trade-in, taxes, and fees, and clarify the mystery appliance in the parking space.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. Still awake? It's a bit late for sensible conversation.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Barely. I'm drinking peppermint tea, so I feel like I should be winding down.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.text: Well, I have a small piece of news. Elise and I are picking up Miso, a rescue dog, on January 7.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, wow! That's 2 days away. Are you ready?

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.text: As ready as we can be. We've bought a yellow leash, which is either cheerful or wildly optimistic.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What are you thinking for when Miso gets home?

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.text: For the first few days, we'll give Miso access to the living room and avoid having visitors. Just keep things quiet.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds nice. No big welcoming committee, then.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.text: No, just me and Elise trying not to make a fuss. We'll see how well we manage that.

details_in_summary: Ingrid mentions that the leash they bought is yellow.
key_facts: Ingrid and Elise are picking up Miso, a rescue dog, on January 7.
For the first few days, they plan to give Miso access to the living room and avoid having visitors.
minor_details: Ingrid mentions that the leash they bought is yellow.
Riley is drinking peppermint tea.

summary: Riley and Ingrid discussed adopting Miso, a rescue dog, arriving January 7. They plan to keep first days low-key with quiet introduction, allowing Miso access to the living room and avoiding visitors. They mention a yellow leash as a hopeful signal. Action items include preparing for Miso’s arrival on January 7 and maintaining a calm environment initially.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: I'm making a list in this small green notebook. It's supposed to help me figure out where to start.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What are you figuring out?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: My Fremont lease ends in February, and Lila plans to move when it ends. So I need to find a place.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, that's coming up pretty soon. Are you looking for another roommate?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: I think I want to live alone. I've never had a place entirely to myself, and I'd like to try it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That makes sense. What's on the list so far?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: Mostly questions. What can I spend, what do I actually need, how many listings can I look at before they all become the same apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Maybe start with the amount you're comfortable spending. Then use the rest to narrow things down.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: Yeah. I keep a spreadsheet for large expenses, so I can start there. I think I also need a list of things I can stop thinking about.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: Well, our kitchen faucet is dripping, and apparently that's enough to make 'faucet condition' feel like a major life decision.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Fair enough. Maybe put it on the list for when you're looking at places, not at the very top.

key_facts: Nora's Fremont lease ends in February.
Her roommate Lila plans to move when the lease ends.
Nora wants to live alone.
minor_details: Nora has started a list in a small green notebook.
She mentions a dripping kitchen faucet.

summary: Riley noted Nora’s Fremont lease ends in February and Nora plans to live alone and find a new place. Nora is building a list of questions (budget, needs, number of listings before saturation) and will start with what she can spend. She uses a spreadsheet for large expenses and wants a list of things to stop worrying about. They discussed the faucet issue as a non-top priority. Action items: Nora finalize budget, define must-haves, and begin evaluating listings; address faucet later.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: Oh, yes, that's the one! The ferry picture we chose on December 27.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The one leaving Bainbridge Island, right? With the bicycle at the railing.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: That's it. I like that you can just make out the bicycle.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It gives you something to look at besides the ferry itself.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: And it was tucked inside that yellow envelope. I almost put the envelope back without looking.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm glad you didn't. It's a small contact print, but at least we can see the image.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: Yes. I think there's a larger original somewhere in the house, though I couldn't tell you where.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: For now, we know which picture you want. That's a start.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: Mm. I keep remembering the barley soup I made for lunch that day, too.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It was good soup. And we did manage to choose a picture.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: A productive lunch. Not every lunch can say that.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The little print has a lot in it, even at that size.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: It does. I think it's the right one for the hallway.

details_in_summary: Lian had made barley soup for lunch that day.
The contact print was tucked inside a yellow envelope.
key_facts: They chose an image of a ferry leaving Bainbridge Island, with a bicycle visible at the railing.
The copy they selected is a small contact print.
minor_details: Lian had made barley soup for lunch that day.
The contact print was tucked inside a yellow envelope.

summary: Riley and Lian discussed selecting a ferry photograph from December 27, featuring a bicycle on the railing near Bainbridge Island. They noted the yellow envelope, the small contact print, and the possibility of a larger original elsewhere. They recalled a barley soup lunch and agreed the chosen image is suitable for the hallway.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You're still looking at those bike cables?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, yes. I bought replacement brake cables. They're in this paper sleeve, which somehow makes them feel more official.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How much did they set you back?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: $22. So with the $38 tire and tube, I'm at $60.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Still comfortably under the $250 replacement bike.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. Though I nearly bought a set with the wrong end fittings. I spent a ridiculous amount of time looking at the little metal ends.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Classic Daniel. Did you actually figure out which ones you needed?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I did, eventually. There were two that looked almost the same, and I had my usual crisis about making a $22 decision.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Well, better than getting home and finding out they don't fit.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: That's what I told myself for the entire comparison.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: When are you going to put them on?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I'm planning to try installing them on January 10, Saturday. Give myself some time, since the tire took longer than I expected.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Especially with that rear brake being sluggish in the courtyard.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. I don't want to take it into traffic like that. The cables are frayed, so they seemed like the place to start.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Makes sense. And at least you got the right little metal ends.

key_facts: Daniel spent $22 on replacement brake cables.
He plans to install them on January 10.
minor_details: The cables came in a paper sleeve.
He nearly bought a set with the wrong end fittings.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Morning, Riley. Someone's left a stack of paper cups by the sink. Very optimistic about how much coffee we're all having.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Morning. Either that or they're building a tiny tower.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: A practical tower, at least. Have you got a minute for Warehouse Words?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. Is that it in your notebook with the blue elastic band?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The notebook's just my notes. The sheet's here. It has 18 examples now, from screens, help articles, and training material.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. So the picking action we talked about is in there?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. 'Pick,' 'collect,' and 'pull.' Seeing them together helps, but a list of words on its own doesn't tell us much about where they're used.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right. We could end up changing a word that makes sense in one place just because it looks odd in the list.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. I added columns for the source and a link to the relevant screen. What if we make sure each example has a location, so we can check a change before recommending it?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. Could we also note whether the word is a button label or explanatory text? That might affect what fits.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Good point. I was thinking source would cover that, but no, not quite. A screen can have both.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And then when we look at 'pull,' we can see what it's actually doing, not just vote on which word we like.

key_facts: The sheet now has 18 examples from screens, help articles, and training material.
Sam added columns for the source and a link to the relevant screen.
Riley suggests noting whether a word is a button label or explanatory text.
minor_details: Sam’s notebook has a blue elastic band.
Someone has left a stack of paper cups by the sink.

summary: Riley discussed with Sam the Warehouse Words project. They reviewed 18 examples (screens, help articles, training material) for words like pick, collect, and pull, emphasizing context over list only. They planned to add columns for source, screen location, and a link, and to note whether terms are button labels or explanatory text. Action items: ensure each example has a location, verify usage on the actual screen before recommending changes, and differentiate by UI function.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, how are things looking for the drive?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Well, the current pass forecast includes a chance of snow. It's still a couple of days out, though.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay. Should we check the road conditions again before we leave?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yeah. Let's check WSDOT road conditions on Friday morning, before I head up to get you.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Friday morning works. We can decide what to do once we see them.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Exactly. No point comparing 6 routes tonight when we don't know what the pass will be like.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Look at you, not comparing routes.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I'm trying a new approach. I've even put a thermos by my keys, so in theory I'll remember it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a solid system. I'll check WSDOT Friday morning too.

details_in_summary: Hannah has put a thermos by her keys.
key_facts: The current pass forecast includes a chance of snow.
They will check WSDOT road conditions on Friday morning.
minor_details: Hannah has put a thermos by her keys.

They will reassess routes based on pass conditions and avoid pre-judging routes. Hannah notes a new memory routine (thermos by keys). Both will check WSDOT Friday morning.

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: Oh, that's good to hear. You're still thinking about the Bluewake opening?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, I am. Do you have a few minutes to talk it through?

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: Of course. How's your evening going?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Pretty good. I'm just putting away a loaf of bread while we talk.

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: Nice. I'm at my desk, squinting because my desk lamp needs a new bulb.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds like a very relaxing place to spend the evening.

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: It's a little like working in a cave, but with more email.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So, at lunch on January 6, you said the designer would work on tools for shipping operations teams, right?

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: That's right. The short version is, it's product design for the people doing shipping operations.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And it includes research with customers, not just interface design?

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: Yes, both customer research and interface design are part of the role.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's the part I keep coming back to. I like being able to talk to the people using what I'm designing.

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: Does the operations side interest you too?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I think so. It sounds like work where the details would matter a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: Mm-hm. Is there anything about it that's giving you pause?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I don't know enough yet to say. But the work sounds worth considering.

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: That's fair. You don't have to make a decision tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good, because I'm still trying to get this bread into a bag.

key_facts: The designer would work on tools used by shipping operations teams.
The role includes research with customers as well as interface design.
Naomi shared those details over lunch on January 6.
minor_details: Riley is putting away a loaf of bread during the call.
Naomi mentions that her desk lamp needs a new bulb.

summary: Riley discussed the Bluewake opening with Naomi, focusing on a designer role for shipping operations that includes customer research and interface design. Riley expressed interest in the operations aspect and potential details, but requested more information and a decision not to be made tonight. Action items: continue discussion to gather role specifics and responsibilities for clarity.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: So you were right about looking at the whole journey, not just the ferry.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, did you map out the Port Angeles route?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. I drew the connections as boxes linked by arrows. Very sophisticated.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: My favorite kind of travel research.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The thing is, I have to get to Port Angeles before taking the ferry to Victoria. And that ground travel could eat up a substantial part of the day.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Especially if the connections don't line up.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Right. My first estimate left only 20 minutes between 2 legs. Which looked fine until I actually thought about it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's not much room for anything to go wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: No. What if the first leg is late? Then the rest of my beautiful boxes are just decoration.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How does the direct crossing compare?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The direct passenger ferry leaves from Seattle, so it's a much simpler trip to picture. Fewer arrows, anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And you wouldn't have to get yourself to Port Angeles first.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. I also prefer to avoid renting a car for the visit, so I'm trying to think about getting around without one.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Makes sense. Are you leaning toward the direct ferry, then?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I think so. Or, well, it looks simpler. I haven't committed to it yet.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Fair. The map did its job, at least.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. It showed me that 20 minutes isn't a connection I want to rely on.

details_in_summary: Sam drew the connections as boxes linked by arrows.
Their first estimate left only 20 minutes between two legs.
key_facts: The Port Angeles option involves getting to Port Angeles before taking the ferry to Victoria.
The direct passenger ferry leaves from Seattle.
Sam prefers to avoid renting a car for the visit.
minor_details: Sam drew the connections as boxes linked by arrows.
Their first estimate left only 20 minutes between two legs.

summary: Sam evaluated travel options from Seattle to Victoria, comparing the Port Angeles route (mapped as boxes and arrows) with the direct Seattle ferry. He noted a 20-minute connection risk and the potential cascading delays, and expressed a preference to avoid renting a car. The direct ferry appears simpler and potentially preferable, but he has not committed yet. The mapping confirmed that relying on a 20-minute connection isn’t reliable.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: I've been thinking about that ferry photograph for the hallway. I don't want to damage it just to put it on the wall.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. The one leaving Bainbridge Island, with the bicycle at the railing?

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: That's the one. The copy we picked is such a small contact print, though.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You could ask a print shop to scan it and make a larger display copy, instead of fastening the photograph into a frame.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: So the photograph itself wouldn't have to stay in the frame at all.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right. You'd frame the new print and keep the photograph somewhere safe.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: I'd want the original returned after it's been scanned. I wouldn't want to leave it with the shop.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Definitely. You could ask them about that before handing anything over.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: I still think there's a larger original somewhere in the house. For now, all we've got to work from is the contact print.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A shop could tell you whether they can get a decent enlargement from that small copy.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: And whether it'll cost a fortune. I'm hoping to keep the whole project under $90.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Then it'd be worth asking for prices on the scan and print first, and seeing how much is left for the frame.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: I do have an empty frame, but the glass has a chipped corner.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh. I wouldn't use the glass as it is. Replacing it might still cost less than buying a whole frame.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: Mm. The empty frame may not be quite the bargain I thought it was.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Can I use the back of this utility bill? I'll sketch what I mean.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: Go ahead. It's paid, and the back is doing nothing useful.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: There. Photograph goes to the shop for scanning, then comes home. The display copy goes in the frame.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: That makes sense. I could ask what they charge before deciding on the size. What do you think?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I think that's a good place to start, especially with the $90 limit.

details_in_summary: Lian says the glass on her empty frame has a chipped corner.
key_facts: Lian wants the original returned after it has been scanned.
She hopes to keep the whole project under $90.
minor_details: Riley sketches the idea on the back of a utility bill.
Lian says the glass on her empty frame has a chipped corner.

summary: Riley and Lian discussed displaying the Bainbridge ferry photograph. They considered scanning the small contact print to create a larger display copy, then framing that copy while returning the original after scanning. They planned to ask the shop about enlargement feasibility, cost, and returning the original. They noted a chipped frame glass and potential frame replacement costs, keeping the project under $90. Riley proposed scanning first, then framing the display copy within budget.

dialogue.speaker: Beatrice
dialogue.text: Oh, that's what I should do with those postcards.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What postcards, Grandma?

dialogue.speaker: Beatrice
dialogue.text: The ones in a box in my hall cupboard. I'm going to look through them and decide which ones are worth keeping.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. Do you remember what's in there?

dialogue.speaker: Beatrice
dialogue.text: Some old views of Spokane, I think. There's a loose rubber band wrapped around the box, though I doubt it's doing much.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: When are you going to sort them?

dialogue.speaker: Beatrice
dialogue.text: Sunday, January 18. I thought I'd give myself the afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You could make a little room on the table before you start, so you can spread them out.

dialogue.speaker: Beatrice
dialogue.text: Yes, I'll clear away the bowl of sewing buttons first. Otherwise I'll be sorting buttons and postcards together.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds like a much longer afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Beatrice
dialogue.text: And the buttons would probably win. I'll make a keep pile and see how many I end up with.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds like a good way to start.

details_in_summary: A loose rubber band is wrapped around the box.
She plans to clear away a bowl of sewing buttons first.
key_facts: Beatrice plans to sort the postcards on Sunday, January 18.
The postcards are in a box in her hall cupboard.
She remembers having some old views of Spokane in the box.

She plans to clear away a bowl of sewing buttons first.

summary: Riley discussed Beatrice's plan to sort postcards from a box in the hall cupboard. Beatrice will decide which to keep, with a keep pile as the goal. dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: The smaller laundry load worked on January 6, at least.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, the working washer was free when we went down at 7 a.m., and we finished the load.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Which was a relief with the left-hand washer out of service.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A relief, but I don't really want to do laundry at 7 a.m. again.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but was it the hour or trying to fit it in before everything else?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Both, I think. It felt like we were squeezing it into the morning.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah. The machine was available, but apparently so were we, against our better judgment.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I did use the last scoop from the detergent box, by the way.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Oh, okay. And I brought the dry clothes upstairs in the green tote, if you're looking for it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Thanks. So, maybe an evening again? Just not as late as December 10.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Right. We didn't finish until 10:45 p.m. that night, even with both washers free.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What about before dinner instead?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but which day? Tuesday evening after dinner didn't work so well last time.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Let's try Wednesday, January 14, before dinner.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Sounds good. We'll see if an early evening is any easier.

details_in_summary: Maya brings the dry clothes upstairs in a green tote.
key_facts: On January 6, the working washer is free at 7 a.m., and they finish their small load.
They plan to try Wednesday, January 14, before dinner.
minor_details: Riley uses the last scoop from the detergent box.
Maya brings the dry clothes upstairs in a green tote.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I've got the pictures spread over a dish towel on the table, and I'm already wondering why I thought this would be straightforward.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You started on the shoebox and the biscuit tin?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yeah. There's a picnic photograph I can't quite place. Beatrice is standing beside a picnic table.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Is there anything else in the background?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Some playground equipment, I think. Hang on, I'll send you a picture of it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, yeah. I recognize that playground. That's at Spokane's Riverfront Park.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Really? I was trying to decide if that was a playground or just a very peculiar fence.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: No, I'm pretty sure it's the playground. The shape of that equipment is familiar.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: That helps. I was also trying to figure out when it was taken. One corner of the print is bent, so I was being a little careful turning it over.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Is there anything on the back?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Oh, there is a date stamped on it. August 1996.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: August 1996. So Beatrice at Riverfront Park, in the summer.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes. Well, that was easier once I actually looked at the back.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: In your defense, you had the front to look at first.

details_in_summary: One corner of the print is bent.
key_facts: Beatrice is standing beside a picnic table in the photograph.
Riley recognizes the playground at Spokane's Riverfront Park.
