dialogue.text: Okay, so, I'm looking at the certificate calendar again. I printed it in grayscale, which somehow makes it look more official.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You found the calendar for the Cascadia Archive Institute one?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, the audio preservation certificate I mentioned. It runs from September 2026 through May 2027.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a decent stretch. What does the week-to-week look like?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: The live online classes meet Tuesdays from 6:30 to 8:30 p.m. So it's a regular evening commitment.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Every Tuesday for that whole stretch would be a thing. But at least you wouldn't have to go anywhere.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Right. The online part makes it feel doable. I'm trying to picture being ready to pay attention for 2 hours at the end of the day, though.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, that's different from just seeing an empty slot on a calendar.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Exactly. My highlighter has done more planning than I have.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The old study-session method: mark everything, understand it later.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Hey, it got us through college. More or less.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So does the format make you more interested?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I think so. It could work, at least on paper. I'm still thinking about that Tuesday commitment, though.

key_facts: The certificate runs from September 2026 through May 2027.
Live online classes meet Tuesdays from 6:30 to 8:30 p.m.
minor_details: Daniel has printed the calendar in grayscale.
He jokes that his highlighter has done more planning than he has.

summary: Riley and Daniel reviewed the Cascadia Archive Institute audio preservation certificate (Sept 2026–May 2027). Classes are online Tuesdays 6:30–8:30 pm. Riley noted the online format could work, but Daniel is concerned about a 2-hour end-of-day commitment. They discussed planning approaches and overall suitability. Action item: Daniel will decide whether to commit to the Tuesday schedule and enroll if feasible.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So how do things stand with the laundry room?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Better, actually. There's a new notice saying the broken washer was repaired on January 20.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good. The left-hand one?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah. I saw the notice downstairs today.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm copying January 20 into my phone note, so we don't forget when it was fixed.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Our very important washer records.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Well, on January 14 the working washer was occupied when we checked before dinner. That wasn't much of an experiment.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: No, and with the other one broken, we didn't have another option.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you happen to see whether both were free today?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I didn't check both. I did spot an empty clothespin bag on the shelf, though, which was less useful.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay. Want to try both machines on Sunday, January 25?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Sure. In the morning?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, before lunch, like we tried last time.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but let's see what's free before we haul everything downstairs.

details_in_summary: Riley copies the repair date into a phone note.
key_facts: On January 14, the working washer is occupied when they check.
A new notice says the broken washer was repaired on January 20.
They plan to try both machines on Sunday, January 25.
minor_details: Riley copies the repair date into a phone note.
Maya spots an empty clothespin bag on a shelf.

summary: Riley discussed laundry room status with Maya. The repaired washer was fixed on January 20; on January 14 the working washer was occupied. They planned to try both machines on Sunday, January 25 in the morning before lunch, after checking which machines are free. Riley will copy January 20 into her phone note as a reminder.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How are things going this morning?

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: Pretty well, apart from my cassette deck. It won't turn anymore, so I can't play my mix tapes. I didn't realize how much I'd miss them.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, no. Does it power on at all?

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: It does, but when I press play, nothing turns. The lights are very reassuring, for a machine that isn't doing its job.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Have you looked into getting it fixed?

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: Yeah, a local repair shop estimated about $90. I'm trying to decide whether that's sensible or whether I should just replace the deck.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Do you know what a replacement would cost?

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: Not exactly. A used one might cost less than the repair, but then I'd be buying another old machine that could have its own problems.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right. And $90 isn't nothing, but at least you'd be keeping the one you know.

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: I've had it since my twenties. Still, I should probably look at replacement prices before I decide. I'll think it over.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds reasonable. Oh, are you getting your coffee with oat milk?

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: I am. And I'm glad we found this table near the window. Rosa's neighbourhood cafe is a good place to weigh the financial future of obsolete technology.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Especially with coffee. No need to decide before we finish it.

details_in_summary: Amara orders coffee with oat milk.
key_facts: Amara's cassette deck no longer turns, leaving her unable to play her mix tapes.
A local repair shop has estimated about $90 for the repair.
Amara and Riley meet at Rosa's neighbourhood cafe.
minor_details: Amara orders coffee with oat milk.
They sit at a table near the window.

summary: Riley discussed Amara's broken cassette deck, which powers on but won't play. A repair estimate of $90 was considered versus replacing the deck, with concerns about used units. Amara planned to compare replacement prices before deciding. They noted enjoying coffee with oat milk at Rosa's neighborhood cafe while weighing options, and agreed to finish the discussion after gathering prices.

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: It's getting to the point where I don't really trust my car for much longer. I'm thinking of replacing it with a used electric one.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. Have you got a budget in mind?

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: Up to $13,000. I'd rather spend less, obviously, but that's the ceiling.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And what do you mostly need it for?

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: Local trips around Seattle, mostly. Nothing heroic. I'd like it to get me to the library and back without a committee meeting.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds pretty doable, depending on the car. What about charging?

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: That's the part I'm trying to figure out. We rent the duplex, and I need to find out whether I can charge in the driveway.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Do you know if there's an outlet you could use out there?

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: I'm not sure what it's connected to, or whether I'd be allowed to use it for a car. I should look properly.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, and ask the landlord before counting on it. Even an ordinary outlet might work, but it'd be slow.

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: Slow might be fine, actually. If it's sitting there overnight, it doesn't need to fill up in 10 minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right. It depends on how much you drive and whether the outlet and circuit are safe for that kind of load.

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: That's what I was wondering. I don't want to buy the car and then discover the driveway is just a decorative rectangle.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You could check the charging requirements for whatever car you're considering, then ask about the wiring.

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: Yeah. And I suppose I'd need to work out who pays for the electricity, too.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Probably worth getting that clear. How's your black tea, by the way?

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: Good, thanks. Though now I can smell that loaf cooling on your kitchen counter, and tea feels a bit lonely.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Give it a little longer and I'll cut you a piece. So are you looking at any particular electric car yet?

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: Not one in particular. I'm comparing what's around in my price range. Battery condition seems important, but it depends on the car.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Makes sense. I'd start with the driveway question, then at least you'll know what charging options you're working with.

key_facts: Oliver's budget is up to $13,000.
He mainly wants a car for local trips around Seattle.
He needs to find out whether he can charge in the duplex driveway.
minor_details: Oliver is drinking black tea.
Riley has a loaf cooling on the kitchen counter.

summary: Riley discussed replacing his car with a used electric vehicle under $13,000 for local Seattle trips. Key concerns: whether he can charge in the rental duplex driveway, landlord permissions, wiring safety, and cost of electricity. Action items include checking available outlet, confirming charging requirements for potential cars, and clarifying who pays for electricity. Riley advised starting with the driveway feasibility to determine charging options.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Oh, finally. There are actual cabinets in Teresa's kitchen.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good! They made it on time?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, they arrived January 22, and installation was completed yesterday, January 24.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: After all that waiting. Does it feel like a kitchen again?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: It's starting to. I walked in and could actually see the shape of the room. I'm so relieved.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And now they can measure for the countertop, right?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Exactly. Countertop templating is booked for January 27. We wanted the cabinets installed first, so nobody was guessing at the measurements.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That seems worth waiting for. Though I bet your mom's tired of waiting.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. She's keeping track of everything, though. She tucked the cabinet care booklet into a green folder.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's satisfying. Meanwhile, what were you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Mostly looking at the cabinets, honestly. I noticed sawdust on the toes of my boots afterward, so apparently I did manage to walk around.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Your contribution was a thorough inspection by boot. Very college of you.

key_facts: The cabinets arrived on January 22.
Installation was completed on January 24.
Countertop templating is booked for January 27.
minor_details: Daniel noticed sawdust on the toes of his boots afterward.
Teresa had tucked the cabinet care booklet into a green folder.

summary: Riley noted that cabinets arrived January 22 and installation finished January 24, with the space starting to look like a kitchen. countertop templating is scheduled for January 27 to ensure proper measurements after cabinets are in. Daniel mentioned the mom is tracking progress and filed the cabinet care booklet in a green folder. No other decisions were recorded.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Oh, that's a relief. Everything actually got dry.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, and we didn't have to wait around for a washer this time.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Both washers were free when we got there this morning, January 25. I almost didn't believe it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: After that notice saying the left one was repaired on January 20, I was hoping we'd get to use both.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: And we did. Towels in one machine, clothes in the other.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It felt weird putting everything in at once instead of making a smaller load.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I set a 35-minute timer so we could get back down there promptly.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Which worked, even with me dropping a dryer sheet on the stairs.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: You did pick it up, though. The stairs remain dryer-sheet-free.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: For now. Thanks for folding the towels, by the way.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Sure. I folded them at the kitchen table. More room than trying to do it downstairs.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: This morning was a lot less annoying than checking before dinner and finding the working washer occupied.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but that was when we only had 1 working washer. Still, Sunday morning seems worth trying more often.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, around the same time, if we're home. It didn't run into lunch or keep us up late.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: And we can set a timer again. The machines have apparently agreed to cooperate, as long as we show up.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm not signing a contract with them yet.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Fair. Let's just call it a useful window for now.

details_in_summary: Maya folds the towels at the kitchen table.
key_facts: On the morning of January 25, both washers are free when they arrive.
They wash towels in one machine and clothes in the other.
Maya sets a 35-minute timer so they can return promptly.
minor_details: Riley drops a dryer sheet on the stairs.
Maya folds the towels at the kitchen table.

summary: Riley and Maya used two free washers on January 25, drying towels and clothes separately. They planned a 35-minute timer to optimize return time, noted past repairs and current cooperation of machines, and saved time by folding towels at the kitchen table. They reflected on prior single-washer days, agreed Sunday mornings are worth trying, and considered repeating the morning window if at home, while avoiding commitments beyond a useful window.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I asked Dad about that photograph with the swing.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, the one where we couldn't tell where it was?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yeah. Walter says it's the swing from our Spokane backyard.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Really? I couldn't place it at all.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Neither could I. He noticed a garden hose in the background, which apparently helped.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I didn't even see the hose.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: It's easy to miss. He also says the photograph was taken in 1993.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: 1993. Okay, that makes sense.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Does it? I was still trying to work out what was going on with that little figure.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The one in the yellow raincoat? That's you.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Wait, that's me? I thought the yellow thing was a blanket.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: No, it's a raincoat. You can just make out your face under the hood.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Oh. Yes, now I see it. I was looking at it as a blanket, so in theory there could've been anyone in there.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A very small mystery person wrapped in a blanket on a swing.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Well, when you put it like that.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: At least now we know: our Spokane backyard, 1993, and you in the raincoat.

details_in_summary: Hannah had initially mistaken the raincoat for a blanket.
key_facts: Walter identifies the swing in the picture as the one in their Spokane backyard.
He says the photograph was taken in 1993.
Riley points out that the small figure in the yellow raincoat is Hannah.
minor_details: Walter noticed a garden hose in the background.
Hannah had initially mistaken the raincoat for a blanket.

summary: Riley and Hannah discussed identifying a photograph: the swing from their Spokane backyard, dated 1993, helped by a garden hose in the background. They clarified that the small figure in a yellow raincoat is Riley, not a blanket, confirming the person on the swing. The conversation resolved the scene: Spokane backyard, 1993, Riley in the raincoat.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, how do things stand with the kitchen renovation?

dialogue.speaker: Wei
dialogue.text: It's scheduled to start on March 2, at our townhouse in Greenwood.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's coming up. What are you having done?

dialogue.speaker: Wei
dialogue.text: We're replacing the counters and the sink. They're pretty worn at this point.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So what do you do for a sink while that's happening?

dialogue.speaker: Wei
dialogue.text: Mei and I are expecting to wash dishes in the bathroom for a few weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, that's going to be a little awkward.

dialogue.speaker: Wei
dialogue.text: Yeah. I've picked out a blue plastic dishpan, at least. It feels like a very small solution to a fairly large problem.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Still, probably better than trying to balance everything in the bathroom sink.

dialogue.speaker: Wei
dialogue.text: That's the theory. Mei's also put a takeout menu on the fridge.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good backup for when you can't face another round of bathroom dishes.

dialogue.speaker: Wei
dialogue.text: Exactly. I'm trying not to calculate how many dishes we'll wash. Some numbers are better left alone.

details_in_summary: Wei has picked out a blue plastic dishpan.
Mei has put a takeout menu on the fridge.
key_facts: The renovation is scheduled to start on March 2.
The worn counters and sink will be replaced.
Wei and Mei expect to wash dishes in the bathroom for a few weeks.
minor_details: Wei has picked out a blue plastic dishpan.
Mei has put a takeout menu on the fridge.

summary: Riley discussed the kitchen renovation planned to start March 2 at the Greenwood townhouse. They will replace the counters and the sink. For the duration, Mei and Wei will wash dishes in the bathroom, using a blue plastic dishpan. A takeout menu was placed on the fridge as a backup reference. Wei noted the situation is a temporary, imperfect workaround and preferred not to calculate expected dish volumes.

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: Oh, wow. I just realized how badly I tangled up that Italian worksheet.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What happened?

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: The class has started practicing the passato prossimo. I mixed up the forms using essere and avere on the worksheet.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Is it remembering the forms, or figuring out which one to use?

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: Mostly choosing the right auxiliary verb. When I read the forms, I can usually recognize them. But when I have to write one, I stop and think, wait, which one goes here?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds frustrating. Were you able to work through it?

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: Some of it. I did the worksheet at my kitchen table, and I kept changing my answers. My pencil eraser left a gray smudge on the page.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A record of the learning process.

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: Yes. Very thorough documentation, not especially legible.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Does seeing the whole sentence help you tell which one's right?

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: Sometimes. It's easier when it's already there in front of me. Coming up with it myself is the part that, well, gets tangled.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A bit different from trying out greetings on our walk.

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: It is. I was pleased I could remember those without checking my notes. This page, on the other hand, looks like it lost an argument.

details_in_summary: Her pencil eraser left a gray smudge on the page.
key_facts: The class has started practicing the passato prossimo.
Amara mixed up forms using “essere” and “avere” in a worksheet.
minor_details: She did the worksheet at her kitchen table.
Her pencil eraser left a gray smudge on the page.

summary: Riley discussed Amara's difficulties with the Italian passato prossimo, focusing on choosing the correct auxiliary (essere vs avere) when writing. Amara mixed up the forms on a worksheet; recognizing them is easier than producing them. She worked at home, repeatedly changing answers, and left a pencil eraser smudge. They noted that seeing the full sentence helps, though generating the form remains challenging. Amara found recall of greetings easier than constructing sentences.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I've been checking the rights on those Tacoma photographs, and there's 1 I can't use for now.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, which one?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: A neighborhood parade. I really liked that one, but the rights holder is unidentified.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's frustrating. Was there anything in the collection information that helped?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Not enough to tell me who holds the rights. So I've taken it out of consideration rather than assume we can use it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, probably not worth guessing. What did you like about it?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: It just had that everyday-life feeling I was looking for. And there's a dog near the edge of the frame, which didn't hurt.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The dog was doing a lot of work for that photograph, apparently.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: It was a strong supporting performance. But I've found enough alternatives to keep working without it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good. With the wall being only 6 feet wide, I guess you still have plenty to choose from.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I do. I'm disappointed about the parade, but I don't need to force it into the selection.

key_facts: A photograph of a neighborhood parade has an unidentified rights holder.
Hannah has removed it from consideration rather than assume she can use it.
minor_details: The parade photograph includes a dog near the edge of the frame.

summary: Riley and Hannah discussed rights issues on Tacoma photos. One photo, a neighborhood parade with an unidentified rights holder, was removed from consideration. The image’s everyday-life feel and a dog in the frame were noted. Riley confirmed there are enough alternatives and will continue selection, given the wall is only 6 feet wide.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, I took the green bike to a shop about that stuck rear brake cable.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good. What did they say?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: They recommend replacing the rear cable housing and truing the rear wheel.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So it's not just a matter of pulling the old cable out?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Apparently not without a lot more trouble than it's worth. I'd rather pay them to deal with it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And the wheel too?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. I asked them to include that. I don't really feel comfortable doing it myself.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Fair. Did they give you an estimate?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: They wrote it on a yellow slip. $110 for the housing and wheel work.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay, and you'd already spent $60 on the tire, tube and cables, right?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Right. So that puts me at $170, still below the $250 I figured a replacement would cost.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Assuming nothing else comes up.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. I'm not calling it a bargain until I get the bike back.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did they suggest anything else?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: An optional drivetrain overhaul. I declined it for now.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Makes sense. Get the brakes sorted first.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Exactly. The front cable's in, but I'm not commuting on it with the rear one still stuck.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: When can they take it?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I booked the bike in for February 4.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Nice. A decision, not another round of comparing options.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I know. I walked home past a florist closing for the day and realized I'd managed to decide before every business in Seattle shut down.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's growth. Let's get lunch.

key_facts: The shop recommends replacing the rear cable housing and truing the rear wheel.
Daniel declines an optional drivetrain overhaul.
He books the bike in for February 4.
minor_details: The shop wrote its estimate on a yellow slip.
Daniel walked home past a florist closing for the day.

summary: Riley reviewed Daniel’s plan to fix the bike. Daniel reported a shop recommended replacing the rear brake cable housing and truing the rear wheel, rather than pulling the old cable. Estimated cost is $110 for housing and wheel work, bringing total to about $170 (including $60 already spent on tire, tube, and cables), below the $250 replacement estimate. An optional drivetrain overhaul was declined. The bike is booked for February 4 to proceed with brakes first.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: There's another problem in Warehouse Words, apart from the pick, collect, pull thing.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh? Hang on, I'm eating an apple. Which row?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: These 2 here. Both warehouse screens use 'hold' when they're asking staff to move goods to a staging area.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Huh. I read 'hold' as restricting the inventory, not moving it somewhere.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. It could mean don't let anyone use it, or it could mean take it over there. Those aren't quite the same instruction.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Are both of them buttons?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: One's a button label and the other's explanatory text. I put that in the column you suggested.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The screen links are handy here. You can see why someone might think the goods are supposed to stay put.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. I've marked both examples for a check with engineering. I want to make sure we're not missing some restriction behind the scenes.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Makes sense. The wording's confusing either way, but we should know what the action actually does.

key_facts: Two warehouse screens use “hold” where staff are being asked to move goods to a staging area.
Sam has marked those examples for a check with engineering.
minor_details: Riley is eating an apple during the conversation.

summary: Riley discussed ambiguity in Warehouse Words where 'hold' appears on two screens, one as a button label and one as explanatory text. The term could mean restricting inventory or moving it to staging. Screens’ linking and wording may mislead staff into thinking goods must stay put. An engineering check was requested to verify any underlying restrictions and to clarify the actual action, with a plan to adjust wording or UI as needed.

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: Hi, Riley. Hard to believe it's already Tuesday, January 27. How's your evening going?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, Naomi. Pretty good, thanks. How's yours?

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: Good. I wanted to follow up about Inez. Remember on the evening of January 22, I told you we'd tried the Seattle Aquarium you suggested?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, and Inez especially liked the jellyfish, right?

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: She did. She's been drawing jellyfish since we went.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, really? That's great.

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: She made this one at home. Here, I've got a photo of the drawing on my phone.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, look at that. The tentacles are purple.

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: Yeah, she used a purple pencil for those.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I love that she came home and started drawing them.

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: Me too. The jellyfish clearly made an impression.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm glad the aquarium worked out.

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: It did. So, thank you for the suggestion.

details_in_summary: Inez used a purple pencil for the tentacles.
Naomi shows Riley a photo of the drawing on her phone.
key_facts: On the evening of January 22, Naomi told Riley that she and Inez had tried the aquarium.
Inez especially liked the jellyfish.
By January 27, Inez has made a jellyfish drawing at home.
minor_details: Inez used a purple pencil for the tentacles.
Naomi shows Riley a photo of the drawing on her phone.

summary: Riley discussed suggesting the Seattle Aquarium for Inez, noting she enjoyed the jellyfish. Naomi shared that Inez has been drawing jellyfish at home, including a purple-tented drawing, and provided a photo. Riley acknowledged the positive impact of the aquarium visit and Naomi thanked them for the suggestion.

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. How's your evening going? Mine's been pretty quiet, which I can't complain about.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, Oliver. Pretty quiet here too. Did you find any cars worth looking at?

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: Actually, yeah. A dealer has a used 2019 Nissan Leaf SV. I called the dealer on my lunch break.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. Are you going to see it?

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: Yeah, I've arranged a visit. The dealer agreed to hold it until I get there.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's good. Gives you a chance to look without rushing.

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: Right. I'm trying not to get attached before I've looked it over, though.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Already caught yourself imagining it in the driveway?

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: Maybe a little. It's very easy to like a car when all you've seen is a listing.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Fair. You can decide how you feel once you've actually seen it.

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: That's the plan. So far my favorite feature is that it exists, but it depends.

details_in_summary: Oliver called the dealer on his lunch break.
key_facts: A dealer has a used 2019 Nissan Leaf SV.
The dealer agreed to hold it until Oliver's visit.
minor_details: Oliver called the dealer on his lunch break.

summary: Oliver informed Riley about a held 2019 Nissan Leaf SV at a dealer and arranged a viewing during lunch. The dealer will hold the car until Oliver arrives. They discussed not getting attached before inspection and deciding after seeing the car. The plan is for Oliver to assess the vehicle and determine interest based on the visit.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Oh, the blue one sold? That's disappointing.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, I just saw it was gone. I found another Bolt, though: a silver 2021 with approximately 35,000 miles.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but what's the price before we get attached to this one?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It's advertised at $18,750, before taxes, fees and the trade-in.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: So it might fit under our $20,000 limit, but we need the actual numbers.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. I don't want to guess what they'll give us for the Subaru, either.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: And now that Omid's given us the outlet conditions, charging at home seems possible. What does the silver one look like?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Pretty good in the photos. There's a small scuff on its rear bumper.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I can live with a scuff. I'd rather know what's happening underneath it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Same. I scheduled an independent inspection for January 31, before we decide whether to buy it.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Saturday, then. I'm circling the inspection appointment on our paper calendar.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Thanks. Once we get the inspection results and the full price, we can decide if it's worth pursuing.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Good. The calendar is earning its keep for once.

details_in_summary: The silver car has a small scuff on its rear bumper.
key_facts: The new candidate is a silver 2021 Bolt with approximately 35,000 miles.
Its advertised price is $18,750 before taxes, fees and trade-in.
An independent inspection is scheduled for January 31.
minor_details: Maya circles the inspection appointment on their paper calendar.
The silver car has a small scuff on its rear bumper.
meta.storyline_title: A plug in the parking space

summary: Riley and Maya discussed a silver 2021 Bolt found after the blue one sold. The car is advertised at $18,750 (pre-tax/fees/trade-in) and may fit a $20k budget, but exact figures are needed. They referenced uncertain Subaru trade-in value and Omid’s home charging suitability. The silver Bolt appears photoset with a minor rear bumper scuff. An independent inspection was scheduled for January 31, and they plan to review inspection results and full pricing before deciding to pursue the purchase. The calendar was noted as useful for tracking timing.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Have you checked keyboard navigation in the staged build of the delivery exception queue?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Not yet. Is something off?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. I turned my laptop trackpad off to test it, and keyboard focus skips the row action.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The 'Review delivery' action? So you can see it, but you can't tab to it?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. The mouse can get there, which is a pretty unhelpful consolation for a keyboard test.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'll flag it for the team. We should get that fixed before we release.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Agreed. We're planning to launch the initial version on February 3, provided the focus issue is fixed.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What if we check the staged build again once the fix is in, before we call it ready?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yes. I'll test it with the trackpad off again, and make sure I can actually reach the row action.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'll check it too. If it's still skipping, we hold the launch.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Sounds good. Better to catch it now than ask a dispatcher to find an invisible tab stop.

details_in_summary: Sam tests with the laptop trackpad turned off.
key_facts: Keyboard focus skips the row action in the staged build.
The team plans to launch the initial version on February 3, provided the focus issue is fixed.
minor_details: Sam tests with the laptop trackpad turned off.

summary: Riley and Sam identified a keyboard navigation focus bug in the staged delivery exception queue where the row action is not reachable via keyboard; mouse can access it. They will flag the issue, fix it before release, and target a February 3 launch contingent on the fix. They will re-test with the trackpad off and, if the issue persists, hold the launch.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So how do things stand with the Bluewake opening?

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: The short version is, I learned today, January 29, that the role requires 3 days a week in the office.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh. That's more than I was hoping for.

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: Yeah. I wanted you to know before we did anything about that introductory call.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I appreciate it. The work sounded interesting, but 3 office days a week doesn't really suit me.

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: That's fair. You don't have to talk yourself into a schedule you don't want.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Then I think I'll pass. Could you not take the inquiry any further?

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: Of course. I'll leave it there, and I'll continue to be discreet about it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Thanks. I know I said the call could be useful, but that changes things.

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: It does. Better to find out now than after you've had 4 conversations about synergy.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Very true. Oh, sorry, I've got this board game spread out on your table. Do you need the space?

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: No, you're fine. I'm just making lentil soup, and I've got plenty of room over here.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay. And thanks for checking on the office requirement.

dialogue.speaker: Naomi
dialogue.text: You're welcome. I'm glad we got a clear answer.

key_facts: Naomi learned on January 29 that the role requires three office days a week.
Riley decides not to pursue the opening.
minor_details: Naomi is making lentil soup while they talk.
Riley has a board game spread out on the table.

summary: Riley discussed Bluewake opening with Naomi Adler. Naomi stated the role requires 3 days per week in the office. Riley decided this schedule doesn’t work and asked to discontinue the inquiry. Naomi agreed to stop and remain discreet. Action: Riley will not pursue the opportunity; Naomi will not proceed with the introductory call and will conclude the matter.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I'm trying to write this on the meeting room whiteboard, but the marker's dried out.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Here, use my pen. Is this about those screens that say 'hold' when they mean moving goods to staging?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. I talked to Mateo about what the inventory actually does behind those labels.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And are the actions different, or is it just different wording?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Different actions. Mateo confirmed that staging records a location without blocking allocation.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So the goods have a staging location, but they can still be allocated?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. An inventory hold, on the other hand, prevents allocation until the hold is removed.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Then we definitely need to distinguish them in the guide. They sound similar if you're just looking at a label, but the effects aren't the same.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Right. I'm planning to give each action its own definition, so we don't treat them as interchangeable.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That should help when we're checking the wording on those screens, too.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. Oh, my tea's gone cold. Another successful meeting room beverage.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It is Friday evening. I think the tea gave up before we did.

key_facts: Mateo confirmed that staging records a location without blocking allocation.
An inventory hold prevents allocation until the hold is removed.
Sam plans to give each action its own definition.
minor_details: A marker has dried out in the meeting room.
Sam’s tea has gone cold.

summary: Riley and Sam discussed inventory actions behind labels on the screens. They clarified that staging records a location without blocking allocation, while an inventory hold prevents allocation until removed. Riley noted the need to distinguish these actions in the guide and to create separate definitions. Action items include updating the guide with distinct definitions and reviewing screen wording to reflect the differences.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How's the apartment search standing this week?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, I found a listing in Fremont. It's a one-bedroom for $1,825 a month.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, that's under your ceiling. When is it available?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: It's advertised as available April 1. I've got a viewing scheduled for February 7.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds promising. How'd you find it?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I noticed the ad while I was drinking coffee at Low Tide. I may have compared the photos for longer than it took to drink the coffee.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did they tell you anything useful, or just make it look nice?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Mostly nice. There's a round mirror in the hallway, which apparently I've decided is important information.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Very important. But don't decide from the photos alone.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. After the footsteps at the Phinney Ridge place, I want to actually stand there and listen.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And try the windows closed, like we talked about. Still, Fremont and under budget is a good start.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: It is. I'll see what it's like on February 7 before I start mentally arranging my furniture.

details_in_summary: The listing photos show a round mirror in the hallway.
key_facts: The Fremont listing is for a one-bedroom apartment at $1,825 a month.
It is advertised as available April 1.
Daniel has a viewing scheduled for February 7.
minor_details: The listing photos show a round mirror in the hallway.
Daniel noticed the advertisement while drinking coffee at Low Tide.

summary: The conversation covers Daniel finding a Fremont 1-bedroom listing at $1,825 under budget, available April 1, with a viewing set for February 7. He found it via coffee, noted a round hallway mirror as potentially important, and emphasized not relying solely on photos. They plan to test the unit with the windows closed and to assess it on February 7 before mentally furnishing. Action: Daniel to view on Feb 7 and report back.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, how do things stand with the holds shelf?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Better, I think. Marisol and I rearranged the holds, and we've got a layout that seems worth a longer trial.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. How did you divide it up?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: The top row is surnames A through F. The middle row is G through M, and the bottom row is N through Z.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And you managed that with the shelf you already had?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes, it's all on the existing shelving. No extra furniture, which was rather the point.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Especially with M being so crowded when you counted.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Exactly. We kept that in mind while we were moving things around. It looks workable, anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What about the signs? Last time the one on the top row was hard to read from a seated position.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I added a matching sign at eye level. And I used a ruler to line up the signs, because apparently I can't be trusted to do that by sight.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I respect the commitment.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: A bookend left a faint scuff on my sleeve, too. Very glamorous work.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So are you happy with the arrangement, or are you still weighing options?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I'm trying not to keep comparing alternatives indefinitely. There are always 3 more ways we could divide it, in theory. This one seems worth trying for a while.

details_in_summary: Hannah used a ruler to line up the signs.
key_facts: The top row now holds surnames A through F.
The middle row holds G through M, and the bottom row holds N through Z.
The arrangement uses the existing shelving without adding furniture.
minor_details: Hannah used a ruler to line up the signs.
A bookend left a faint scuff on her sleeve.

summary: Riley discussed shelf holds reorganization with Hannah. They rearranged the holds onto existing shelving and split rows by alphabet: top A–F, middle G–M, bottom N–Z. Signs were updated to eye level and aligned with a ruler. Riley noted the improvement and that M remains crowded but manageable. They plan a longer trial of this layout and avoid endless comparisons, though three alternative divisions exist in theory. Action: monitor trial and collect feedback before any further changes.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: The map still makes me want to turn the page sideways to follow it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Let me move the fruit bowl off the table so we can spread it out. There.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Thanks. This first mock-up has that tiny dotted line, and I don't like it. It just disappears against the street names.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. What if the library stays at the bottom of the page and 57th is at the top? Then you can follow the route without rotating anything.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but how do we show that people come back the same way without drawing 2 lines right next to each other?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Use a single heavy line for the route and an arrow at the turnaround. The description can say it's an out-and-back.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: So the arrow goes at NW 57th Street, and the line runs along 22nd Avenue NW?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right. One line there and back, not a dotted maze.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Good. The dotted maze is officially rejected.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And the distance and seating note can stay next to the map, where people can see them before deciding.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yes. About 0.3 miles, and no public bench on that stretch. I'll keep the time as an estimate too.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The rest of this text feels like instructions for the group, though, not a description of the route.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but I still need room for both. I'll put the group instructions on the reverse of the map.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That works. You'd flip it to read those, but you wouldn't have to turn the page around to understand the route.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Exactly. The front can tell someone what the walk is like, and the back can tell the group what to do.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a lot easier to find your way through. On paper, anyway.

key_facts: The draft map uses a single heavy line for the route and an arrow for the turnaround.
Maya puts group instructions on the reverse of the map.
minor_details: Riley moves the fruit bowl off the table to make room.
Maya rejects a tiny dotted line from the first mock-up.

summary: Riley and Maya discussed redesigning the walking-route map. They decided to rotate the page orientation for easier following, remove the dotted maze, and depict the route with a single heavy line plus an arrow at the turnaround for an out-and-back path along 22nd Avenue NW with the arrow at NW 57th Street. They noted distances (0.3 miles) and time as an estimate, and stated no public bench on that stretch. Group instructions will be on the reverse; front describes the walk, back provides directions.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Oh, good, Owen's up for it. I just asked him about taking a weekend away in late spring.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. Where are you thinking?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Well, we were tossing around places, but Astoria, Oregon, keeps coming up.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Astoria sounds fun. What got you thinking about a trip?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I first brought it up over a bowl of tomato soup. I thought it would be nice to get away for a couple of days without taking the car.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So you don't want to drive at all?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Right. Neither of us wants to drive. We just want a proper break from it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And Owen's happy with Astoria?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: He is. He wants to see the river, which seems like a reasonable thing to want in Astoria.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, that does narrow it down less than you'd think.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Exactly. Now we just need a weekend that works for both of us. Late May, maybe?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Have you got a particular one in mind?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Let's see. Friday, May 29, through Sunday, May 31. Owen, does that work for you? Yes, apparently it does.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And does it work for you?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: It does. I was trying to compare every weekend in May, which is a very efficient way to never pick one.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Then go with that one. May 29 through May 31.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: All right, that's settled. Owen and I are going to Astoria for the weekend, without driving.

details_in_summary: Owen wants to see the river.
key_facts: Hannah and Owen plan to visit Astoria, Oregon.
They choose Friday, May 29, through Sunday, May 31.
They want to travel without driving.
minor_details: Hannah first raised the idea over a bowl of tomato soup.
Owen wants to see the river.

summary: Riley discussed with Hannah a weekend trip to Astoria, Oregon, in late May. They prefer not to drive and plan a short break for two days. Owen is on board to see the river. The proposed dates were May 29–31, which Hannah confirmed as suitable for both.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How are things standing with the ferry piece?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, Louise listened to the cut. She thinks the sequence of voices works.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good. Even that transition you were worried about?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, she seemed happy with how the voices follow each other. But she's worried about the noise from the gallery entrance.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Like people coming in and talking over it?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. She thinks the quiet speech could be hard to follow with all that noise nearby.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's tricky. It's not like people will be listening in a quiet room.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Exactly. I jotted her feedback down with a green pen, which somehow makes it look more reassuring than it is.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Green means everything's fine, obviously.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Right. I'll spend 20 minutes deciding what color the problem actually is.

details_in_summary: Daniel jotted the feedback down with a green pen.
key_facts: Louise thinks the sequence of voices works.
She is concerned that noise from the gallery entrance could make quiet speech hard to follow.
minor_details: Daniel jotted the feedback down with a green pen.

summary: Riley discussed the ferry piece with Daniel. Louise listened and approved the voice sequence and transitions, but raised concerns about gallery entrance noise affecting intelligibility. Riley noted that quiet speech may be hard to follow in a noisy lobby. Daniel mentioned recording feedback with a green pen, implying some color-coding optimism, and plans to spend 20 minutes assessing the problem’s severity and color.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So where do you think we stand on the dog question?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I still really want one. But I don't think we're ready to bring one home yet.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. I've been thinking about that week in February. I'd only be home Monday and Tuesday.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: And I can't take leave that week. Okay, but even if we get through those first 2 days, that's not much time for a dog to settle in.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Especially if Wednesday would mean being alone from about 8:30 to 4:30. We said we shouldn't just assume a friend could cover it.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Right. A walker could help, but 3 weekday visits at $30 each would add up to about $90 a week.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And that's on top of the $325 adoption fee. There'd be other pet expenses too.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: The dog would presumably expect more than a lease and a pleasant view of the bookcase.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Pretty demanding, honestly. I'm waiting for the kettle to boil, by the way, so if I wander off, that's why.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay. So do we say no application for now?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. Let's not submit an adoption application now. The money and the time we'd have for a new dog just don't feel settled enough.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I agree. I don't want to rush the first week and hope it all works out.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It's disappointing, though. I keep picturing an adult dog curled up beside the bookcase.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: And I keep picturing one coming with me to Golden Gardens. We can still want that without doing it this month.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How about we revisit the dog question in June?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: June sounds good. And could we set aside $40 a month toward future pet expenses in the meantime?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, let's do that. It won't cover everything, but it's a start.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I'll add a reminder to the shared note: $40 a month for future pet expenses.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Thanks. June it is, then.

details_in_summary: Maya adds the savings reminder to a shared note.
key_facts: They decide not to submit an adoption application now.
They agree to revisit the dog question in June.
They plan to set aside $40 a month toward future pet expenses.
minor_details: Maya adds the savings reminder to a shared note.
Riley is waiting for the kettle to boil during the conversation.

summary: Riley and Maya discussed adopting a dog but concluded not to submit an adoption application now due to time, custody, and cost constraints. They identified weekly walker costs (~$90) plus a $325 adoption fee, and other pet expenses. They agreed to revisit the decision in June and to set aside $40 per month for future pet expenses, with a reminder added to a shared note.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, Nora, how's the car search standing?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: It's a little less overwhelming. On January 23, I settled on the Chevrolet Bolt as the model to look for.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. What made you land on that one?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: I think it fits what I'm looking for in an electric car for weekend trips. And I've been comparing the listings against the $19,000 I have saved.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That must make the search more manageable.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: A bit. There are still a lot of listings, but at least I'm comparing the same model now.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Have you figured out the charging side?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: Yeah. I've been checking charging networks on my phone during bus rides.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Find anything that would work for you?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: I did. There's public Level 2 charging in Fremont, and a public fast charger in Everett.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good. So you have a couple of options.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: I think so. That was one of the things I needed to know before I could take the search seriously.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And are the listings giving you enough information?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: Some more than others. One described a scratched cup holder in surprising detail.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Very thorough.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: Yes. I feel like I know the cup holder better than the rest of the car.

details_in_summary: One listing described a scratched cup holder in surprising detail.
key_facts: Nora settled on the Chevrolet Bolt as the model to look for on January 23.
She found public Level 2 charging in Fremont and a public fast charger in Everett.
minor_details: She has been checking charging networks on her phone during bus rides.
One listing described a scratched cup holder in surprising detail.

summary: Riley discussed Nora settling on the Chevrolet Bolt as the target model within a $19,000 budget. Nora is comparing Bolt listings and has identified charging options: Level 2 in Fremont and a fast charger in Everett. She plans to proceed once charging feasibility is confirmed. Some listings vary in detail, with one unusually thorough description of a cup holder.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. How's your afternoon going?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, Sam. Pretty good. I'm ready for the end of the day, though.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah, same. My brain's starting to put up the closed sign.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Fair. Have you heard anything more about visiting Ada?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I have, actually. We settled on Friday, May 15, through Monday, May 18, for the Victoria visit.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. Does that weekend work well for her?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah, Ada's free for much of it. We sorted the dates out on a 10-minute call, which might be a record for travel planning.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a pretty efficient call. Did you get them on your calendar?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I did. Marked the days in green, so now they look very official.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And are you still leaning toward the direct ferry?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. If the crossings fit, I intend to take the direct ferry from Seattle to Victoria and back. Both directions, not the Port Angeles route.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Makes sense. Hopefully the sailing schedule lines up with your dates.

details_in_summary: Sam marked the days in green on their calendar.
key_facts: The visit is planned for Friday, May 15, through Monday, May 18.
Sam intends to take the direct ferry in both directions.
Ada is free for much of that weekend.
minor_details: They settled the dates over a ten-minute call.
Sam marked the days in green on their calendar.

summary: Riley discussed planning a Victoria visit for Ada from Fri May 15 to Mon May 18. Sam confirmed the dates after a brief call and marked them on his calendar in green. They prefer the direct Seattle–Victoria ferry in both directions if schedules align, not the Port Angeles route. Next steps: verify sailing times fit the dates and finalize travel arrangements.

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: I'm thinking of starting a beginner-friendly tabletop-game group at the Greenwood library. Got any ideas?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds fun. When's the first meeting?

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: February 10. I'm trying to figure out what to bring without turning it into a seminar.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'd keep the group small, for one thing. It's easier to teach when everyone's at the same table.

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: Yeah, I was thinking I'd cap it at 4 players. Enough for a game, not enough to form a committee.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a good size. What game are you considering?

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: Ticket to Ride. The rules seem manageable, but it depends on how much explaining people want.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You could bring a shorter game as a backup, just in case. Something you can explain quickly.

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: Right. I keep getting caught up in which edition to bring, and that's probably not the important part.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Probably not. Oh, you could use folded paper name cards, too. Makes it easier for people to talk to each other.

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: Good idea. I'm planning to bring pencils, so paper's not much more to carry.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: There you go. Keep the explanation simple and let people ask questions as they play.

details_in_summary: Oliver plans to bring pencils.
Riley suggests using folded paper name cards.
key_facts: The first meeting is planned for February 10 at the Greenwood library.
Oliver plans to cap the group at four players.
Oliver is considering Ticket to Ride for the group.
minor_details: Oliver plans to bring pencils.
Riley suggests using folded paper name cards.

summary: Riley and Oliver discussed starting a beginner-friendly tabletop-game group at the Greenwood library, with a Feb 10 kickoff. They planning a small group capped at 4 players to ease teaching. Ticket to Ride proposed as the main game, with a shorter backup. Riley suggested folded name cards and keeping explanations simple, while considering which edition to bring as secondary. Action items include finalizing materials (backup game, name cards, pencils) and keeping the session concise.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Morning, Nora. How's the apartment search going?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: Morning. Better than I expected, actually. I viewed a Greenwood studio on January 27, and I keep thinking about it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. What did you like about it?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: It has a separate kitchen. I think that makes the studio feel a little less like I'd be sleeping in the kitchen.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That seems like a reasonable standard. What was the rent?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: The advertised rent is $1,575 a month. So it's under the $1,650 ceiling.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That leaves a little room, though you'd want to check what else you'd be paying each month.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: Yeah. I don't want to decide it's affordable and then discover the rent has friends.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Fair. And how does it work for the Route 40 commute?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: I still need to check that carefully. I don't want to assume it's manageable just because it's in Greenwood.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Makes sense. Was there anything about the place that worried you?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: A radiator clicked during the viewing. I couldn't tell if that was normal or if it was going to hold a conversation with me all winter.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You could ask about the heating and the noise. Anything else stick in your mind?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: The building's mailboxes are painted dark red. Not exactly a deciding factor, but I noticed them. I think I liked the place enough to consider applying, though I'm not sure when I've asked enough questions.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Maybe start with the total monthly cost, the commute and the radiator. If those check out, it sounds worth considering an application.

details_in_summary: A radiator clicked during the viewing.
The building's mailboxes are painted dark red.
key_facts: Nora viewed a Greenwood studio on January 27.
The advertised rent is $1,575 a month.
The studio has a separate kitchen.
minor_details: A radiator clicked during the viewing.
The building's mailboxes are painted dark red.

summary: Riley discussed Nora's Greenwood studio viewing (Jan 27). Nora likes the separate kitchen and notes rent at $1,575/month, under $1,650. They agreed to verify total monthly costs, commute viability to Route 40, and heating/noise (radiator) concerns. Nora observed dark red mailboxes as a minor detail. Decision: Nora is considering applying if questions about cost, commute, and radiator are resolved; action item: confirm total costs, commute feasibility, and radiator reliability before applying.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Oh, good, I think I've finally got a simple way to check on the holds shelf.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. What are you going to do?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: A tally sheet for staff. We can mark down requests for help finding holds, and holds we find in the wrong place.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I like that. You'll have something to look back at instead of trying to remember how busy it felt.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Exactly. I'm not asking anyone to write a whole account of what happened. Just a mark in the right column.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And no patron names?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: No patron names on the sheet. We don't need to know whose hold it was to count it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's good. You can review it without collecting information about people.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: That's the idea. I've clipped the sheet to a blue clipboard, and I drew the columns with a green pen. Very sophisticated.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Well, as long as the columns are labeled. You'd never forgive yourself otherwise.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: No, I really wouldn't. I'm planning to review the results through the end of March, so we have more than a few days to go on.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds manageable. And you can actually take a lunch break instead of comparing 12 more layouts.

details_in_summary: The tally sheet is clipped to a blue clipboard.
Hannah drew the columns with a green pen.
key_facts: Staff will tally requests for help finding holds and holds found in the wrong place.
The tally sheet will not include patron names.
Hannah plans to review the results through the end of March.
minor_details: The tally sheet is clipped to a blue clipboard.
Hannah drew the columns with a green pen.

summary: Riley summarized that Hannah proposed a simple tally sheet on a blue clipboard with green-ink columns to track holds shelf requests and misplacements, without patron names. The goal is to provide a verifiable record rather than memory. They will review results through the end of March. Action items include implementing the sheet and conducting periodic reviews; Riley noted the potential for better lunch breaks once the system is in place.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. Okay, so, how's your evening going?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Pretty good. How about yours?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Good. I got a workload estimate from the certificate program, and now I'm doing that thing where I try to fit an entire week into a mental spreadsheet.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Our old study-session method. How much work are they talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: They estimate 6 to 8 hours of assignments a week, in addition to class. I wrote it on the back of a grocery receipt, so it's officially part of my filing system.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a decent chunk on top of the Tuesday class. Did they say what the assignments involve?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Students complete a preservation project using a small collection of recordings. So it's not just reading and showing up online.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Where do you think you'd fit the independent work?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Maybe a couple of longer blocks during the week, rather than trying to squeeze in an hour every night. Though 6 to 8 hours is a pretty wide range when you're looking at a freelance schedule.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. At least now you've got a better sense of what that Tuesday commitment would come with.

key_facts: The program estimates six to eight hours of assignments a week, in addition to class.
Students complete a preservation project using a small collection of recordings.
minor_details: Daniel wrote the estimate on the back of a grocery receipt.

summary: Riley and Daniel discussed a certificate program's workload: 6–8 hours of weekly assignments plus class, including a preservation project with a small recording collection. They considered scheduling two longer blocks during the week rather than daily short slots and assessed how the Tuesday class would fit into a freelance schedule.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Morning. Is there any coffee left?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Morning. Yeah, I left you some.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Thanks. Oh, that box on the dining table is full of family photographs. Lian gave it to me.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Your mom's photos? I was wondering what was in there.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah. I want to digitize them before the prints deteriorate. Some have already started to yellow at the edges.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, that's a shame. Do you know who's in them?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Some of them. Others, I'm not sure. And apparently there's a loose paper clip among the prints.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The family archive's security system.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Very sophisticated. Okay, but I don't want to guess at who's who.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I can help you sort them. We can separate the ones we can identify from the ones we need Lian's input on.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: That'd be great. Even if we recognize a face, we might not know where the picture was taken.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Then we can put those with the ones to ask her about.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah, that makes sense. Thanks for helping.

details_in_summary: Maya finds a loose paper clip among the prints.
key_facts: Lian gave Maya the box of family photographs.
Some prints have started to yellow at the edges.
Riley will help Maya separate identifiable pictures from those that need Lian's input.
minor_details: The box is sitting on the dining table.
Maya finds a loose paper clip among the prints.

summary: Riley noted coffee, discussed a box of family photographs to digitize, and highlighted that some images are unidentified and some contain a loose paper clip. They planned to separate photos they can identify from those needing Lian’s input, and to note locations or context to confirm with Lian later.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The delivery exception queue is live. The initial version shipped on February 3 to 6 pilot dispatch teams.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good. Have we heard anything yet?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: One dispatcher reported that some arrival times were missing from the new list.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Ah. That's one of the things we wanted people to see without opening each delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Right. The feedback came in a message with a screenshot attached.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Do we know if the times were missing from the delivery data, or just from the list?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Not yet. What if we check that once we have a bit more usage data? See whether it's happening across more deliveries.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. I don't want to assume it's a display problem.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Me neither. A blank space is very good at not explaining itself.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'll keep the missing times in mind when we look at the data.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Sounds good. For now, at least we have the screenshot to start from.

key_facts: The initial version shipped on February 3 to six pilot dispatch teams.
One dispatcher reported that some arrival times were missing from the new list.
minor_details: The feedback arrived in a message with a screenshot attached.

summary: Riley and Sam discussed the live delivery exception queue, noting the pilot deployment dates (Feb 3–6) and a report that some arrival times are missing from the new list. They reiterated the need for visibility of times without opening each delivery and considered whether the issue is data or display-related. The plan is to gather more usage data to determine if the problem appears across more deliveries, using the received screenshot as a starting point, and to keep missing times in mind during data review.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: I've decided to apply for the Greenwood studio. I'm getting the paperwork together.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good. Did you find out what the lease terms are?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: Yeah. It's a 12-month lease, beginning March 1.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay. And is the rent still the $1,575 you saw advertised?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: That's what's in the application information, yeah. The application fee is $40.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What do they need from you for the application?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: I need to provide proof of income. I'm checking what I have for that.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did they give you instructions for it?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: They did. I saved the application instructions as a PDF.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a start.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: I think my folder has more subfolders than documents. It's a very organized shortage of paperwork.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Well, at least you know where everything goes.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: In theory. I'm also trying not to research this decision indefinitely.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds wise. You'd already narrowed it down by budget and the bus route.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: Right. And I keep coming back to the separate kitchen. I think I have enough information to make a choice.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Then you can let the spreadsheet rest for a bit.

details_in_summary: She saved the application instructions as a PDF.
She jokes that her folder has more subfolders than documents.
key_facts: The available lease is for 12 months, beginning March 1.
Nora needs to provide proof of income with her application.
The application fee is $40.
minor_details: She saved the application instructions as a PDF.
She jokes that her folder has more subfolders than documents.

summary: Nora decided to apply for the Greenwood studio. Lease terms: 12 months starting March 1, rent $1,575, application fee $40. Proof of income required; instructions saved as a PDF. Nora notes her files are well organized but may have more folders than documents. She aims to avoid over-researching and focuses on budget, bus route, and a separate kitchen. Next steps: gather proof of income and review application instructions; consider proceeding with the application.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, how are things looking with the car search?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: I booked a test drive for February 10, at a used-car dealer in Lynnwood.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Nice. Is it a Bolt?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: Yeah. Since I settled on that model, I figured I should actually drive one.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That seems like a reasonable next step.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: I think so. The spreadsheet can only tell me so much about how it feels to drive.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did the dealer tell you what to bring?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: My driver's license. Which I probably would have brought anyway, but I'm glad we covered it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Anything else you're going to check while you're there?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: I put a reminder in my calendar to check the tire tread. Otherwise I'll get distracted by the dashboard or something.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And if you like it?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: I'd want to request an independent inspection before I committed to buying it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, that's worth leaving room for in the schedule.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: I think so too. I don't want a test drive to turn into a decision just because I'm already there.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Makes sense. You've got the charging options in Fremont and Everett to consider too.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: Right. At least I know where I could charge it. Now I just have to see how it drives.

details_in_summary: The dealer asked her to bring her driver's license.
She put a reminder in her calendar to check the tire tread.
key_facts: Nora has booked a test drive for February 10 at a used-car dealer in Lynnwood.
She plans to request an independent inspection if she likes the car.
minor_details: The dealer asked her to bring her driver's license.
She put a reminder in her calendar to check the tire tread.

summary: Riley discussed car search logistics with Nora. Nora scheduled a test drive for February 10 at a Lynnwood used-car dealer to try a Bolt. She will bring her driver’s license, set a calendar reminder to check tire tread, and plans an independent inspection if she likes the car. They noted charging options in Fremont and Everett and emphasized not letting the test drive become a purchase decision.

dialogue.speaker: Yuki
dialogue.text: I brought that college photograph I scanned, but I can't remember where we took it. Do you recognize it?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Let me see. Oh, that bench looks familiar.

dialogue.speaker: Yuki
dialogue.text: It's from 2012. I got that much from the other photos, but the place is a blank.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The bench has green slats and those fish-shaped metal armrests. I'm pretty sure it's at Gas Works Park.

dialogue.speaker: Yuki
