details_in_summary: Sam marked the decision on a yellow sticky note.
key_facts: Sam will frame each shopfront straight on from roughly across the street.
They will keep the full doorway in each composition.
minor_details: Sam marked the decision on a yellow sticky note.

summary: Sam proposed framing each shopfront straight on from across the street, keeping the full doorway in every image to create a consistent series. Riley noted the approach and acknowledged the need to evaluate sign readability, especially where brighter signs lost detail. Sam said the framing rule was written on a yellow sticky note. Action items: review the framing rule, test compositions to ensure the doorway boundary is clear while signs remain legible.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So how do you think things stand with the laundry now?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Honestly, better. Going down around 9:15 on Sunday mornings seems to be working for us.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. We've been doing that for a few weeks now, and it feels less like a whole expedition.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but we shouldn't count on both machines being free every time.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right. On February 15, 1 washer was busy when we got there.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: And we managed fine by putting our combined load in the other one.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Which is a lot less annoying than standing around waiting for a second machine.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Especially after that Sunday when we waited 20 minutes for one.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Or the late Wednesday when we were up until 10:45.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: The machines have finally agreed to office hours.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Very generous of them. So, 9:15 Sunday as the usual time?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yes. One combined load if there's only 1 washer free, and we don't have to assume we'll get both.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What about when Sunday morning's inconvenient?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: We could try Saturday afternoon instead. As a fallback, not another appointment with the laundry gods.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay, Saturday afternoon. I'll write the fallback on the wall calendar.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Can you put it as an alternative to Sunday, so it doesn't look like we're doing laundry twice?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yep. I'm writing 'Saturday afternoon if Sunday morning doesn't work.'

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Perfect. And on Sundays, we'll still set a timer so we're back promptly.

details_in_summary: Riley writes the fallback on their wall calendar.
key_facts: By February 20, they have been going down at about 9:15 on Sunday mornings.
On February 15, one washer was busy, but they managed by washing their combined load in the other.
They choose Saturday afternoon as a fallback when Sunday morning is inconvenient.
minor_details: Riley writes the fallback on their wall calendar.
Maya jokes that the machines have finally agreed to office hours.

summary: Riley and Maya discussed laundry scheduling. They settled on Sundays at 9:15 as the usual time, with a single combined load if only one washer is available. They agreed Sundays may not always have both machines, and a prior fallback is Saturday afternoon, documented on the wall calendar as an alternative. Riley will note the Saturday fallback and ensure Sundays have a timer to start promptly.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, how are things with you tonight?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Pretty good. I'm eating lentil soup, and I had an idea I wanted to run by you.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay, what's the idea?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: What if we got away to the Olympic Peninsula sometime this spring? Just for a little change of scenery.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, I like that. I'd want to keep it really low-key, though.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Same. I'm thinking easy walks, not an ambitious hiking trip where we have to get up at 5.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yes, exactly. Walk a little, sit around a little. How long were you thinking?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Maybe 2 nights away? Enough time to settle in without turning it into a whole expedition.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: 2 nights sounds good. Hang on, I'm writing that on the back of an envelope so I don't forget.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so that's the official planning document. I promise not to make a spreadsheet comparing envelopes.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'd hold you to that, but I know you too well.

key_facts: They want easy walks rather than an ambitious hiking trip.
They are aiming for two nights away.
minor_details: Daniel is eating lentil soup while they talk.
Riley writes the idea on the back of an envelope.

summary: Riley discussed a low-key spring trip to the Olympic Peninsula with Daniel Reyes. They agreed on easy walks, no early starts, and a 2-night stay. They will treat the envelope as the planning document, avoiding a detailed spreadsheet. Action item: finalize the 2-night itinerary and keep the plan informal on the envelope.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: The directions are on the back. Can you read them without looking at the map?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. 'Start at the Ballard library branch, then follow the line to the turnaround.' Wait, which line?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: The heavy one on the map. Okay, but that doesn't help if you haven't looked at it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm marking that sentence with a paper clip. The turnaround isn't named here either.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: It's NW 57th Street. I put it on the map and apparently decided that was enough.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Could you name the street you're walking along too? Then say what to do after the turnaround.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah. I'm eating toast while I revise, so this page might get a few crumbs.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'll keep my map-free hands off it. Start with the library, then 22nd Avenue NW?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Right. 'Start at the Ballard library branch. Walk along 22nd Avenue NW to NW 57th Street.'

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And then separately, 'Turn around at NW 57th Street.'

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but I can put the turnaround in that second sentence: 'Walk along 22nd Avenue NW and turn around at NW 57th Street.'

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That works. Then say, 'Return along 22nd Avenue NW to the Ballard library branch.'

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Good. Starting point, turnaround, return. I'm removing 'follow the line' altogether.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Much clearer. I can understand the route without having to find the map first.

key_facts: The written directions name the starting point, turnaround and return separately.
Maya removes the phrase 'follow the line' because it is unhelpful without the map.
minor_details: Riley marks the confusing sentence with a paper clip.
Maya eats toast while revising.

summary: Riley and Maya reviewed route directions. They clarified the path: start at Ballard library branch, walk along 22nd Avenue NW to NW 57th Street, turn around there, then return along 22nd Avenue NW to the Ballard library branch. They decided to remove phrases like 'follow the line' and ensure each step is explicit. Action: finalize and publish the updated text.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Hi, Riley. How's your Sunday afternoon going?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey! Pretty quiet, which I'm not complaining about. How about yours?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Good. I cleared a space on the dining table before sorting the photos. That took longer than it should have.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A necessary first step. How are the groups looking?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: They're coming along. The childhood, family gathering and trip groups are a useful start, and I'm keeping the undated ones separate.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good. I was thinking we shouldn't try to scan everything at once.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I agree. In theory, everything is a lovely number, but I think 30 photographs would be manageable for the first round of scanning.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, let's choose 30. We can pick a few from each group.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Including the undated ones, if there are some we like?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Sure. We don't have to guess a date just to include them.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: All right. I'll keep the 30 selected prints in an acid-free paper folder, separate from the others.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And let's not write directly on the backs of the photographs, okay?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Agreed. I'm making a note of that, and I'll use a soft pencil on the folder to label it, not on the prints.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Perfect. 30 feels like a much better start than the whole shoebox and biscuit tin.

details_in_summary: Hannah uses a soft pencil on the folder.
key_facts: They choose 30 photographs for the first round of scanning.
Hannah will keep the selected prints in an acid-free paper folder.
They agree not to write directly on the backs of the photographs.
minor_details: Hannah uses a soft pencil on the folder.
She clears a space on the dining table before sorting.

summary: Riley and Hannah planned a first scanning batch of 30 photos, rather than the whole collection. They grouped prints into childhood, family gathering, and trip categories, with undated photos kept separate. They agreed not to guess dates, and to select a few from each group, including some undated if desirable. They will store the selected prints in an acid-free folder, label with a soft pencil on the folder (not the backs), and avoid writing on prints.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How are things coming along with the ferry ticket album?

dialogue.speaker: Victor
dialogue.text: Pretty well, I think. In January, I scanned 3 faded ticket stubs at 600 dpi, just to see what I'd get.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Could you read them once they were scanned?

dialogue.speaker: Victor
dialogue.text: Mostly. One date was still a little hard to make out, though, so I asked Isabel about it today.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, did she remember?

dialogue.speaker: Victor
dialogue.text: She did. It was the Bainbridge Island trip. She confirmed it was in 1994.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How'd you ask without giving away the album?

dialogue.speaker: Victor
dialogue.text: I just brought up the trip casually, like I was trying to remember when we'd gone. I didn't mention the album.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And she didn't get suspicious?

dialogue.speaker: Victor
dialogue.text: No, she seemed to take it as ordinary reminiscing. I'm relieved, honestly. I thought maybe I'd be a little too obvious.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You managed to ask your mother about an old family trip. Very subtle work.

dialogue.speaker: Victor
dialogue.text: Thank you. I'll put it on my résumé, maybe.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Were you over there this afternoon?

dialogue.speaker: Victor
dialogue.text: Yeah. I stopped at the produce stand afterward and bought pears. Then my bus was running about 10 minutes late.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: At least you had pears while you waited.

dialogue.speaker: Victor
dialogue.text: And a date for the album. Not a bad afternoon, I think.

key_facts: In January, Victor scanned three faded ticket stubs at 600 dpi.
Isabel confirmed that the Bainbridge Island trip Victor asked about was in 1994.
Victor asked about the trip casually, without revealing the album.
minor_details: Victor bought pears at the produce stand.
His bus was running about ten minutes late.

summary: Riley discussed progress on the ferry ticket album with Victor. Victor scanned 3 faded stubs at 600 dpi in January; most readings were clear, with one date clarified by Isabel as 1994 Bainbridge Island trip. Riley noted how Victor asked subtly without revealing the album. Victor mentioned a pleasant afternoon with pears and a late bus, and considered adding the task to his résumé.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, Sam, how's your Sunday going so far?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Pretty good. Just checking the mail before I head upstairs. How's yours?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good, nice and quiet. Oh, the strap on your canvas tote is getting a little frayed.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah, slightly. It's holding on, though. Unlike whatever lives in my mailbox and keeps sending me flyers.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Mine's full of those too.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Oh, while I've got you here by the mailboxes, I wanted to ask you something. Would you be interested in a small tabletop-game group?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, I think so. Who were you thinking?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Just 3 of us: you, me and my friend Inez. She used to work with me at the library, and she enjoys tabletop games.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds fun. I like the idea of keeping it small.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Me too. Easier to find a game, and, well, a time that suits everybody.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Should we check when we're all free?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. I'll ask Inez and we can see if we can find a time, if that works for you.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Works for me. Let me know what she says.

details_in_summary: Sam has a canvas tote with a slightly frayed strap.
key_facts: Sam proposes a group of three: Sam, Riley and Inez.
Inez is Sam's former library coworker and enjoys tabletop games.
minor_details: They are talking by the building's mailboxes.
Sam has a canvas tote with a slightly frayed strap.

summary: Riley discussed mail clutter and a fraying tote strap with Sam. They considered a small tabletop-game group with Sam and Inez, noting it would be easier to coordinate. Sam said he would ask Inez and check for a suitable time; Riley asked to be informed once Inez’s availability is known.

dialogue.speaker: Fatima
dialogue.text: Hi, Riley. It's a bit of a gray evening, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, Fatima. Yeah, and my mug of mint tea's going cold while I complain about it.

dialogue.speaker: Fatima
dialogue.text: A very efficient use of tea.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So, about the June book club discussion. We said we'd keep it pretty informal, right?

dialogue.speaker: Fatima
dialogue.text: Right. For A Psalm for the Wild-Built. I was thinking we could divide up the practical bits without making it feel too organized.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. We can still start by inviting everyone's first impressions.

dialogue.speaker: Fatima
dialogue.text: Exactly. I can welcome the group and start the discussion, if that works for you.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Definitely. I can keep an eye on the time and help move the conversation along.

dialogue.speaker: Fatima
dialogue.text: Good. Not in a 'you have 30 seconds left' way, presumably.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: No, I promise not to bring a buzzer. Just a gentle nudge if we're stuck or going long.

dialogue.speaker: Fatima
dialogue.text: That sounds right. And could we leave a few minutes at the end for final thoughts?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, I'll watch for that. We can ask if there's anything people wanted to say before we wrap up.

dialogue.speaker: Fatima
dialogue.text: Perfect. Actually, wait, I was going to put that in my phone, but my bus pass is tucked into the back of the phone case. I keep trying to open the case instead of the app.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: At least you know where your bus pass is.

dialogue.speaker: Fatima
dialogue.text: Today, yes. I won't make any broader claims.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So you'll open, I'll watch the time and help us move along, and we'll save a few minutes at the end.

dialogue.speaker: Fatima
dialogue.text: That's the list. Short enough that even I don't need to write it down.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Not bad for February 22. We've got the jobs sorted without scheduling every minute.

dialogue.speaker: Fatima
dialogue.text: Good. Let's leave room for people to take the conversation where they want.

key_facts: On February 22, Fatima volunteers to welcome the group and start the discussion.
Riley will handle timekeeping and help move the conversation along.
They agree to leave a few minutes at the end for any final thoughts.
minor_details: Riley has a mug of mint tea going cold.
Fatima's bus pass is tucked into the back of her phone case.

summary: Riley and Fatima planned a casual June book club discussion for A Psalm for the Wild-Built. They agreed to split practical tasks without rigid structure, begin with first impressions, and keep time with gentle nudges rather than a buzzer. Fatima will welcome the group; Riley will monitor time and guide the flow, leaving a few minutes for final thoughts. They also aimed to allow organic discussion and avoid over-scheduling; a minor bus pass issue was noted.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Oh, that's encouraging. The first queue numbers just came in.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah? What are we looking at?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: From February 9 through February 20, the median time from queue entry to opening a delivery was 4.5 minutes. It was 7 minutes in the 2 weeks before launch.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'll write that comparison on the whiteboard in black marker: 7 minutes before launch, 4.5 minutes from February 9 through February 20.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Thanks. And that's time to first open, not time to resolve a delivery. The number isn't telling us how long the whole job takes.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right. It does look like the queue might be quicker to scan, though.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: It does, though I'd be careful about calling it a win across the board. We still have those missing arrival times.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, especially since we wanted arrival time visible in the list. What if the source data's incomplete?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: That's worth checking. We should investigate whether the missing arrival times come from incomplete source data.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Let's do that before we draw any broader conclusions from the comparison.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Agreed. I'm putting a paper star beside the investigation item in my notes. Very sophisticated prioritization system.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hard to miss, at least. I'll keep the time-to-first-open distinction next to the numbers.

details_in_summary: Sam puts a paper star beside the investigation item in their notes.
key_facts: From February 9 through February 20, the median time from queue entry to opening a delivery was 4.5 minutes, compared with 7 minutes in the two weeks before launch.
The comparison measures time to first open, not time to resolve a delivery.
The team will investigate whether the missing arrival times come from incomplete source data.
minor_details: Riley writes the comparison on a whiteboard in black marker.
Sam puts a paper star beside the investigation item in their notes.

summary: Riley and Sam discussed queue metrics: median time from queue entry to first open was 7 minutes before launch and 4.5 minutes from Feb 9–20. Riley notes this is time to first open, not total delivery time, and that scanning may be quicker. They flagged missing arrival times as a data issue to investigate before drawing conclusions and planned to verify data completeness. Riley will keep the time-to-first-open distinction with the numbers; Sam added a paper star for the investigation item.

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: I've got an update on the Leaf. My landlord approved using the driveway outlet on February 12.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good. That was the big question after the test drive, right?

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: Yeah. I liked how smoothly it accelerated, but I didn't want to assume I could charge it at home.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And did you get the battery checked?

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: I did. The battery inspection on February 21 showed 85% state of health.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How do you feel about that?

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: Pretty comfortable, actually. For the local trips I want it for, it seems reasonable, but it depends on how much driving I'm doing.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Between that and the outlet, it sounds a lot less uncertain.

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: Definitely. I'm more comfortable proceeding with the purchase now. The inspection waiting room even had a puzzle magazine, so the suspense was manageable.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you get any puzzles done?

dialogue.speaker: Oliver
dialogue.text: A couple. I was less thorough with those than I was with the car.

details_in_summary: The inspection waiting room had a puzzle magazine.
key_facts: Oliver's landlord approved use of the driveway outlet on February 12.
A February 21 battery inspection showed 85% state of health.
minor_details: The inspection waiting room had a puzzle magazine.

summary: Riley and Oliver discussed Leaf details: driveway outlet approval on Feb 12, battery inspection on Feb 21 showed 85% health, Oliver comfortable for local trips, and more confident about purchasing. No further actions noted beyond proceeding with the purchase; Oliver mentioned puzzle magazine in waiting room during inspection.

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: I've started trying to describe an ordinary week in Italian, out loud. It's different from filling in the blanks.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What do you want to be able to say without stopping?

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: I'm aiming for a 5-sentence account of my week. Just ordinary things, nothing terribly literary.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What kind of things?

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: Errands, getting to work. I'm collecting vocabulary for errands and commuting, because I keep getting halfway through a sentence and realizing I don't know a word.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Are you writing the words down?

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: On index cards, the unfamiliar ones. One card fell behind my radiator, so that word may be lost to history.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Do you remember what was on it?

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: No, which rather proves I needed the card.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How's the past tense going when you say things out loud?

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: Slowly. I'm still having to think about whether I need 'essere' or 'avere,' like on that worksheet. When I read the forms, I usually recognize them.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So you're trying to put the pieces together without the blanks there to guide you.

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: Exactly. A small, practical report on my week. Ideally with fewer pauses than this conversation.

details_in_summary: One card fell behind her radiator.
key_facts: Amara is aiming for a five-sentence account of her week.
She is collecting vocabulary for errands and commuting.
minor_details: She writes unfamiliar words on index cards.
One card fell behind her radiator.

summary: Riley discussed Amara's plan to describe an ordinary week in Italian, aiming for a five-sentence account about errands and commuting. She is compiling vocabulary on index cards, noting one card fell behind a radiator and may be lost. Past tense usage (essere vs avere) remains slow, though forms are recognized when read. Action items: continue practicing with fewer pauses, maintain vocabulary cards, and attempt to retrieve the lost card or replace it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How's the ferry piece standing now?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, better, I think. I've been working on the mix since we tried it in the gallery.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Because the fan was swallowing that low voice?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. I adjusted the speech equalization to make the words clearer over the room noise. Not just turning everything up again.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right, since the louder bits were already uncomfortable.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Exactly. I also reduced the background ambience underneath the quietest words, so they're not competing with it as much.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Can you still hear the deck between the voices?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, it's still there. I just pulled it back where the speech gets quiet. I spent a frankly ridiculous amount of time deciding how much.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: College Daniel would like a spreadsheet of all the possible amounts.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: College Daniel would have 3 spreadsheets. I listened to the revised version while standing beside the suite door, just to hear it from a little farther away.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And it held together?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: It did there, yeah. The words feel easier to follow without losing that sense of being on the ferry.

details_in_summary: He listened to the revised version while standing beside the suite door.
key_facts: He adjusted the speech equalization to improve clarity over the room noise.
He reduced the background ambience beneath the quietest words.
minor_details: He listened to the revised version while standing beside the suite door.

summary: Riley discussed the ferry piece with Daniel, noting improvements in the mix. Daniel described adjusting speech EQ to clarify words, reducing background ambience under quiet phrases, and pulling back the deck noise when speech quiets. Riley asked about still hearing the deck; Daniel confirmed it remains but is less prominent. Riley and Daniel tested the revised version near the suite door, confirming the words are easier to follow while maintaining the ferry atmosphere.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm waiting for the kettle to boil. What are you drawing on that receipt?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Just sketching an idea on the back of the grocery receipt. I want to propose an oral-history display for the Ballard library branch.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, what would be in it?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Short audio clips of neighborhood residents talking about places they remember. Everyday places, like a shop they used to stop at or a corner where they waited for the bus.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That could get pretty big. How will you keep it manageable?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but I don't want it to be a comprehensive local history. Just a few people's memories of ordinary neighborhood places.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How many people are you thinking?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: My initial goal is 3 resident contributions. Small enough that I can actually get started.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And short clips, so people can listen to a little at a time?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah. More like a glimpse of a place than somebody's entire life story.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds good. You've got the whole idea on a grocery receipt?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Most of it. The receipt is enforcing a very strict word limit.

details_in_summary: Maya sketches the idea on the back of a grocery receipt.
key_facts: Maya proposes the display for the Ballard library branch.
She wants to collect memories of everyday neighborhood places rather than a comprehensive local history.
Her initial goal is three resident contributions.
minor_details: Maya sketches the idea on the back of a grocery receipt.
Riley is waiting for the kettle to boil.

summary: Riley discussed Maya's idea for a Ballard library oral-history display. Plan: short audio clips from residents about ordinary places, not a comprehensive history. Start with 3 contributions, brief clips, a glimpse rather than full lives. The grocery receipt enforces a strict word limit on the idea. Action items: Maya to gather 3 resident contributions and keep the project small and manageable within the word limit.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I've made some progress on the rights for the Tacoma photo display.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good. How many of the 6 can you use?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: 4 of the selected images are verified as public domain. The other 2 need permission, so I've requested it from the rights holder.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Is that 1 request for both?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yeah, both are with the same rights holder. I sent the request just before leaving for lunch, so I'm waiting on that 1 response.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds pretty straightforward, at least.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: In theory, yes. I'm glad I started the rights part early, though. It takes a while to be sure what you can actually use.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Especially after you had to take that parade photo off the list.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Exactly. I'd rather check than make an assumption and have to undo it.

details_in_summary: She sent the request just before leaving for lunch.
key_facts: Four selected images have been verified as public domain.
Hannah has requested display permission from the rights holder for the other two.
minor_details: She sent the request just before leaving for lunch.

summary: Riley discussed rights for the Tacoma photo display with Hannah. Of 6 images, 4 are public domain; 2 require permission from the same rights holder. A single permissions request was sent before lunch, and they are awaiting a response. Riley noted starting the rights process early and avoiding assumptions, referencing the parade photo that was removed.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. Is it just me, or did today have about 3 extra meetings in it?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey. It definitely felt longer than a Thursday.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. I was just about to head out, but I wanted to tell you: I booked the suite for Victoria.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice! The self-catering one you were looking at?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: That's the one. It's in James Bay, and I booked it for 3 nights.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So the kitchen won over the inn?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The kitchen helped. And the cancellation terms made it easier to commit. I can cancel through April 30 without a lodging charge.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's reassuring. You don't have to feel completely locked in.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. I kept reading that line to make sure I hadn't missed a 'but' somewhere.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The traditional booking-page 'but.'

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Right. The confirmation arrived at 8:14 p.m., and I checked it again. Still no 'but.'

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Does it look like a comfortable place to hang out, too?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I think so. The listing shows a small round table beside a window. Not much to go on, but it looks like a decent spot for breakfast.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And you can make breakfast there instead of having Ada take care of every meal.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. That's what I was hoping for. It also has its own entrance.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, that's nice. You can come and go without feeling like you're disturbing anyone.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. And I'll have somewhere to retreat between visits with Ada. Not because I want less time with her, just—

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A little room to reset.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. A long weekend feels more manageable that way. Also, somewhere to leave my breakfast dishes until later.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: An important feature. I'm glad you found a place.

details_in_summary: The confirmation arrived at 8:14 p.m.
key_facts: Sam booked a self-catering suite in James Bay for three nights.
The reservation can be canceled without a lodging charge through April 30.
The suite has its own entrance.
minor_details: The confirmation arrived at 8:14 p.m.
The listing shows a small round table beside a window.

summary: Riley and Sam discussed booking a self-catering suite in James Bay for three nights for Victoria. Key points: cancellation terms allow free change through April 30; confirmation received at 8:14 p.m. Features include a private entrance, a small breakfast table, and the ability to cook breakfast, plus a space to retreat between visits with Ada. Overall, a plan to have a reset space during the long weekend.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Well, that's a bit of a letdown. I just heard back from the Cascadia Archive Institute about financial help.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh. No luck?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: No scholarships available for this certificate cohort. So if I enroll, I'll have to cover the cost myself.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Ah, I'm sorry. Did they say anything else about how the payments work?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. There's a $200 enrollment deposit, but it's credited toward the first tuition installment.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay, so it's not another $200 on top of the $2,400?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Right. The first installment is $800, so after the deposit it'd be $600 left on that one.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's something, at least. How are you feeling about it?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Still interested. Just need to think about paying for it myself. I took the call standing beside my apartment window, and I was doing the math in my head instead of listening for a second.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The classic Daniel math pause.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Exactly. My specialty is making a simple subtraction feel like a research project.

key_facts: The institute has no scholarships available for this certificate cohort.
A $200 enrollment deposit is credited toward the first tuition installment.
minor_details: Daniel took the call standing beside his apartment window.

summary: Riley and Daniel discussed Cascadia Archive Institute certificate funding. There are no scholarships for the cohort. Enrollment deposit is $200 and is credited toward the first tuition installment. The first installment is $800, leaving $600 after the deposit. Daniel remains interested but needs to decide how to cover the costs himself. No immediate commitment; Riley acknowledged the math calculation as part of Daniel’s decision process.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: Oh, I actually did it. I signed the lease for the Greenwood studio.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You got it? Nora, that's great!

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: Yeah. I was accepted on February 17. I think it took until signing the lease for it to feel real.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: After all that waiting on the reference check, I can imagine.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: Exactly. And I'm moving tomorrow, February 28. So it's feeling very real now.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Tomorrow! How's the packing going?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: It's going. I'm labeling boxes with a black marker, which makes me feel more organized than I actually am.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, being able to find things counts.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: I think so. And I borrowed a hand truck, so at least I don't have to carry every box.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good call. I'm really glad the studio worked out for you.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: Me too. A place of my own, with a separate kitchen. I think I can finally stop comparing listings.

details_in_summary: She has borrowed a hand truck.
She is labeling boxes with a black marker.
key_facts: Nora was accepted on February 17 and has signed the lease.
She is moving on February 28.
minor_details: She has borrowed a hand truck.
She is labeling boxes with a black marker.

summary: Nora signed the Greenwood studio lease, accepted February 17, with moving scheduled for February 28. She is packing, labeling boxes with a black marker for organization, and has borrowed a hand truck to move items. The separate kitchen is noted, and she aims to stop comparing listings now that the lease is in place.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: The garden replied about the vacant bed. The email came in while I was eating toast.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. What did they say?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Canal-side Community Garden asks prospective gardeners to complete a short application. Applications for the vacant bed are due March 6.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay, that's next Friday. Do you want to apply for it together?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah, I do. We were looking at sharing one bed for the season, right?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right. I think one would be good for us.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but let's actually fill it out before March 6. The deadline seems unlikely to move out of politeness.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Fair. Let's apply.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: All right. I'll pull up the application.

key_facts: The garden asks prospective gardeners to complete a short application.
Applications for the vacant bed are due March 6.
minor_details: The reply arrived while Maya was eating toast.

summary: Riley and Maya discussed the Canal-side Community Garden vacant bed and the application deadline of March 6. They decided to apply together for one bed to share for the season and will fill out the application before the deadline. Maya will pull up the application to begin the process.

dialogue.speaker: Wei
dialogue.text: Morning, Riley. It's a bit chilly in here today.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Morning. Yeah, I was hoping it'd warm up after I got to my desk.

dialogue.speaker: Wei
dialogue.text: My tea had the same hope. Hang on, I'm moving this cold mug of tea away from the keyboard.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Probably wise. I wanted to ask about the timestamp check.

dialogue.speaker: Wei
dialogue.text: Right. By February 3, I'd checked the underlying scan and receipt timestamps. The summary uses the receipt timestamp.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So it's when the scan record arrives in the system, not the time on the delivery scan itself?

dialogue.speaker: Wei
dialogue.text: Exactly. In the example we looked at, the delivery scan showed 9:50 a.m., before the 10:00 a.m. expected delivery time.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: But the record arrived at 10:12 a.m., so it got counted.

dialogue.speaker: Wei
dialogue.text: Yes. Calling the summary 'Late shipments' makes that sound like a conclusion about the shipment itself. The receipt timestamp doesn't establish that.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's what I was trying to address in the wording I brought you on February 19.

dialogue.speaker: Wei
dialogue.text: The longer label?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. I've got the document open here, the one with the pale green header. The proposed label is 'Shipments with delivery scans received after expected delivery time.'

dialogue.speaker: Wei
dialogue.text: That names the thing we're actually counting. It's long, but it's precise.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And the explanation says the count does not establish whether the shipment itself arrived late.

dialogue.speaker: Wei
dialogue.text: Good. A record can arrive late even when the scan time is before the expected delivery time. Those are different timestamps.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I was worried people might read 'received' as the customer receiving the shipment.

dialogue.speaker: Wei
dialogue.text: Mm. The explanation could make it clear that the system receives the scan record. Then 'received' has somewhere to point.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That makes sense. I'll make sure the explanation says that.

key_facts: By February 3, Wei checked the underlying scan and receipt timestamps and confirmed that the summary uses the receipt timestamp.
On February 19, Riley brought Wei the proposed label “Shipments with delivery scans received after expected delivery time.”
Riley’s accompanying explanation says the count does not establish whether the shipment itself arrived late.
minor_details: Riley has the wording open in a document with a pale green header.
Wei pauses to move a cold mug of tea away from the keyboard.

summary: Riley discussed the timestamp check, clarifying that the summary uses the receipt (system arrival) timestamp, not the delivery scan time. Example: a 9:50 delivery scan with a 10:12 record arrival is counted as late. They agreed on the label: 'Shipments with delivery scans received after expected delivery time.' The explanation should state the count does not imply the shipment itself was late, and that 'received' refers to the system receiving the scan. Action: update the February 19 document to reflect this clarification.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: You're still at your desk. Can I borrow your brain for a minute?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Sure. What's that you've got?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: A program I found on a community noticeboard. The one with the blue border. It's for a little film series, and I can't decide what to see.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, Neighborhood Frames. Where is it?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The Beacon Hill Screening Room, March 14–15. There are 3 films, but I want to see 2, not spend the entire weekend at the series.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Fair. What are the choices?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The Long Way Home, Low Tide Market, and A Place for Rain.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Low Tide Market is the title that jumps out at me. Does the program say what it's about?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: It does, but I'm still torn. The Long Way Home sounds appealing too, and A Place for Rain has a good title. This is a very scientific process.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Well, you could start with Low Tide Market and see which of the other 2 you're more curious about.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: What if I pick based on the times as well? I don't want to rush from one straight into another.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, leave some time free between screenings. You might want a break instead of making a whole shift of it.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Right. I'll check the times before I choose. That's already more of a system than staring at the titles.

key_facts: The Neighborhood Frames series is at the Beacon Hill Screening Room on March 14–15.
The program has three films: The Long Way Home, Low Tide Market, and A Place for Rain.
Sam wants to see two films rather than spend the entire weekend at the series.
minor_details: Sam found the program on a community noticeboard.
The printed program has a blue border.

summary: Riley discussed Neighborhood Frames at the Beacon Hill Screening Room (Mar 14–15) with Sam. They narrowed choices to The Long Way Home, Low Tide Market, and A Place for Rain, with a plan to watch two films. Riley suggested starting with Low Tide Market and evaluating the other two, and emphasized checking showtimes to allow breaks between screenings.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, how are things standing with the Astoria hotel search?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I've narrowed it down to 2 downtown hotels: Hotel Elliott and the Norblad Hotel. I'm still comparing the rooms, though.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Do you have a favorite yet?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Not quite. Owen and I definitely want a private room, not a shared sleeping space, so I'm checking the room descriptions carefully.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That seems like a good thing to check before you book.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes. In theory, the listings make it clear. In practice, I've opened so many tabs that I've lost the one I wanted.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Is it the one with the room you liked?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I think so. Or it might be the one with the photograph of a particularly ornate headboard. Which is not, strictly speaking, a useful way to compare hotels.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Depends how much you care about headboards.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Apparently enough to remember that and not the room details.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What are you weighing besides the rooms?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Mostly location and price. We'd prefer to be within walking distance of downtown. Do you think being able to walk places is worth paying a little more?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I probably would, especially since you're not driving. It'd be nice not to have to figure out another ride every time you go out.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: That's what I keep coming back to. A cheaper room isn't quite as appealing if getting around is a nuisance.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Maybe compare the private rooms first, then see how much extra the more convenient one actually costs.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes. Once I find that tab again, I'll do exactly that.

key_facts: Hannah is comparing Hotel Elliott and the Norblad Hotel.
She and Owen want a private room rather than a shared sleeping space.
They prefer lodging within walking distance of downtown.
minor_details: One listing has a photograph of a particularly ornate headboard.
Hannah has opened so many browser tabs that she loses the one she wants.

summary: Riley discussed the Astoria hotel search with Hannah. Two downtown options—Hotel Elliott and the Norblad—are under comparison, focusing on private rooms. Hannah is sorting room details but has tabs scattered. They prioritized location and price, valuing walkability over extra cost. Riley suggested comparing private rooms first and then evaluating whether a central location justifies the price. Action item: Hannah will locate the private-room tab again and proceed with the side-by-side comparison of options and, if relevant, cost of walking convenience.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So how do things stand with work?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, I picked up a separate commission for Willow Bend Salmon Hatchery, near Monroe.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A hatchery? What are you making for them?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: A 3-minute soundscape for the visitor center. Something that gives people a sense of the working site.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a lot to fit into 3 minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. And I don't want it to sound like a factory tour, you know? It's a working place, but that's not the whole feeling of it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right. You could let the water be there without making it all big and majestic.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Exactly. Not 3 minutes of heroic river. But not just a catalog of machines, either.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Who are you working with there?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Their visitor coordinator is Maren Holt. She's the contact on the brief.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And what does the brief say about the space?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Well, there's a cork noticeboard by the visitor center entrance. That little detail stuck with me. It sounds like a place people actually use, not some polished lobby.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a good thing to keep in mind. People might be coming in with kids, looking at the board, talking over it.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, it doesn't have to demand complete silence and attention.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Have you got ideas down yet?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: A few. I read the brief over a bowl of tomato soup and put my first notes in a green spiral notebook.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you spend an hour deciding which notebook to use?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: No, I grabbed the nearest one. I'm as surprised as you are.

details_in_summary: The visitor center has a cork noticeboard by its entrance.
His first notes are in a green spiral notebook.
key_facts: Willow Bend Salmon Hatchery is near Monroe.
The commission is for a three-minute visitor-center soundscape.
The hatchery's visitor coordinator is Maren Holt.
minor_details: Daniel read the brief over a bowl of tomato soup.
The visitor center has a cork noticeboard by its entrance.
His first notes are in a green spiral notebook.

summary: Riley discussed a Willow Bend Salmon Hatchery commission: a 3-minute soundscape for the visitor center aiming to convey a working site without a factory-tour feel. Daniel will coordinate with Maren Holt; brief notes a cork noticeboard near the entrance to guide tone. Audience includes families; not requiring silence. Initial ideas exist in a green notebook; next steps involve refining concepts per the brief.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: The permission came through for the last 2 photographs for the Tacoma display.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good. Both of them?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes. The rights holder granted permission to display both images at the Swasey branch. So I can use the full selection.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a relief. Was there anything you have to include with them?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: A credit line beside each of those 2 images. Which is perfectly reasonable, I just need to leave room for it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Especially with the captions and that 6-foot wall.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Exactly. The reply came as a PDF attachment, so I've got the wording there. Now I'm trying to make the captions useful without writing 6 miniature essays.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Do you have a length in mind?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: No more than 40 words each. I'm drafting them in a plain-text document, which is not glamorous, but at least I can see how much I'm writing.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What are you trying to fit into those 40 words?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: The place and date, if we know them, and enough about what's happening that somebody isn't left guessing. Then the credit where it's required.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds like a good order. You could leave out anything that's already obvious from looking at the picture.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes. I don't need to tell people there's a building in the photograph when they're looking directly at the building.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Unless the building is the interesting part.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Right, if there's something worth knowing about it. Short captions are easy, in theory. Apparently I can use 40 words just explaining why a caption should be short.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You've got a limit now, at least. And all 6 pictures can stay.

details_in_summary: The reply arrived as a PDF attachment.
key_facts: The rights holder granted permission to display both remaining images at the branch.
The permission requires a credit line beside each of those images.
Hannah is aiming for captions of no more than 40 words each.
minor_details: The reply arrived as a PDF attachment.
Hannah has been drafting captions in a plain-text document.

summary: Riley noted that permission was granted for the last 2 Tacoma display photos at the Swasey branch, with a required credit line. Hannah will draft 40-word captions per image, including place/date if known and a concise description, while reserving room for credits. Captions should avoid redundant details; six photos can stay. Action: finalize two captions with credits ready for PDF wording.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. Quiet Sunday evening, isn't it? The elevator's almost suspiciously quick.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, Sam. Yeah, I didn't even have time to check my phone.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: A rare building amenity. Oh, I've started a beginner Italian class.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice! Where are you taking it?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: At the neighborhood community center. It meets on Tuesday evenings.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How's it going so far?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Good, I think. There's a lot to remember, so I've put Italian vocabulary notes on my fridge.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's smart. You see them every time you go for food.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. I'm hoping some of the words will, uh, stick. Unlike the notes, which need a little help.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What kind of words have you got up there?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: One says 'finestra.' That's the Italian word for window.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A window on the fridge. That might actually make it more memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Maybe. A blue magnet's holding that one in place, at least.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you make them on little scraps of paper?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah, and I wrote them in pencil, so I can change them around. Very sophisticated system.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, whatever works. I like 'finestra,' actually.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: It is a good one. Anyway, have a good evening, Riley.

details_in_summary: Sam wrote the notes in pencil.
A blue magnet holds one of the notes in place.
key_facts: Sam's beginner Italian class meets on Tuesday evenings at a neighborhood community center.
Sam has put Italian vocabulary notes on their fridge.
One note says 'finestra,' the Italian word for window.
minor_details: Sam wrote the notes in pencil.

summary: Riley greeted Sam and noted a quiet Sunday. Sam shared starting a beginner Italian class at the neighborhood community center, meeting on Tuesday evenings. He uses fridge-mounted vocabulary notes—pencil, scraps of paper, blue magnet—to help memorize words like 'finestra' (window). Riley commented on the system and expressed a positive stance. No immediate decisions or next steps were made.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: What if we put a few cooking herbs out on the balcony?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, I like that. Close enough to grab while we're making dinner.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah, just snip a little when we need it, instead of buying a whole bunch.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'd put them on scrambled eggs all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but which herbs do you actually want on your eggs?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Chives, probably. Maybe parsley too.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Parsley would be useful for a lot of things. I like the idea of having something we can use every day.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And we could do it separately from our community garden bed. Just a little experiment here.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Right, containers on the balcony at our Ballard apartment, not in the garden bed.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: We wouldn't have to go anywhere when we want a handful.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Or put on shoes to get dinner. A major advance in agriculture.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Where would we put them, though?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Well, that unused folding chair is taking up space out there. We could move it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I keep forgetting that's even there. Yeah, let's make room.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Good. A few herbs within arm's reach sounds pretty nice.

details_in_summary: Maya notices an unused folding chair taking up balcony space.
key_facts: The herbs will grow in containers on the Ballard apartment balcony, not in the community garden bed.
Maya and Riley want herbs they can snip for everyday cooking.
minor_details: Riley mentions putting herbs on scrambled eggs.
Maya notices an unused folding chair taking up balcony space.

summary: Riley and Maya discussed growing herbs on the Ballard apartment balcony in containers separate from the community garden bed. They settled on chives and parsley for daily use and quick access. Action items: move the unused folding chair to create space and set up a few balcony containers for herbs to keep within arm's reach.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. Afternoon's moving along at its usual dramatic pace.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, Sam. Yeah, I could use a little more afternoon in this afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Same. Oh, I finally replaced the cookbooks under my monitor.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. What did you get?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: A bamboo monitor riser. It was $18, and it lifts the monitor 4 inches.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Does that feel better than the cookbooks did?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah, it does. I compared 3 options at a hardware store before picking it. The practical bonus is my pencil tin now fits beneath the riser.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's handy, especially with the folding table being only 32 inches wide.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. Now the next problem is the lighting. It's uneven, so one side of the workspace is much brighter than the other.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What if you look at where the light's coming from before you change anything?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah, that makes sense. I'll have a look on my next home-working day.

details_in_summary: Sam compared three options at a hardware store.
A pencil tin now fits beneath the riser.
key_facts: Sam bought a bamboo monitor riser for $18.
The riser lifts the monitor four inches.
minor_details: Sam compared three options at a hardware store.
A pencil tin now fits beneath the riser.
