Travel will involve train and bus connections, with flexibility for a walk if weather is dry.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so I bought a used Technics SL-B2 turntable for the new apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. How much was it?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: $45. It seemed like a pretty good deal until I plugged it in.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What's it doing?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: There's this hum. Not loud enough to drown everything out, just loud enough that I can't stop listening for it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Is it only when a record's playing?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: No, that's the irritating part. I can hear it before the needle reaches the record.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay. What have you got it connected to?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I set it up in my Fremont apartment with an external phono preamp and powered speakers.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Could be a cable, maybe? Or a ground wire?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, I was wondering about the ground. I should check whether it's actually secure instead of just staring at the back of the thing.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The staring method has gotten us through a lot, though.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: College shorthand for 'we haven't started yet.'

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Exactly. You could also try moving the cables away from the power cords, see if anything changes.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, ground first, then cables. Otherwise I'll spend 3 hours deciding which wire looks the most suspicious.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Apart from the hum, how is it?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Looks decent. The dust cover has a cloudy patch near one hinge, but I don't really mind that.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, I could live with a cloudy patch. The hum would drive me nuts, though.

details_in_summary: The turntable cost $45.
Its dust cover has a cloudy patch near one hinge.
key_facts: Daniel bought a used Technics SL-B2 turntable.
He has set it up in his Fremont apartment with an external phono preamp and powered speakers.
The hum is audible before the needle reaches the record.
minor_details: The turntable cost $45.
Its dust cover has a cloudy patch near one hinge.

summary: Riley discussed Daniel’s used Technics SL-B2 purchase for $45 and a persistent hum audible even before a record plays. They identified possible causes, focusing on grounding and cabling. Action items include verifying the turntable ground connection is secure and rearranging cables away from power cords. They also noted the unit’s overall condition, including a cloudy patch on the dust cover, but did not raise further issues. No final fix determined yet.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So how do things stand with the bed now?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Pretty good, actually. We pulled the winter weeds and loosened the soil by hand, so bed 7 finally looks ready.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And more than ready, I guess. We got the peas in.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Right, a short row of peas along the back of the bed.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I kept thinking that row looked tiny after all that weeding.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but it's a short bed. A very ambitious row would have run out of bed.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Fair. And the chard starts are in the front half.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah. I was looking at the labels afterward, and I'd written them with that blunt marker.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, that's why the letters looked so squashed together.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I could still read them, just about.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did the empty plant pots make it home?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: They did. I brought them home in the canvas bag.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good. That drizzle started just as we were putting the tools away.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: At least it waited until then. I'll take that as a very modest victory.

details_in_summary: The chard labels were written with a blunt marker.
Maya brought the empty plant pots home in a canvas bag.
A drizzle started as they were putting the tools away.
key_facts: They pulled the winter weeds and loosened the soil by hand.
They sowed a short row of peas along the back of the bed.
They planted chard starts in the front half.
minor_details: The chard labels were written with a blunt marker.
Maya brought the empty plant pots home in a canvas bag.
A drizzle started as they were putting the tools away.

summary: Riley discussed bed 7 preparation: pulled winter weeds and loosened soil, bed now ready. They planted a short row of peas along the back and placed chard starts in the front half. Maya noted labeling with a blunt marker looked squashed but readable. They confirmed empty plant pots were brought home in a canvas bag. A drizzle began as tools were put away; both viewed it as a modest victory.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: And this time the score actually opened up. I used the razor like you suggested.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice! How was the middle?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Fully baked. No gummy patch. I kept looking at it like I needed a second opinion, but it was done.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a pretty good improvement from the first one.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Much better. I ate the heel with butter while the loaf was still slightly warm, so I didn't wait very long to check.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I wouldn't have waited either. Did the schedule feel any easier this time?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: It did. Feeding on Friday evening, mixing and shaping on Saturday, then putting the dough in the fridge overnight worked without keeping me up half the night.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And you baked it yesterday morning?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yeah, Sunday morning. I think I'll stick with feeding the starter on Friday evenings and baking on Sunday mornings.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What are you doing with the starter you're not using?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: After I feed it, I return the remaining starter to the refrigerator. I cleared a small spot for the jar on the upper shelf, so it has an actual home now.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A good loaf and a designated shelf. That's a solid routine.

key_facts: The repeat loaf had an open score and a fully baked center.
Hannah plans to feed the starter on Friday evenings and bake on Sunday mornings.
She returns the remaining starter to the refrigerator after feeding it.
minor_details: She ate the heel with butter while the loaf was still slightly warm.
She has cleared a small spot for the jar on the upper refrigerator shelf.

summary: Riley discussed the loaf improvements, noting a fully baked middle and no gummy patch. Decisions included sticking with feeding Friday evenings and baking Sunday mornings, and the schedule feeling easier. Riley also outlined starter management: feed, return the remainder to the fridge, and maintain a designated upper-shelf home for the jar. Action items: continue the Friday feed / Sunday bake routine and keep the starter on the assigned shelf.

dialogue.speaker: Chloe
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. How's your evening going?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, Chloe. Pretty quiet, actually. How's yours?

dialogue.speaker: Chloe
dialogue.text: Quiet here too. I've been working on captions for those cinema programs.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. Are these for the 4 you scanned?

dialogue.speaker: Chloe
dialogue.text: Yeah. They're still drafts, but I'm trying to say a little about each film and the design of its program.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What have you got for Singin' in the Rain?

dialogue.speaker: Chloe
dialogue.text: Just that it's a musical, and then a bit about the lettering on the program. I'm trying not to make each one a whole essay.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds good. Enough to give someone a reason to look closer.

dialogue.speaker: Chloe
dialogue.text: Maybe. The first drafts are on the backs of scrap envelopes, so they look very official.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The finest archival stationery.

dialogue.speaker: Chloe
dialogue.text: Mm. And my pen ran out midway through a sentence, which really adds to the effect.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You could call it an unfinished thought and leave it there.

dialogue.speaker: Chloe
dialogue.text: Tempting. The actual thing I'm unsure about is one undated program. I can't verify when that screening was.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Could you just say the screening date is unknown? Better than guessing.

dialogue.speaker: Chloe
dialogue.text: Yeah, that's what I was thinking. I'll label its date as unknown rather than guess. It feels more honest.

details_in_summary: She wrote the first drafts on the backs of scrap envelopes.
key_facts: Chloe's captions describe the films and the programs' designs.
She cannot verify the screening date for one undated program.
She plans to label that program's date as unknown rather than guess.
minor_details: She wrote the first drafts on the backs of scrap envelopes.
Her pen ran out midway through a sentence.

summary: Riley discussed Chloe’s work on captions for four cinema program drafts, focusing on film content and program design. They noted drafts are on scrap envelopes and will remain concise rather than full essays. For Singin’ in the Rain, captions mention it is a musical and comment on lettering. A decision was made to label an undated program’s screening date as unknown instead of guessing, improving honesty in the captions.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I've got 5 images on the shortlist for the group to consider. They're in this translucent folder, if you want to have a look.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. Is the shoe-repair shop in there?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah, the wider one with the whole awning. The florist made it in too.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That shoe-repair frame still feels much better with the pavement at the bottom.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: It gives the shop a little room to breathe. Which is more than I can say for this folder.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Are these the captions for the submission?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: They are. Sorry about the small dent in the caption sheet. A paper clip did that.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I think it'll survive. When do you have to send everything in?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The submission deadline is April 24, so I'm trying to get it ready this morning.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You've got the locations under each one. Wait, is this block number right?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Which one?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The shoe-repair caption says the 3700 block, but the street sign in the photo says 3800.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Oh, you're right. I must've typed the wrong block number. What if I check the other captions against the photos too, before I send them?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, good idea. The colors look more consistent across these, by the way.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Thanks. Revisiting the edits together on the same screen helped. Now I just need the captions to agree with the pictures.

key_facts: Sam has shortlisted five images for the group to consider.
The submission deadline is April 24.
Riley notices that one caption gives the wrong block number.
minor_details: Sam carried the shortlist in a translucent folder.
A paper clip left a small dent in the caption sheet.

summary: Riley reviewed Sam's shortlist of 5 images, including a shoe-repair shop and florist. They confirmed captions, noted a dent in the caption sheet, and discussed a submission deadline of April 24. A block-number discrepancy (3700 vs 3800) was identified; Sam will verify all captions against the photos. They emphasized consistency in colors and plan to revisit edits on the same screen to ensure captions align with images before submission.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You're still looking at apartment listings?

dialogue.speaker: Jamal
dialogue.text: Yeah, just comparing a couple before I get back to work. The Northgate place didn't make my shortlist.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, what ruled it out?

dialogue.speaker: Jamal
dialogue.text: The commute, mostly. From that apartment I'd need 2 bus transfers to get to work.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oof. Did you check it for a weekday?

dialogue.speaker: Jamal
dialogue.text: I did, yeah. Used a weekday departure time, since that's the trip I'd actually be making. I thought maybe I was reading it wrong, but no.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a lot of chances to miss a connection.

dialogue.speaker: Jamal
dialogue.text: Exactly. The floor plan looked practical, but the trip kind of canceled that out.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Anything else look promising?

dialogue.speaker: Jamal
dialogue.text: Maybe. I've scheduled a viewing for a Roosevelt apartment on April 25.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Nice. Does the listing tell you much about it?

dialogue.speaker: Jamal
dialogue.text: Not a ton. It does show a small entry shelf, which is a nice touch. I'll have a better idea after I see it.

details_in_summary: The new listing shows a small entry shelf.
key_facts: The commute from the apartment he viewed would require two bus transfers.
He has scheduled a Roosevelt apartment viewing for April 25.
minor_details: He checked the trip using a weekday departure time.
The new listing shows a small entry shelf.

summary: Riley discussed apartment options with Jamal. Northgate was dropped due to a long, multi-transfer weekday commute and unreliable connections, despite a practical floor plan. Jamal scheduled a Roosevelt apartment viewing for April 25; listing provides limited details beyond a small entry shelf. Next step: Jamal to evaluate Roosevelt after the viewing and report back.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So, how are things with you?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Pretty good. I took a pottery class over the weekend.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. Was it a whole course?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: No, just a one-off class on Saturday, April 18. 2026 will be remembered as the year I fought a pottery wheel.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Who won?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: The wheel, I think. Here, this is a photo of the cup I made on it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, I see what you mean. That rim's going on a little journey.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Yeah. Uneven is the polite word for it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I kind of like it, though. It has character.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: That's very generous. I had a hard time keeping the clay centered. Every time I thought I had it, it started wobbling again.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you have fun, at least?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: I really did, actually. It was frustrating, but in a good way. I liked getting my hands into it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And probably everything else, too?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: My watch strap had clay on it afterward. I somehow missed that until I got home.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You were saving a little souvenir.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Apparently. The cup still has to be fired, and I'm not sure I'll even recognize it once it's done.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You might recognize the wobble.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: If it keeps that rim, definitely. Oh, I ordered the lentil soup, by the way. I couldn't decide until the last second.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good choice. We can compare it to the cup's shape when it gets here.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, I'm taking my shoes off, if that's all right.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, come in. How did the hatchery visit go?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Pretty well, actually. On April 16, Nikhil Sethi and I got a cleaner stretch of channel water while the intake pump was off.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good. Was it as quiet as you'd hoped?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Quieter, definitely. You could hear the water without that low hum sitting underneath it. But the window went fast.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you get anything besides the water?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, we captured the clatter of a feed dispenser too, from a safe marked position. I want to layer a little of that in deliberately.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So some machinery is allowed in the piece after all.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Some! Just not a pump hum draped over everything. There's a difference, which I can explain in a 40-minute lecture.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'll take your word for it. Did you get over to the outdoor spillway?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: No, the maintenance window ended before we could get to it. That was the one thing we missed.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Was it just too much to fit in?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Pretty much. One microphone stand had a stubborn adjustment knob, too. I spent a ridiculous amount of time persuading it to move.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And I assume you considered 6 different ways to persuade it.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: At least. Also, a staff member lent me a pair of orange ear defenders. Very fetching.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Sounds like a productive day, though.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: It was. Nikhil and I ate cheese sandwiches in the car afterward and sat there for a minute.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A solid end to a day of negotiating with machinery.

details_in_summary: They ate cheese sandwiches in the car afterward.
One microphone stand had a stubborn adjustment knob.

They also captured the clatter of a feed dispenser from a safe marked position.
The maintenance window ended before they could record the outdoor spillway.

They ate cheese sandwiches in the car afterward.

Small setup issues included adjusting a stand and receiving orange ear defenders. They ended with cheese sandwiches in the car.

dialogue.speaker: Elena
dialogue.text: Oh, that's interesting. I've just been looking at the interview results, and there's a pattern already.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What did you find?

dialogue.speaker: Elena
dialogue.text: 3 participants interpreted a missing shipment status as a delay.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh. So they thought the shipment was delayed, rather than noticing there wasn't a status?

dialogue.speaker: Elena
dialogue.text: Right. They treated the absence of a status as information about the shipment.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a pretty different conclusion from 'we don't know.'

dialogue.speaker: Elena
dialogue.text: It is. And since we asked them to identify shipments that needed attention, that distinction matters.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. I was watching for whether they picked a shipment, but not necessarily what they thought the missing status meant.

dialogue.speaker: Elena
dialogue.text: That's the useful part of hearing them explain it. The selection alone can look more straightforward than it is.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Are these still preliminary findings?

dialogue.speaker: Elena
dialogue.text: Yes. I want to go through my notes again before I draw any bigger conclusions.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Makes sense. Oh, the meeting-room window is slightly open. Is that breeze bothering you?

dialogue.speaker: Elena
dialogue.text: No, it's fine. Though I see you've got a folded umbrella beside your chair. A very Seattle morning.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, I wasn't trusting the weather on the way in. Anyway, are you sharing this with the team?

dialogue.speaker: Elena
dialogue.text: I am. I'll share the findings with the team tomorrow, April 23. I'll be clear that they're preliminary.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Great. The missing-status confusion is worth making sure they hear.

key_facts: Three participants interpreted a missing shipment status as a delay.
Elena plans to share the findings with the team on April 23.
minor_details: The meeting-room window is slightly open.
Riley has a folded umbrella beside their chair.

summary: Riley discussed preliminary interview findings with Elena: 3 participants interpreted a missing shipment status as a delay, indicating a misinterpretation of missing data. They noted the distinction between absence of status and unknown status matters for identifying shipments needing attention. Elena plans to re-check notes and share preliminary findings with the team tomorrow, April 23, explicitly labeling them as preliminary.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How are things looking for you in June?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Pretty open, actually. I was looking through a regional guidebook, and it gave me an idea for a day trip to Whidbey Island.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. What did you find?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: The Island County Historical Museum in Coupeville. I thought we could go up and have a look.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'd like that. Could we do a walk while we're there too?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah. Ebey's Landing would be my pick.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Mine too. A museum and a walk sounds like a good day.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but which Saturday works for you? I don't want to just say June and leave it floating there.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How about Saturday, June 6? I'm free that day.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: June 6 works for me too. Let's pick that.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Great. I'll make a note on the back of the grocery list.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Perfect. The grocery list has become our travel department.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It's a very small department. Whidbey, June 6, museum and Ebey's Landing.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Can you put Coupeville next to the museum? Just so we remember where it is.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yep. Island County Historical Museum, Coupeville.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Thanks. I'm glad you like the idea.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Definitely. It'll be nice to spend a day up there with you.

details_in_summary: Riley makes a note on the back of a grocery list.

They want to visit the Island County Historical Museum in Coupeville.
Their preferred walk is at Ebey's Landing.

Riley makes a note on the back of a grocery list.

dialogue.speaker: Gabriel
dialogue.text: I'm still deciding what to order. Everything on this menu sounds good.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm getting the noodles. Oh, did you ever take those apartment negatives in?

dialogue.speaker: Gabriel
dialogue.text: I did, yeah. I took the sleeve to Northlight Photo for scanning.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Nice. All 24 frames?

dialogue.speaker: Gabriel
dialogue.text: The whole sleeve. They expect the files to be ready on April 25.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's Saturday, right? Pretty quick.

dialogue.speaker: Gabriel
dialogue.text: Yeah. I asked for scans at 2400 dpi. It seemed like a reasonable choice.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did they give you anything to keep track of the order?

dialogue.speaker: Gabriel
dialogue.text: The receipt. They put it in a blue envelope, which should make it easy to find. Assuming I don't put it in a box.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Maybe keep it away from the shoebox of ticket stubs.

dialogue.speaker: Gabriel
dialogue.text: Exactly. Actually, wait, I had plenty of time to think about where to put it. My bus was running late on the way home.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Well, at least the negatives are in the right place now.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, I submitted my application to the Cascadia Archive Institute yesterday, April 21.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You did? Daniel, that's great.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. I'm mostly relieved I can't keep adjusting the wording now.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How many times did you look at that statement?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Enough that the words stopped looking like words. Very rigorous process.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And did you get a confirmation?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I did. At first I mistook the confirmation email for a newsletter, so I almost skipped over it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That would've been a very quiet ending to all that proofreading.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. But the email says applicants should hear back by May 15.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay, so now you wait.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Now I wait. Which is somehow less satisfying than pressing submit.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you at least celebrate?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I bought a cinnamon roll. Seemed like the appropriate level of ceremony.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Honestly, after all that wording, you earned it.

details_in_summary: Daniel celebrated by buying a cinnamon roll.

The institute's confirmation email lists May 15 as the date by which applicants should hear back.
minor_details: Daniel celebrated by buying a cinnamon roll.
He initially mistook the confirmation email for a newsletter.

No further action items were identified; the next step is awaiting the response deadline.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: The shorter one seems better, I think. I compared a few walks for Bainbridge, and some of them get us farther from the ferry than we really need to be.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, I'd rather have time to wander than spend the whole day trying to finish a route.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: That's what I thought. I've written the options on the back of an envelope, which is, in theory, an organizational system.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: As long as you can still read it.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Mostly. So, for Saturday, May 16, we could walk from the terminal to Waterfront Park first.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds good. We can hang around there a bit if we feel like it.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Exactly. Then afterward, browse along Winslow Way and find lunch somewhere nearby.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Perfect. A bakery stop would be welcome, too.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes, definitely. We don't have to pick a place now, though. We can just see what looks good.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm happy with that. Is there anything on your envelope that we'd be missing?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Well, there are longer walks, but then we'd be watching the time more. I'd rather leave room to stop wherever looks interesting.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Same. And since we're walking on the Seattle–Bainbridge ferry, we don't have to think about getting a car over.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Right. Ferry, park, Winslow Way, lunch. In whatever pace suits us.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's my kind of route. Enough of a plan that we won't stand at the terminal debating it.

Riley says a bakery stop would be welcome.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How do things stand with the returns exception queue?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: We're just starting to scope it. The idea is a separate queue for returned goods with label problems.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right, returned goods, not outbound deliveries. I want to keep that boundary clear.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Agreed. Otherwise 'exception queue' could mean almost anything. A very efficient way to confuse everyone.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And are we putting missing and damaged labels together?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yes, same queue for items with missing labels and items with damaged labels. We can still identify which problem an item has.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay. I'm going to sketch a first layout on this dot-grid paper.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I'll move my chipped blue mug out of your way. It's already contributed enough character to the meeting.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Thanks. So where do we want to draw the line for this first bit of work?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: What if we focus on getting warehouse staff from identifying the item to inspecting it? Not the whole returns process.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. Start with what they can use to identify it, then make the move to inspection clear.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: And we shouldn't assume a label is readable. For a missing one, there's nothing to read; for a damaged one, there might be something.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good point. I can leave room in the flow for either situation without splitting the queue.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I'll draft the warehouse-facing language while you sketch the flow.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Perfect. Can you make it clear what the person is looking at before asking them to identify it?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yes. I want the language to say what information is available without pretending it's complete.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And then inspection should feel like the next step, not another queue they have to find.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Right. A clear handoff from identification to inspection. Or, sorry, not a handoff between people necessarily—just a clear next step.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Got it. I'll keep the first sketch to that path, with both label conditions entering the same queue.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: And I'll keep the wording focused on that path too. We can start there.

key_facts: The new queue is for returned goods, not outbound deliveries.
Items with missing labels and items with damaged labels will enter the same queue.
Sam will draft the warehouse-facing language while Riley sketches the flow.
minor_details: Sam brings a chipped blue mug to the meeting.
Riley sketches the first layout on dot-grid paper.

summary: Riley discussed establishing a returns exception queue specifically for returned goods with label problems, clarifying that outbound deliveries should remain separate. The initial focus is on guiding warehouse staff from item identification to inspection, not the full process, with clear language and handoff cues. Action: Riley to sketch flow; Sam to draft warehouse-facing wording.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I've organized the photo files and made a Google Drive folder called Morgan Family Photos. I just sent you the link.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, great. I'll try it on my phone.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I gave you editing access through your Google account, so you should be able to get in without requesting anything.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yep, the folder's open. I can see the TIFFs and the JPEGs.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Good. Can you open one, not just see the list? I managed to spend an embarrassing amount of time staring at the sharing settings.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, the JPEG of the picnic's open. And the TIFF opens too.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Excellent. Now, the names are a bit inconsistent. I was thinking, for files where we know the date, start with the year and then a short description.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That makes sense. So the picnic could be '1996 Riverfront Park picnic'?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes, exactly. Easier to browse than a string of numbers and whatever I happened to type that day.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And the school concert could start with 2001. We can leave that person at the edge unnamed until we're sure.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Right. No need to turn a guess into a filename.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What about the ones where we scanned the backs? Could the front and back have the same name, with 'front' or 'back' at the end?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes, that'll keep the pairs together. Oh, I just noticed I put an underscore in the picnic filename by accident. I'll replace it with a space.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I can see the updated name. And for the undated ones, we can just use a short description without a year.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: That works. A year where we know it, and no invented year where we don't. In theory, even I'll be able to find things now.

details_in_summary: Hannah replaces an accidental underscore in one filename.
key_facts: Hannah creates a Google Drive folder called Morgan Family Photos.
She gives Riley editing access through their Google account.
Files with known dates begin with the year, followed by a short description.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Oh, that's worse than I thought.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The noise in the room?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah. In that small meeting room at the Ballard branch, I thought we could talk over it. But the ventilation is audible throughout the whole sample.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It competes with both of our voices. Especially when you ask a question.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but could you make out your answer about the bus stop?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Mostly. I was trying to sound like an interviewee describing an imaginary bus stop, not somebody shouting directions across a street.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: You did fine. The room was less cooperative.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The fan gave the longest answer.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: And it didn't wait for a question. Very efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I didn't realize it was that loud while we were talking.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Me neither. I could hear it, but I thought our voices were clearer than that.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So is that first take useful at all?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: It told me there's a problem, but I'm not going to use it as a model for the project.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That makes sense. People shouldn't have to struggle to hear the words.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Oh, and I brought the folded room-reservation slip home. It's in my bag.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A souvenir of our very chatty meeting room.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How's the turntable situation now?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, I tried those straightforward fixes you suggested. It's better, but not quiet.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What did you try first?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I plugged the turntable, the preamp and the powered speakers into the same power strip. That didn't eliminate the hum.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay. And the ground wire?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Connecting the turntable's ground wire to the preamp reduced the hum, but it didn't stop it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Is it still there before the needle gets to the record?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, just not as loud. I had to get a small screwdriver from my kitchen drawer to connect the wire.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: At least that part helped.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: It did. I also put a folded towel under the turntable while I was checking the connections.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: To keep it from getting scratched?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. And while I was looking at the cables, I noticed split insulation near the right RCA plug.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh. Can you see the wire inside?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I couldn't really tell. It's a little split, and I didn't want to start pulling at it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Probably wise. That cable could be part of the hum, but it's hard to say just by looking.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Right. I spent a while staring at it, which is my preferred method of electrical diagnosis.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Very scientific. You could have someone check the cable before you mess with the plug.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, that sounds better than me making the split bigger with a screwdriver.

details_in_summary: He had put a folded towel under the turntable while checking the connections.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Oh, that's the last one checked. We have 86 photographs in the labeled collection.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: 86? That feels pretty good for one box.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah. And the uncertain dates still say 'approx,' so we're not pretending we know more than we do.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The notes file explains that too, right?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: It does. Okay, but did we check the unidentified folder as well?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, I went through it. Those are labeled without guessing who's in them.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Good. Could you put a backup on the external drive before I send the link to Lian?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Sure. The one with the scratched silver case?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: That's the one. It's not pretty, but it doesn't have to be in the photographs.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: All right, I've copied the folder to the external drive.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: And I've sent Lian a link to the folder. She can see the whole collection now.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Nice. Are the paper duplicates still in their sleeve?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yep. I've closed the photo box with a length of cotton ribbon. I think we're finished.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So, how do things stand with the dog you were considering?

dialogue.speaker: Tessa
dialogue.text: I'm still considering him. His name's Pippin. He's a small adult rescue dog.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What's making you hesitate?

dialogue.speaker: Tessa
dialogue.text: Mostly the walks. I have 2 library shifts a week that start at 8:30 a.m., and I want to be sure I can manage his schedule around those.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Could you walk him before you leave?

dialogue.speaker: Tessa
dialogue.text: Maybe. I'm also looking into a paid dog walker for those early-shift days. I'm comparing the cost with what I could reasonably do myself.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds sensible. Do you know how much walking he needs?

dialogue.speaker: Tessa
dialogue.text: Not enough to make a decision yet. I've got a folded shelter printout in my bag, but I need to ask them more about his routine.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You came prepared.

dialogue.speaker: Tessa
dialogue.text: I did. Actually, wait, I also ordered my coffee with oat milk. That's the full extent of my preparation.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Both important. Would the walker come in the morning?

dialogue.speaker: Tessa
dialogue.text: That's one option I'm looking at. I don't want to commit to Pippin until I know I can give him a decent routine, not just hope the bus and the dog cooperate.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, worth figuring out before you decide.

key_facts: The dog is named Pippin and is a small adult.
Tessa has two library shifts a week that start at 8:30 a.m.
She's looking into a paid dog walker for those early-shift days.
minor_details: Tessa orders her coffee with oat milk.
She has a folded shelter printout in her bag.

summary: Riley discussed Tessa’s consideration of adopting Pippin, a small adult rescue dog. The main concern is managing daily walks around two 8:30 a.m. library shifts. Tessa is weighing walking the dog herself vs hiring a paid walker, and plans to confirm Pippin’s routine with the shelter. Riley noted the need to determine a feasible morning schedule before deciding and suggested comparing costs and options for a morning walker as next steps.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: I keep meaning to look through that old box for stuff from the college radio show.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The one we used to listen to when we were roommates at the University of Washington?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Yeah, that one. I think I might've taped some of it, but I can't remember what I kept.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I remember the show, but I have no idea what you might still have from it.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: It's probably in the cardboard box in the hall closet at my Fremont duplex, if it's anywhere.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Is that the box with the receipt on it?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Yeah, the old receipt's still taped to the lid. Apparently that was important to me at some point.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Or you just didn't want to throw it away.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: That's a pretty safe guess. I sort things professionally and then come home and do the opposite.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So are you going to look today?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Not today. I'll check for the show the next time I sort through the box.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Fair enough. Your iced coffee's probably a better use of lunch anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: It is. The box has waited this long; it can wait a little longer.

details_in_summary: An old receipt is taped to the box's lid.
key_facts: Marcus plans to check a cardboard box in the hall closet of his Fremont duplex.
The recordings are from a radio show he and Riley listened to while rooming together at the University of Washington.
He intends to look the next time he sorts through the box.
minor_details: Marcus is drinking an iced coffee.
An old receipt is taped to the box's lid.

summary: Riley and Marcus discussed locating old college radio show tapes. They recall the box is in the hall closet at Marcus’s Fremont duplex, with an old receipt taped to the lid. Marcus indicated he would check for the show the next time he sorts the box (not today). No immediate retrieval; box waiting for later sorting.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. How's your afternoon going? We made it past lunch, at least.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, Sam. Not bad. I'm still waking up from that design review.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah, it had a lot of slides for a meeting about making things simpler.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How's the Victoria planning going?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Good. I booked a table for 2 at a restaurant near the Inner Harbour for Saturday dinner.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Nice. So Ada doesn't have to cook that evening.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. And we're still cooking that vegetable pasta together at her place on Sunday.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you find something you want on the restaurant menu?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: There's a mushroom dish that caught my eye. I also requested a table away from the door. Less of a breeze, hopefully.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good call. Are you walking back afterward?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Maybe. Ada and I agreed we'll take a taxi after dinner if we don't feel like walking. A very sophisticated transportation plan.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The best kind: you don't have to decide until you're done eating.

details_in_summary: Sam requested a table away from the door.
key_facts: Sam booked a table for two at a restaurant near the Inner Harbour for Saturday dinner.
Sam and Ada plan to take a taxi after dinner if they don't feel like walking.
minor_details: The restaurant's menu includes a mushroom dish that caught Sam's eye.
Sam requested a table away from the door.

summary: Riley and Sam discussed progress on Victoria planning and a design review. Sam booked a table for two near the Inner Harbour for Saturday dinner, with a table away from the door. Ada won’t cook Saturday; Sunday will be vegetable pasta at Ada’s place. Sam showed interest in a mushroom dish, and they may take a taxi home after dinner if they don’t want to walk.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How are things standing with the island trip?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, we have the ferry reservations now, but not quite the ones we wanted.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What happened?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: There wasn't a vehicle reservation available for the Friday morning sailing we wanted from Anacortes. That's June 19.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, bummer. Did you find another one?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. Ben and I reserved a late-afternoon sailing on Friday, June 19, and a midday return on Monday, June 22, for Ben's car.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So you still get the car over, just a later start.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Exactly. We'll have less time there that first day, but it seemed like the simplest compromise.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Was it a whole ordeal to book?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I had the reservation page open on my laptop through lunch. I was comparing options like the ferry was going to award me a degree.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Ah, the old elective in Advanced Ferry.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I would've taken that instead of making a decision, yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Does the later crossing mess with the guesthouse?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: No, we've still got the Friday Harbor guesthouse for the 3 nights. And Ben suggested bringing a deck of cards for the crossing.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds good. A little less island time, but at least the crossing's sorted.

details_in_summary: Ben suggested bringing a deck of cards for the crossing.
key_facts: No vehicle reservation was available for their preferred Friday morning sailing from Anacortes.
They reserve a late-afternoon Friday sailing and a midday Monday return for Ben's car.
minor_details: Daniel had the reservation page open on his laptop through lunch.
Ben suggested bringing a deck of cards for the crossing.

summary: Riley discussed the island trip logistics with Daniel. They secured ferry reservations but missed the Friday morning vehicle slot from Anacortes on June 19, opting for a late-afternoon crossing and a midday June 22 return for Ben's car. The Friday Harbor guesthouse remains booked for 3 nights. They plan to accommodate less island time and consider bringing a deck of cards for the crossing; no further actions were defined beyond keeping the bookings.

dialogue.speaker: Yuki
dialogue.text: Oh! I just realized I never told you what happened with that garden bed.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The corner at Canal Street? Inez had suggested you take it over, right?

dialogue.speaker: Yuki
dialogue.text: Yeah. I asked the garden group first, like I said I would, and they approved me taking it over on March 19.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice! Have you done anything with it yet?

dialogue.speaker: Yuki
dialogue.text: I have. I cleared the bed on April 16, and I sowed radishes in it that same day.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You got straight to planting, then.

dialogue.speaker: Yuki
dialogue.text: Once it was clear, yes. I had a borrowed hand fork, which was just about the right size for it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Was it a lot of work?

dialogue.speaker: Yuki
dialogue.text: Not too bad. It's a small corner, so I could get through it without feeling like I'd taken on an entire farm.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And why radishes?

dialogue.speaker: Yuki
dialogue.text: They seemed fairly straightforward. In theory.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a very reassuring endorsement.

dialogue.speaker: Yuki
dialogue.text: I'm trying not to oversell my expertise.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Fair. What kind of seeds did you get?

dialogue.speaker: Yuki
dialogue.text: I don't remember the variety. The packet had a red stripe across the top, though. That's apparently the detail my brain kept.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The important botanical information.

dialogue.speaker: Yuki
dialogue.text: Exactly. Red stripe, radishes. I can be precise about 2 things.

details_in_summary: Yuki used a borrowed hand fork.
The seed packet had a red stripe across the top.
key_facts: The garden group approved Yuki taking over the bed on March 19.
Yuki cleared the bed on April 16.
Yuki sowed radishes in the cleared bed on April 16.
minor_details: Yuki used a borrowed hand fork.
The seed packet had a red stripe across the top.

summary: Riley discussed Yuki taking over the Canal Street garden bed after approval on March 19. Yuki cleared the bed on April 16 and sowed radishes the same day using a borrowed hand fork. She described the task as manageable due to the small space. When asked about seed varieties, Yuki only recalled a red-striped seed packet and noted realism about her expertise, without overstatement.

dialogue.speaker: Jamal
dialogue.text: Morning, Riley. Coffee's doing its job today, more or less.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Morning. How did the Roosevelt viewing go on Saturday?

dialogue.speaker: Jamal
dialogue.text: Pretty well, actually. The layout makes sense to me, and I'm getting an application together.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. What did you like about the layout?

dialogue.speaker: Jamal
dialogue.text: It just felt practical. The living room has a broad windowsill, too. Not exactly a requirement, but I liked it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A good windowsill is a bonus. Is there laundry?

dialogue.speaker: Jamal
dialogue.text: Yeah, there's laundry in the building. That's one less thing to work around.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And you're going to apply?

dialogue.speaker: Jamal
dialogue.text: That's the plan. The property manager asked for some documents, so I'm gathering those now. The application requires recent pay stubs.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: When are you hoping to send it in?

dialogue.speaker: Jamal
dialogue.text: May 1. I want to get everything together first, make sure I'm not missing anything.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Fair. Anything else catch your eye while you were there?

dialogue.speaker: Jamal
dialogue.text: There was a cork noticeboard beside the mailboxes. Not a reason to pick an apartment, obviously, but I noticed it. Anyway, the layout's good and the laundry's there, so, fair enough.

details_in_summary: The living room has a broad windowsill.
He noticed a cork noticeboard beside the mailboxes.
key_facts: The apartment has laundry in the building.
Jamal plans to submit the application on May 1.
The application requires recent pay stubs.
minor_details: The living room has a broad windowsill.
He noticed a cork noticeboard beside the mailboxes.

summary: Riley discussed Jamal Carter’s Roosevelt viewing, noting the layout as practical and the living room windowsill. Jamal confirmed laundry is available in the building and that he plans to apply, gathering required documents such as recent pay stubs and aiming to submit by May 1. Riley mentioned a cork noticeboard near the mailboxes as a minor observation. No other major issues were identified.

dialogue.speaker: Arjun
dialogue.text: The awkward bit is, I keep switching between my laptop and looking out at the street. So I ordered my first pair of progressives today, April 29.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. You're hoping they'll work for both?

dialogue.speaker: Arjun
dialogue.text: Yeah. Laptop distance and, you know, the street farther away. That's the idea.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What kind of frame did you choose?

dialogue.speaker: Arjun
dialogue.text: Dark brown. Fairly plain, which seemed right for something I'll be looking through all day.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A sensible interface choice.

dialogue.speaker: Arjun
dialogue.text: Exactly. No unnecessary animations.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So are the different distances all in the same lenses?

dialogue.speaker: Arjun
dialogue.text: Right, the prescription changes gradually through the lenses. You look through different parts depending on the distance.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds handy for working by a window.

dialogue.speaker: Arjun
dialogue.text: Yeah, I like being able to look up from the screen and see what's happening outside.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And you managed to pick a frame without asking me for a design review?

dialogue.speaker: Arjun
dialogue.text: I know, reckless. Anyway, this tomato sandwich at Larch Cafe is pretty good.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It does look good. Mine's got me thinking I should've ordered that.

details_in_summary: Arjun has a tomato sandwich at Larch Cafe.
He chose a dark brown frame.
key_facts: Arjun ordered his first progressive glasses on 29 April.
He hopes to use them for both laptop work and distance vision.
minor_details: Arjun has a tomato sandwich at Larch Cafe.
He chose a dark brown frame.

summary: Riley noted Arjun ordered progressive lenses for laptop and street distances, with a dark brown, plain frame and no animations. Arjun explained the progressive design covers multiple distances within one lens. Riley commented on potential window-view usefulness and teased the design-review joke. Arjun mentioned a tomato sandwich at Larch Cafe, and Riley considered ordering it.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, I've started putting the hatchery soundscape in order.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How's it coming together?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I'm building it around an arrival, then a walk alongside the channels, and a return outdoors. Just enough of a path that it feels like you're moving through the place.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And are you using the quieter water from when the pump was off?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, that's giving me room to work. But I'm leaving some machinery audible too. Otherwise it starts to sound unnaturally tranquil, like the hatchery is a spa.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A spa with a feed dispenser. Very exclusive.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Exactly. The dispenser might come in briefly, but I don't want it to take over. I've chosen a short valve click as a transition between sections.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. Just a little cue that you're moving somewhere else?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: That's the idea. My editing notes have blue sticky tabs all over them now. I spent a while deciding which notes deserved tabs, which is a perfectly normal use of time.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You did take a break, though, right?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I did. I went to the corner shop and bought a pear. Then I came back and reconsidered the tabs.

details_in_summary: His editing notes use blue sticky tabs.
He took a break to buy a pear at the corner shop.
key_facts: Daniel is building the piece around an arrival, a walk alongside the channels, and a return outdoors.
He has chosen a short valve click as a transition between sections.
minor_details: His editing notes use blue sticky tabs.
He took a break to buy a pear at the corner shop.

summary: Riley and Daniel discussed progress on the hatchery soundscape, planned around an arrival, a walk along channels, and a return outdoors. They decided to use quieter pump-water and keep some machinery audible to avoid an overly tranquil effect, with a short valve click as a transition cue. Daniel noted extensive editing notes marked with blue tabs. Next steps include finalizing the transition cue, balancing sounds, and continuing tab-driven edits; Daniel took a break to buy a pear before reconsidering the tabs.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How's the Tacoma photo display looking now? Is it up?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: It is. Marisol and I installed it on April 20, before the branch opened.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. Did the 2 rows of 3 work out?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: They did. The bigger prints have enough room around them, which was the whole point of cutting back to 6.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And did the mounting strips behave?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: They did, thank goodness. The overnight test was reassuring, but I still wasn't entirely convinced.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What about the captions? You were trying to keep them short.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I carried the finished captions in a manila folder, feeling very organized. Then Daphne saw them on the wall and asked us to raise the lettering size.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Ah. They were readable up close, but not from where people stood?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Exactly. On a table they seemed fine. On the wall, not so much.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Was it a pain to change them?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Not too bad. We made the lettering larger, and they're much easier to read now. In theory, I'd have thought of that myself.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Well, that's what seeing it on the wall is for. Have people been stopping?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes. I overheard 1 visitor stop and point out a familiar street to a companion. They were looking at it together for a while.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's lovely. That's the kind of thing you were hoping for, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: It is. I wanted the everyday Tacoma pictures to give people something they could recognize, not just dates to read.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And now they can actually read the dates too.

key_facts: Hannah and Marisol installed the display on April 20.
Daphne asked them to raise the caption lettering size after seeing it on the wall.
One visitor stopped to point out a familiar street to a companion.
minor_details: Hannah carried the finished captions in a manila folder.
The installation took place before the branch opened.

summary: Riley discussed the Tacoma photo display: installed April 20 before the branch opened. The 2x3 layout with six prints works, and mounting strips passed an overnight test. Captions were initially too small on the wall; after Daphne and feedback, lettering was enlarged and now reads more easily. A visitor paused to view a familiar street, indicating the goal of recognizable, everyday Tacoma images is being met. Dates are readable now, fulfilling the intended effect.

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: It's turning again. Sound Bench replaced the worn drive belt.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. So that was the problem?

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: Yeah. The belt had worn out. They replaced it, and the deck seems happy enough now.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How much did it end up costing? You had that estimate for about $90.

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: I paid $78 for the completed repair. Less than the estimate, which was a pleasant surprise.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Definitely. You can finally hear those tapes again.

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: That's the hope. Do you want to pick one? I've got pear slices on this small plate, by the way.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Thanks. How about this one? It's labelled 'Rainy Bus Rides.'

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: Oh, yes. Let's see if it remembers how to do its job.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Should I move that blue mug with the chipped handle? It's right beside the deck.

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: Please. I'd rather not introduce pear juice or tea to the mechanism.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay, here goes. Oh, there it is.

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: It sounds steady, doesn't it? Before, it wouldn't turn at all.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. Let's give it the whole first song.

dialogue.speaker: Amara
dialogue.text: There. It played through the first song without slowing down. I think that's a reasonably good test.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'd say so. And it's evening already. I'm glad we got it playing.

details_in_summary: A blue mug with a chipped handle sits beside the deck.
key_facts: Sound Bench replaced the deck's worn drive belt.
Amara paid $78 for the completed repair.
They test a tape labelled 'Rainy Bus Rides,' and it plays through the first song without slowing down.
minor_details: Amara serves pear slices on a small plate.
A blue mug with a chipped handle sits beside the deck.

summary: Riley and Amara confirmed a worn drive belt on Sound Bench was replaced; repair cost $78, under the $90 estimate. They tested playback with a cassette labelled 'Rainy Bus Rides,' noting the deck now runs steadily. Actions: move the chipped blue mug away to prevent spills, avoid liquid exposure to the mechanism, and run through the first song to verify performance.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Training's feeling more manageable. I did 8 miles on April 26, and I felt steadier afterward.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good. Especially after that 7-mile run wiped you out.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. Easing back was the right call. I wasn't trying to prove anything to the pavement this time.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did the run itself feel better too?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: It did. I noticed a row of tulips near the turnaround point, which probably means I had enough attention left to notice things.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a pretty good sign. Is the next long run still on Saturday?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I moved the 9-mile run from Saturday to Sunday, May 3, to make room for plans with Leila.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So you're giving up the open Sunday this once?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah, just shifting things around. What if the beginner plan can survive one Sunday run? I suspect it can.

key_facts: Sam completed eight miles on April 26 and felt steadier afterward.
Sam has moved the next nine-mile run from Saturday to Sunday, May 3, to make room for plans with Leila.
minor_details: Sam noticed a row of tulips near the turnaround point.

summary: Riley and Sam discussed training progress, noting 8 miles on April 26 with steadier performance after easing back from a 7-mile setback. Sam observed improved focus, evidenced by noticing tulips. The next long run was moved from Saturday to Sunday, May 3, to accommodate plans with Leila, with Riley considering whether the beginner plan can handle one Sunday run.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How are we looking for slug protection at the garden?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Why, did you see slugs in the bed?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: No, but several pea shoots have appeared, and I spotted a snail on the outside of the gate.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but the snail wasn't actually in bed 7?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: No, it was just outside the gate. Still, I'd rather not wait until something finds the peas.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Fair. And how do the chard starts look?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: They're still there. I didn't see any obvious damage.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I'll put copper tape around the bed's wooden edge. That should give the young plants some protection from slugs.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good. We can check whether it's staying attached, too.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah. A very small fence for very slow intruders.

details_in_summary: Riley spotted a snail on the outside of the gate.
key_facts: Several pea shoots have appeared.
Maya will put copper tape around the bed’s wooden edge.
minor_details: Riley spotted a snail on the outside of the gate.

summary: Riley noted pea shoots and a snail outside the gate, not in bed 7. Chard starts appear undamaged. Decision: apply copper tape around the garden bed’s wooden edge to deter slugs and protect young plants. Action items: install copper tape and verify it remains attached; monitor slug activity and plant protection.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Oh, that's tempting. I just spotted a narrow bookcase at a neighborhood porch sale here in Tacoma.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh yeah? Are you thinking of getting it?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Maybe. It's painted pale blue, and they're asking $35. I'm just not sure it's worth the trouble of getting it home.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How big is it?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: It's 24 inches wide. Narrow enough that, in theory, I have a place for it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: In theory sounds a little uncertain.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Well, I haven't measured that space. I keep looking at it and thinking, surely that's about 2 feet. Very scientific.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'd measure the space before you decide. If it's too tight, that answers the question for you.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yeah, and if it isn't, I still have to work out how to get the thing home.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right, but at least you'd know whether it was worth thinking about.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Fair. I'll measure first. I can compare transportation problems after that.

details_in_summary: The asking price is $35.
The bookcase is painted pale blue.
key_facts: The porch sale is in Tacoma.
The bookcase is 24 inches wide.
minor_details: The asking price is $35.
The bookcase is painted pale blue.

summary: Riley and Hannah discussed a pale blue bookcase for sale in Tacoma, priced at $35 and 24 inches wide. They evaluated fit and transport challenges, with Riley urging measurement of the space to determine viability. The decision is to measure first and then assess transportation logistics if it seems worth pursuing.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. Is it lunchtime already? Friday took its time getting here.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It really did. Want to look at the draft at the standing table?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. I've got an early attempt at naming the identification step for the returns queue.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Is that the phrase you've highlighted in orange?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: It is. My first proposed status is 'Needs identification.' Not exactly poetry, but that might be a feature.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It's clear about what needs to happen. I wonder if people will know which return they're looking at, though.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Right. Especially with missing and damaged labels going into the same queue. The status doesn't distinguish them.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What if we show the return reference beside the status when one is available?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I like that. Though 'Needs identification' next to a reference might make someone think we already identified it. Or maybe not.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Let's test the wording with warehouse staff instead of settling it here.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Agreed. We can see what they think needs identifying, with and without the reference.

key_facts: Sam's first proposed status is “Needs identification.”
Riley suggests showing the return reference beside the status when one is available.
minor_details: They review the draft at a standing table.
Sam has highlighted one phrase in orange.

summary: Riley and Sam discussed naming the identification step for the returns queue. Sam proposed status 'Needs identification,' but noted it may be unclear for missing/damaged labels. They considered showing the return reference beside the status to aid identification. Riley suggested testing wording with warehouse staff rather than deciding now. Action: test wording with and without the reference among warehouse staff to determine clarity.

dialogue.speaker: Jonas
dialogue.text: How's your back been since we talked about noticing when you get tired at the gym?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Sore, actually. I stayed longer than usual at my April 24 session, about 90 minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Jonas
dialogue.text: When did you first notice the soreness?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The next day, April 25. It's been sore all week, right through today, May 1.

dialogue.speaker: Jonas
dialogue.text: Is it in the same lower-back area you've mentioned before?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, same area. I kept thinking it'd settle down, but it's still there.

dialogue.speaker: Jonas
dialogue.text: And during that 90-minute session, did you notice the descent getting less controlled?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, toward the end. I don't know exactly when it started, though. I wasn't keeping a very close eye on the time.

dialogue.speaker: Jonas
dialogue.text: That's all right. The 90 minutes gives us something to work with. I'd suggest taking a break from climbing until the soreness settles.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay. I was wondering if I should just do a shorter session, but a break makes sense.

dialogue.speaker: Jonas
dialogue.text: And you don't need to make up the missed climbing afterward. Once things have settled, we can look at a shorter visit and see how your back responds.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good. I can get into that mindset of, 'Well, I missed a day, so I should stay longer.'

dialogue.speaker: Jonas
dialogue.text: Your back may not appreciate the accounting. Let's see what a break does first.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Fair enough. I even packed an orange in my gym bag that day, like I was preparing for a whole expedition.

dialogue.speaker: Jonas
dialogue.text: A sensible snack, at least. Was there anything else about that session you think might be useful to note?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Nothing else I'm sure about. Oh, and there was a delivery truck blocking the clinic's usual loading space when I got here. I had to go around it.

dialogue.speaker: Jonas
dialogue.text: Thanks for telling me. So for now, take the break, and pay attention to whether the soreness settles. We can work out the climbing length from there.

details_in_summary: Riley had packed an orange in their gym bag that day.
key_facts: Riley's April 24 climbing session lasted about 90 minutes.
Their lower back became sore the following day and remained sore through May 1.
Jonas suggests taking a break from climbing until the soreness settles.
minor_details: Riley had packed an orange in their gym bag that day.
A delivery truck was blocking the clinic's usual loading space.

summary: Riley discussed persistent lower-back soreness after a 90-minute gym session on April 24, with onset the next day and ongoing through May 1. The descent during the session was less controlled toward the end. Jonas advised taking a break from climbing until the soreness settles, with no requirement to make up the session and to reassess shorter visits afterward. Riley noted a possible distraction from a delivery truck and an orange snack as ancillary details.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How are the herbs looking?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: The parsley soil is crumbly and dry. Did you check it this week?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: No, I thought you were checking it. I figured you'd tell me if it needed water.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Oh. I thought you were checking it, especially since we moved it to the brighter east corner.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Well, we were both very confident in each other. I'll water it now.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but let's divide up the checks so the pots don't get forgotten again. Would Mondays and Thursdays work for you?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, I'll check the pots on Mondays and Thursdays. Can you take Saturdays?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I can. I'll check them on Saturdays. That gives us a reasonably well-staffed parsley department.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And we'll check the chives and mint at the same time, not just the parsley?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Right, all the pots. I'm setting a Saturday reminder with a little leaf icon.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Perfect. I'll put my Monday and Thursday checks in too.

details_in_summary: Maya sets a reminder with a little leaf icon.
key_facts: The parsley soil is crumbly and dry after both assumed the other was checking it.
Riley will check the pots on Mondays and Thursdays, and Maya will check them on Saturdays.
minor_details: Maya sets a reminder with a little leaf icon.

summary: Riley discussed herb care with Maya. The parsley soil was dry; Riley will water it now. They agreed to split checks: Riley on Mondays and Thursdays, Maya on Saturdays, to prevent missed pots. They will also check chives and mint during each round. Maya will set a Saturday reminder with a leaf icon; Riley will add Monday/Thursday reminders. All pots will be checked.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How are things standing with the Astoria trip?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Pretty good. I've been checking the bits between the stations and the hotel, because apparently buying the tickets wasn't enough for my brain.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Fair. Did you figure out where you catch the bus in Portland?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes. I confirmed the outbound POINT bus picks up at Portland Union Station, so we don't have to get ourselves to another stop after the train.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good. And you gave yourselves some time between them, right?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: That's the idea, yes. I wanted room for the train to be delayed, not a dramatic sprint to the bus.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What about once you get to Astoria?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I'm expecting we'll walk from the Astoria Transit Center to Hotel Elliott. I checked the walking route using street view.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Does it look straightforward?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Mostly. There's a steep-looking block near the hotel, though. Hard to tell quite how steep from a picture.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Could be a fun surprise with luggage.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Exactly. Owen and I decided on 1 backpack each. No wheeling a suitcase uphill, in theory.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds manageable, even if it rains.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I think so. And if that block turns out to be a hill in disguise, at least we'll have both hands free.

details_in_summary: She notices a steep-looking block near the hotel.
key_facts: Hannah confirms that the outbound bus picks up at Portland Union Station.
She expects to walk from the Astoria Transit Center to the hotel.
Hannah and Owen plan to take one backpack each.
minor_details: Hannah checks the walking route using street view.
She notices a steep-looking block near the hotel.

summary: Riley and Hannah reviewed the Astoria trip logistics. They confirmed the outbound POINT bus picks up at Portland Union Station and planned a time buffer between train arrival and bus departure. They assessed the walk from Astoria Transit Center to Hotel Elliott and noted a potentially steep block near the hotel. They agreed on taking one backpack each and avoiding suitcases, aiming for hands-free travel, and preparing for possibly rainy conditions.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: This bench has a chipped green slat right where I'm sitting.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, we picked the premium seating. At least it's nice out here.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Have you managed to stop thinking about the certificate application?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Not entirely. I'm waiting to hear by May 15, and meanwhile I'm trying to picture what my weeks would look like if I got in.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: With the Tuesday class and the assignments?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. The class is 6:30 to 8:30, and they estimate another 6 to 8 hours a week for assignments. That's not just a little gap I can fill.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What do you already have on your calendar for the fall?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I've got that recurring monthly exhibit-audio update contract. It takes up space, even if it's not every week.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Then maybe make room for the course before you accept more fall work, instead of assuming you'll find spare time later.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Right. I keep thinking I can just move things around, but I haven't actually left anything to move them into.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You don't have an answer yet, though. What would holding some room look like now?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I think I'll hold off on taking any new multi-day installation work for September until I have an answer. I can look at the calendar again once I know.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds easier than promising those days and trying to squeeze the course in afterward.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. Look at me, making a decision before comparing 14 versions of the same calendar. Oh, I packed an apple and forgot to eat it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You can save it for later. You've already made your 1 decision for the afternoon.

details_in_summary: They talk on a bench with a chipped green slat.
key_facts: Daniel's current freelance calendar already includes a recurring monthly exhibit-audio update contract.
