dialogue.text: That's the weakness in the system, yes. I'm thinking of hanging the calendar beside the kitchen door.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That'd be a nice spot for it. Do you want the captions to be really detailed?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I don't think so. Just enough that we know who or what we're looking at. I don't want a paragraph under each photo.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Fair. And if we're not sure about something, we can leave it out.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Exactly. Thanks for being willing to help, especially this late in the evening.

details_in_summary: Hannah is thinking of hanging it beside the kitchen door.
She has been making notes on the back of an envelope.
key_facts: Hannah is making the calendar for 2027.
She plans to use some of the photographs she and Riley sorted earlier.
minor_details: Hannah is thinking of hanging it beside the kitchen door.
She has been making notes on the back of an envelope.

summary: Riley discussed collaborating with Hannah to create a 2027 family photo calendar, selecting photos for each month and writing brief captions. They will verify identities, review captions, and leave uncertain items out. Riley acknowledged Hannah’s envelope-note organizational system and warned against discarding the envelope. They plan to hang the calendar beside the kitchen door. Action items: help choose pictures and captions, confirm who/what is in each photo, and keep the envelope for reference.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Oh, good, our neighboring gardener agreed to check bed 7 on June 24 while we're away.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a relief. Especially with that far end drying out faster.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but we should leave a note about how to check it. The surface might look dry even when the soil underneath isn't.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right. Just a finger in the soil, like we've been doing?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah. I've written it on an orange index card. I'll leave it for the gardener, asking them to water deeply if the soil is dry below the surface.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Could you put the hose hours on there too? Before 9 a.m. or after 6 p.m.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Good idea. Nothing like a watering schedule with office hours.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And maybe mention the straw, so they know why it's there.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Sure. I'll say we left the carrot row clear of it, too.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Perfect. I'm glad someone can take a look on Wednesday.

details_in_summary: The note is written on an orange index card.
key_facts: A neighboring gardener agrees to check their bed on June 24.
Maya will leave a note asking the gardener to water deeply if the soil is dry below the surface.
minor_details: The note is written on an orange index card.

summary: Riley discussed arranging a neighbor gardener to check bed 7 on June 24 while away. They will leave an orange index card with soil-moisture checks (finger test) and instructions to water deeply if dry below the surface. They will add hose hours (before 9 a.m. or after 6 p.m.), note the straw, and indicate the carrot row is clear. Action items: Maya to place the note and details; gardener to check on Wednesday.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: My reading lamp's started flickering, and I can't tell if the bulb's just wearing out.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The one by your chair?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yeah, beside my reading chair in the Tacoma apartment. The one with the cream-colored shade.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: When did you notice it?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I was reading a mystery novel, and the light kept flickering. At first I thought I was imagining it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What kind of bulb is in it?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: It's a 60-watt-equivalent LED. I thought those were supposed to last ages, but I suppose they don't last forever.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: No, they don't. Did you try another outlet?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I did. I moved the lamp to another outlet, and it still flickered.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay, so maybe try a different bulb and see if that changes anything.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: That's what I was thinking. I was looking at the options and somehow managed to make choosing a bulb feel complicated.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You could just look for another 60-watt-equivalent LED.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Right. In theory, I can handle that. I'll unplug the lamp before I swap it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good. Hopefully it's just the bulb.

key_facts: The lamp is beside Hannah's reading chair in the Tacoma apartment.
The current bulb is a 60-watt-equivalent LED.
The flicker persists when Hannah moves the lamp to another outlet.
minor_details: Hannah noticed it while reading a mystery novel.
The lamp has a cream-colored shade.

summary: Riley and Hannah discussed a flickering lamp in the Tacoma apartment. The 60-watt-equivalent LED bulb was suspected; outlets were tested with no fix. Riley suggested trying a different bulb and unplugging before swapping. Hannah planned to look for another 60W-equivalent LED and proceed with unplugging prior to replacement. Next steps: replace bulb and retest to determine if the issue is bulb- or socket-related.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: This one's hibiscus tea. I steeped it for 3 minutes and added strawberries.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a big change from the black tea and lemon.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. After the 6-minute steep last time, I thought I'd try a shorter one.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And I called that one a little bitter. Okay, let me try this.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I brought 2 mismatched cups, by the way. The office collection is apparently very eclectic.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I don't mind. Oh, the paper label on your bottle has curled at one corner.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: It has, hasn't it? I'll need to find a better way to stick it on.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay, I like the hibiscus, but the strawberry flavor is too faint.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah, I get a little of it at the end, but not much. Or maybe that's just because I know it's there.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I might not have guessed strawberry if you hadn't told me.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: What if I used more strawberries? Although, hmm, that might not be the only thing to change.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, the tea itself is pretty strong. Not bitter, though.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: That's something. Still, I don't think I'll repeat this batch. I'll keep experimenting.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm happy to taste another one. Once I finish closing out this file, anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Fair. I'll put the bottle away and let you finish up. Thanks for judging.

details_in_summary: Sam brought two mismatched cups.
A paper label on the bottle has curled at one corner.
key_facts: Sam steeped hibiscus tea for three minutes and added strawberries.
Riley says the strawberry flavor is too faint.
minor_details: Sam brought two mismatched cups.
A paper label on the bottle has curled at one corner.

summary: Riley and Sam discussed a hibiscus tea batch: 3-minute steep with added strawberries, contrasting with prior black tea and lemon (6-minute steep). They noted the strawberry flavor was faint, the tea was strong but not bitter, and addressed mismatched cups and a curling bottle label. Sam plans further experimentation and likely won’t repeat this batch; Riley offered to taste another after finishing a file.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: I'm sitting at the kitchen table with my noodle recipe. Is this a good time?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, of course. What are you making?

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: Cold sesame noodles for a small lunch. My recipe serves 2, but I need enough for 6. I thought I'd check the numbers with you.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Sure. For 6, we just multiply everything by 3. What does the original use?

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: For 2 servings, it's 6 ounces of dry noodles, 2 tablespoons of sesame paste, 1 tablespoon of soy sauce and 1 teaspoon of rice vinegar.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay, so for 6 servings that's 18 ounces of dry noodles and 6 tablespoons of sesame paste.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: 18 ounces and 6 tablespoons. I'm writing this on the back of an envelope. And the soy sauce would be 3 tablespoons?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's right, and 3 teaspoons of rice vinegar.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: Got it. I'll scatter toasted sesame seeds over the noodles, too. No measuring those, I think.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Sounds good. The envelope can handle a little mystery.

details_in_summary: She plans to scatter toasted sesame seeds over the noodles.
key_facts: Lian's two-serving recipe uses 6 ounces of dry noodles, 2 tablespoons of sesame paste, 1 tablespoon of soy sauce and 1 teaspoon of rice vinegar.
For six servings, they write down 18 ounces of dry noodles, 6 tablespoons of sesame paste, 3 tablespoons of soy sauce and 3 teaspoons of rice vinegar.
minor_details: Lian writes the amounts on the back of an envelope.
She plans to scatter toasted sesame seeds over the noodles.

summary: Riley and Lian reviewed scaling a cold sesame noodle recipe from 2 to 6 servings. They confirmed multiplying ingredients by 3: 18 oz dry noodles, 6 tbsp sesame paste, 3 tbsp soy sauce, and 3 tsp rice vinegar. Lian will scatter toasted sesame seeds as garnish, with no precise measurement. Riley noted the envelope can accommodate the notes and confirmed the final quantities.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Morning, Riley. How's your morning going?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Pretty good, thanks. How's yours?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Not bad. My tea's gone lukewarm already, though. Ready to look at the filter?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. I've marked the relevant screen with a blue sticky note. So, this is the shipment list with a filter selected.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: And what happens when someone opens a shipment?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: They can open it, then come back to the list, and the selected filter stays in place as long as they're in the same browser tab.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: All right. So they don't have to select it again when they come back.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right. That's the small fix I wanted to explore after we talked about the filter disappearing.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Does the proposal cover a different browser tab?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: No, I'm just proposing we preserve it in the same tab.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: That feels clear and contained. It's ready to take into sprint planning. All right, so we have a plan.

key_facts: The proposed behavior keeps the selected filter when the user returns to the list in the same browser tab.
Priya agrees the proposal is ready to take into sprint planning.
minor_details: Riley has marked the relevant screen with a blue sticky note.
Priya's tea has gone lukewarm.

summary: Riley noted that the shipment list filter should persist when opening a shipment and returning, within the same browser tab. They confirmed the filter does not need to persist across tabs. Priya approved the approach and it is ready for sprint planning. Action: implement the small fix to preserve the filter in the same tab.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. How's your lunch break going?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey! Pretty good. It's nice to step away for a bit. How's yours?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Good, thanks. I've been looking at printing options for that 2027 family calendar.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, did you find one you like?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I compared a few, and I think I'm going with an 8.5-by-11-inch wall calendar. It should fit the space in the apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds like a good size. Are the date boxes big enough to write in?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I think so. The sample has a decent amount of space in each box, and a pale blue border around the page.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, from the dimensions you're describing, there should be enough room to write appointments.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: That's what I thought. I was worried the pictures would take up all the useful space. Beautiful in theory, less helpful on a Tuesday.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Is there a minimum order?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: No, the printer I'm considering offers a single-copy order, which is just right for me.

details_in_summary: The sample page has a pale blue border.
key_facts: Hannah chooses an 8.5-by-11-inch wall calendar.
The printer she is considering offers a single-copy order.
minor_details: The sample page has a pale blue border.

summary: Riley discussed calendar printing options with Hannah. Hannah is choosing an 8.5x11-inch wall calendar for 2027, aiming for sufficient writing space in each date box and a pale blue border. She was concerned that pictures might reduce usable space, but Riley confirmed layout should work. The printer offers single-copy orders and has no minimum order. No further actions are specified.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How's the herb idea going?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, I finally brought home some plants. Basil and thyme.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. You went with starters?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, starter plants, like I was thinking. No seeds to negotiate with.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Where'd you put them?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: On the kitchen sill, where it gets that afternoon light.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And did you get pots for them too?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Not yet. I left them in their original nursery pots on the sill.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That seems sensible. You can see how they fit there first.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Exactly. I want to see how they do before I buy larger pots.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You could've spent 2 hours comparing pots.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I could've spent 2 hours comparing shades of the same pot. This is growth.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How much were the plants?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: $9.50 altogether. I carried them home in a paper bag.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's not bad for both.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. And now the basil and thyme have the best seats in the kitchen.

details_in_summary: The two plants cost him $9.50 altogether.
key_facts: Daniel bought basil and thyme starter plants.
He has left them in their original nursery pots on the kitchen sill.
He plans to see how they do before buying larger pots.
minor_details: The two plants cost him $9.50 altogether.
He carried them home in a paper bag.

summary: Riley and Daniel discussed herb ownership, with Daniel having purchased basil and thyme starter plants for $9.50. The plants are placed on the kitchen sill to receive afternoon light, still in nursery pots. They decided to observe how the herbs perform before buying larger pots. Riley noted the idea of pot comparisons, but they will wait to see growth first. The plants are described as occupying the best seats in the kitchen.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, Carmen, how are things standing with the window card?

dialogue.speaker: Carmen
dialogue.text: Pretty much where we left them. We've got that 8-inch by 10-inch clear patch, and we agreed on a 6-inch by 8-inch card.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good. I brought 2 rough layouts, folded inside my notebook. Can we take a quick look?

dialogue.speaker: Carmen
dialogue.text: Sure. Oh, that delivery cyclist just rang their bell outside. Nearly made me jump.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So this one has a centered heading, and the other one aligns all the text to the left.

dialogue.speaker: Carmen
dialogue.text: I think the left-aligned one is easier for me to follow. Is there room for both a phone number and a web address?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, there should be. What do you want them to be?

dialogue.speaker: Carmen
dialogue.text: My booking number is 206-555-0148, and the web address is junipercut.example/carmen.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Got it. Do you want your name in the heading, or just something like 'Book an appointment'?

dialogue.speaker: Carmen
dialogue.text: My name, please. What if we just put 'Book with Carmen' at the top?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That works. I can make the number and web address easy to pick out underneath.

dialogue.speaker: Carmen
dialogue.text: Good. The current notice has enough trouble competing with the glare; it doesn't need tiny writing helping it lose.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'll use those details to refine the left-aligned layout.

key_facts: One layout uses a centered heading; the other aligns all the text to the left.
Carmen wants her booking phone number, 206-555-0148, and web address, junipercut.example/carmen, on the card.
minor_details: The sketches are folded inside Riley’s notebook.
A delivery cyclist rings a bell outside while they talk.

summary: Riley and Carmen discussed window card specs: an 8x10 clear patch with a 6x8 card. They reviewed two rough layouts—centered heading and left-aligned text—favoring the left-aligned option for readability. Carmen provided contact details: booking number 206-555-0148 and web address junipercut.example/carmen, and requested the heading to read 'Book with Carmen' including Carmen's name. Riley will refine the left-aligned layout to emphasize the phone number and web address and address glare issues.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: That tabletop group Becca invited me to was really relaxed. We played Cascadia.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. How was it?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Good. We needed a little time to learn the scoring, though.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Was it confusing, or just a lot to keep track of?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: A bit of both. I kept forgetting to score the wildlife patterns until the end of each round.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's the sort of thing I'd remember right after moving on.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. My brain was very interested in placing things, less interested in remembering why.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did it get easier once you'd played a little?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: It did. Once we slowed down and checked the scoring, it made more sense. Also, someone brought a bag of salted almonds, so we were well supplied for the learning curve.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Essential gaming equipment.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. The almonds were easier to score.

key_facts: The group played Cascadia.
Sam kept forgetting to score the wildlife patterns until the end of each round.
minor_details: Someone brought a bag of salted almonds.

summary: Riley discussed a Cascadia game with Becca's invited group. The session was relaxed but required time to learn the scoring, with confusion over wildlife-pattern scoring early on. It helped to slow down and check the scoring; understanding improved after practice. Snacks (salted almonds) aided the learning curve, and Riley noted that the scoring was easier once players focused on the rules. Action: consider using a scoring checklist for new games.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I think that's why the Whidbey day felt so manageable. We didn't have every minute spoken for.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, even with the ferry line, it never felt like we were trying to catch up.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: How long did we wait on the way out? About 35 minutes?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, about 35 minutes in the vehicle line for the outbound ferry.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but would you use that as the estimate next time, or give it more room?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'd allow at least 45 minutes for the vehicle queue on a future Saturday. It's first come, first served, so 35 isn't much of a promise.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Right. The queue has declined to sign our itinerary.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And leaving Ballard at 7:30 helped. If we'd gone at 8:30, I think I would've been watching the clock more.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Especially with the museum and lunch before the walk. It was nice not having to hurry through either.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Or trying to squeeze in another stop after Ebey's Landing.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I liked having that unplanned stretch after the walk before we headed home. It made the day feel less like a list.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Even though the shower sent us back toward the car earlier than we'd planned.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah. We could just let the walk be shorter, instead of rearranging everything around it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And we had that late snack from a paper bag while we waited for the return ferry. That felt pretty good too.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: It did. Oh, I kept the museum's small printed brochure, by the way.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Nice. The maritime history exhibits were worth the stop, even without trying to add anything else.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Definitely. I think the extra space was more useful than another stop would've been.

details_in_summary: They ate a late snack from a paper bag while waiting for the return ferry.
Maya had kept the museum's small printed brochure.
key_facts: They waited about 35 minutes in the ferry line on the outbound trip.
Riley would allow at least 45 minutes for the vehicle queue on a future Saturday.
Maya liked having an unplanned stretch of time after the walk before heading home.
minor_details: They ate a late snack from a paper bag while waiting for the return ferry.
Maya had kept the museum's small printed brochure.

summary: Riley discussed trip planning for Whidbey, noting a 35-minute outbound ferry queue and recommending allowing at least 45 minutes. Leaving Ballard at 7:30 helped avoid clock-watching. They appreciated not rushing through museum and lunch, the unplanned stretch after the walk, and a late snack while waiting for the return ferry. Riley kept the museum brochure, and agreed the extra space was more useful than another stop.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: Hello, Riley. Come in. It's a lovely evening, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It is. Nice to have a little light left.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: Now, the ferry print. I thought the hallway wall opposite the coat hooks. What do you think?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That'll look good. Let's shift this pair of shoes out of the way first.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: I'll put them over here. And here's a pencil from the ceramic cup, if you need one.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Thanks. I'll use this small level to line it up, then mark where the picture hook should go.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: Is that high enough? I don't want to have to crane my neck at it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I think so. Can you hold the frame there for a second? Yeah, that looks about right.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: All right. I'll move it while you put the hook in.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: There. The picture hook's in, and I'll hang the print on it.

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: Let's step back. It looks a little tilted to me, but that might be the hallway.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Let me check with the level. You're right, just a little. How's that?

dialogue.speaker: Lian
dialogue.text: Straight now. I'm pleased to have it up, and the original is safely put away. Thank you, Riley.

key_facts: They hang the print on the hallway wall opposite the coat hooks.
Riley uses a picture hook and a small level to position it.
minor_details: Lian hands Riley a pencil from a ceramic cup.
They shift a pair of shoes out of the way before starting.

summary: Riley and Lian discussed hanging a ferry print on the hallway wall opposite the coat hooks. They cleared shoes, used a pencil and small level to mark the hook position, and held the frame while Riley set the hook. After hanging, they checked alignment, adjusted the tilt, and confirmed the print was straight and the original kept safely away.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. Okay, so, nice evening, isn't it? Finally cooled off a little.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, it's nice out. How did the hatchery kiosk test go?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Mostly okay, but the June 24 kiosk test produced a 6-second silence before playback restarted. It was pretty awkward at the end.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: 6 seconds? That's a long time to stand there wondering if it's finished.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. I timed the pause with my phone's stopwatch. I was standing there next to this stack of folded chairs against one wall, just staring at the kiosk.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Could it be something at the end of the file?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: That's what I'm checking. My copy loops without that silence in my editing software, so I'm also looking at the kiosk's playback settings.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: At least you know it isn't happening everywhere.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Right. Though I can already feel myself comparing every setting 12 times. Very efficient use of my life.

key_facts: A June 24 kiosk test produced a six-second silence before playback restarted.
Daniel's copy loops without that silence in his editing software.
minor_details: He timed the pause with his phone's stopwatch.
The test room had a stack of folded chairs against one wall.

summary: Riley and Daniel discussed the hatchery kiosk test from June 24, noting a 6-second silence before playback restarted. They are investigating whether the issue lies at the end of the file or in kiosk playback settings. Daniel will compare settings and test end-of-file behavior; goal is to confirm if the issue is isolated and identify a fix.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Morning, Sam. How are things looking with the lead-handoff instructions?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Morning. I've revised the copy for the 'Can't identify item' path. I'll read it aloud once before I send it: 'Set the item aside for a lead. You can add a note about any identifying marks.'

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds clear. And the note's optional?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yes. If there aren't any marks to describe, they can carry on without adding one.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'd rather give that handoff its own screen than bury it in an error message.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Agreed. It's a next step, not just an error. What if the note field sits right under the instruction?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, with 'optional' next to the field label so nobody has to guess.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: That works. Oh, that delivery cart is rattling past the meeting-room door. Very subtle.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hard to miss. For the note, let's keep it focused on identifying marks.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Right. I'll send you the revised copy now, with the optional label on the field.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Great. I'll make room for it on the handoff screen.

details_in_summary: Sam reads the copy aloud once before sending it.
key_facts: The handoff instruction asks the worker to set the item aside for a lead.
The revised screen includes an optional note about identifying marks.
minor_details: Sam reads the copy aloud once before sending it.
A delivery cart rattles past the meeting-room door.

summary: Riley discussed revising the lead-handoff instructions. Sam revised the 'Can't identify item' path copy, including an optional note about identifying marks. They agreed the note should be on its own screen, with the note field labeled optional and placed under the instruction. Action items: Sam will send the revised copy with the optional label; Riley will allocate space for the handoff screen.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I kept going back and forth between those 2 patches, but I finally picked the water-based satin polyurethane.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Over the paste wax? What tipped it for you?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Cup rings, mostly. The polyurethane should give the top better protection, and I like how the satin looks.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That makes sense. You didn't want to have to worry every time you put a mug down.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Exactly. I could be a person who always uses a coaster, in theory.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And did you find a small enough can?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I did. A half-pint can for $12. I didn't want to buy a huge tin for 1 desk.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's not bad. Did you need a brush too?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: No, I already had a usable synthetic brush in a kitchen drawer. Which was a pleasant surprise.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Your kitchen drawer came through for you.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: For once. Anyway, I'm glad I tested both finishes underneath before deciding.

details_in_summary: She already had a usable synthetic brush in a kitchen drawer.
key_facts: Hannah chose the water-based satin polyurethane for better protection against cup rings.
She bought a half-pint can for $12.
minor_details: She already had a usable synthetic brush in a kitchen drawer.

summary: Riley and Hannah discussed finishing two desk patches, choosing water-based satin polyurethane over paste wax for better cup-ring protection and a satin look. They found a half-pint can for $12 and already had a suitable synthetic brush. They tested both finishes before deciding. Action items: proceed with polyurethane application using the existing brush; use the purchased half-pint can.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm just stopping in for a minute. I've got my canvas grocery bag with me, so I won't stay long.

dialogue.speaker: Carmen
dialogue.text: Good timing. I've been thinking about those 2 window card layouts you brought by.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The centered heading and the one with everything aligned left?

dialogue.speaker: Carmen
dialogue.text: Yeah. I prefer the left-aligned layout. My eye finds the booking details a little faster.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay, I can work from that one. Do you have a preference for the colors?

dialogue.speaker: Carmen
dialogue.text: What if we just use dark lettering on a light background? The glare's already doing enough work against us.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Makes sense. I'll keep your phone number and web address easy to pick out.

dialogue.speaker: Carmen
dialogue.text: Good. I don't need anything fancy, just something people can actually read.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Left-aligned, dark lettering, light background. I've got it.

key_facts: Carmen prefers the left-aligned layout.
She asks Riley to use dark lettering on a light background.
minor_details: Riley is carrying a canvas grocery bag.

summary: Riley discussed two window card layouts with Carmen, and they agreed to use the left-aligned version. They decided on dark lettering on a light background to reduce glare. Riley will ensure the phone number and web address are easy to read and prominent. The outcome is a left-aligned card with high readability and clear contact details.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Oh, right, the island trip! Okay, so, we're back, and it was actually kind of perfect at a slower pace.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good! How did the walk at Lime Kiln go?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Shorter than we planned. The wind was really coming in, so Ben and I turned back earlier.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Ah, that's a shame. Did you get to see much before you turned around?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, we watched harbor seals from shore. So it still felt worth taking the taxi out to Lime Kiln Point State Park.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Seals are a pretty good consolation prize.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: They seemed completely unbothered by the wind, which felt a little smug.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And did you do the Jackson Beach walk on Sunday?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: We did. It was nice not having to hurry back for anything except dinner.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How was the seafood place?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Good. We shared lemon cake after dinner, which was probably my favorite part.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a strong endorsement of the seafood.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I know. Very thoughtful review. Oh, and I found sand in 1 of my shoes after I got home.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A little souvenir. How was the ferry back?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Delayed by about 40 minutes. But leaving Ben's car at Anacortes and walking on worked out, especially for the budget.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you manage to stay under $400?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, I spent $365, so $35 under my personal budget. I may have checked that number more than once.

details_in_summary: They shared lemon cake after dinner.
Daniel found sand in one of his shoes after he got home.
key_facts: Wind made the Lime Kiln walk shorter than planned, but Daniel and Ben watched harbor seals from shore.
Their return ferry was delayed by about 40 minutes.
Daniel spent $365 on the trip, $35 under his personal budget.
minor_details: They shared lemon cake after dinner.
Daniel found sand in one of his shoes after he got home.

summary: Riley discussed the trip with Daniel: a slower pace overall; Lime Kiln walk shortened by strong wind; harbor seals seen from shore; Jackson Beach walk completed; seafood dinner with lemon cake noted; sand found in a shoe after returning home. Ferry back delayed ~40 minutes. They stayed under budget at $365 (out of $400).

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How are things standing with the apartment pictures?

dialogue.speaker: Gabriel
dialogue.text: I've been looking through the scans again, trying to work out what to say under them. Some need more explanation than others.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. Oh, I'm just waiting for a loaf of bread to cool, by the way.

dialogue.speaker: Gabriel
dialogue.text: No rush. I was looking at the picture of our kitchen window, with that jar of basil on the sill.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, that one. What about 'Basil that somehow survived.'?

dialogue.speaker: Gabriel
dialogue.text: I like that. It's about as much as I remember of it, honestly.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Same. I can picture it on the sill, but that's about it.

dialogue.speaker: Gabriel
dialogue.text: Then let's use 'Basil that somehow survived.' I'll put that down as the caption.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good. Nice to have one settled.

details_in_summary: Riley is waiting for a loaf of bread to cool.
key_facts: The picture shows their kitchen window with a jar of basil on the sill.
They settle on the caption “Basil that somehow survived.”
minor_details: Riley is waiting for a loaf of bread to cool.

summary: Riley discussed the apartment photos with Gabriel and reviewed captions for the scans. They focused on the kitchen window photo with a basil jar. After considering options, they settled on the caption 'Basil that somehow survived.' Gabriel will record that caption, and Riley noted a settled caption as a positive step. A passing note about waiting for bread was mentioned.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Hey. Is there any tea left?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, there's enough for another cup. I'm glad we're home tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Me too. That beach walk was lovely, though. Salt Creek was worth getting out of the car for.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Definitely. We walked for about 45 minutes, right? Even with the wind and light drizzle.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: About 45, yeah. The shells and warm layers were a good call.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And the ferry queue on the way out added about 50 minutes. We allowed time for it, but still.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but at least we knew there could be a wait. The queue was very committed to being a queue.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The drive home via Tacoma was long too. About 4.5 hours, including the stop.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Including our very important stop to split a cinnamon roll at that roadside cafe.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: An essential part of the journey. Oh, I found sand in the car's footwell, by the way.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: A souvenir. Okay, but for another 1-night trip, how much driving would feel reasonable?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'd aim for under 3 hours each way. More time walking, less time getting there.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Agreed. Under 3 hours of driving each way sounds much better for a short break.

details_in_summary: Riley found sand in the car's footwell.
key_facts: The outbound ferry queue added about 50 minutes to the journey.
Their beach walk lasted about 45 minutes, with wind and light drizzle.
They drove home via Tacoma, taking about four and a half hours including a stop.
For a future one-night trip, they would aim for under three hours of driving each way.
minor_details: They split a cinnamon roll at a roadside cafe.
Riley found sand in the car's footwell.

summary: Riley and Maya discussed a recent trip: tea, beach walk at Salt Creek, 45-minute walk, 50-minute ferry queue, a 4.5-hour drive via Tacoma with a cinnamon-roll stop, and finding sand in the car. They considered future trips: for a 1-night trip, aim for under 3 hours driving each way, with more time spent walking and less time en route; plan to carry a souvenir-free car, and confirm driving time targets for shorter breaks.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I've made a start on the pottery bowls, and keeping the walls even is harder than I thought.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How many have you made so far?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I've formed 2 bowls and started a third. We're using the pinch-pot method, so it's all done by hand.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Is that where you start with a ball of clay and pinch it into a bowl?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes. You press your thumb into the middle and work around it. In theory, you pinch the walls to roughly the same thickness.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And in practice?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: One bowl has a noticeably thicker wall on one side. I kept going around it, thinking I'd evened it out, and then I'd feel that bit again.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Could you tell while you were looking at it, or only when you touched it?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Both, once I noticed. From one angle it looks fairly normal, and then you turn it and there's this thick side.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Is the other one more even?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: More even, yes. Not perfectly even. I'm trying not to spend the whole class measuring it with my fingers.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What are you aiming for, size-wise?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I've been looking at the cereal bowls in my kitchen for ideas. They're a good size, but now I'm noticing how thin their walls are.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: They're probably not a fair comparison for your first hand-built bowls.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: No, probably not. I had this idea that I'd make a little set and they'd all look alike.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What if they're a useful mismatched set instead? They don't have to be identical to belong together.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I like that. I could concentrate on making each one a useful size instead of trying to copy the first one exactly.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And the thick side can just be part of that bowl's personality.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Its very solid personality. I also came home with a smudge of clay on my watchband, so apparently I wasn't as careful as I thought.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a pretty good souvenir of getting started.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: A temporary one, at least. I'm glad I've got 2 formed, even if they're a bit lopsided.

key_facts: Hannah has formed two bowls and started a third.
She is using the pinch-pot method.
One bowl has a noticeably thicker wall on one side.
minor_details: Hannah came home with a smudge of clay on her watchband.
She has been looking at cereal bowls in her kitchen for ideas.

summary: Riley discussed with Hannah the progress on pinch-pot bowls. Hannah has formed 2 bowls and started a third, noting one side is thicker and one is more even. They discussed aiming for useful sizes rather than identical bowls and embracing a intentionally mismatched set. Riley suggested treating the thick side as part of each bowl’s character. Action items: continue forming bowls, focus on practical sizes, and avoid over-measuring; use non-identical designs as a feature.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Morning. Did you sleep okay?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, pretty well. My butter's unusually soft this morning, though. I could barely spread it.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: It's already warm in here. I left my slippers beside the sofa, and even they feel warm.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The living room reached 81°F at 5 p.m. on Sunday. It gets pretty uncomfortable in the afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but is it the sun coming in, or is the whole apartment just warming up?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm not sure. The living-room window faces west, so the afternoon sun could be part of it.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Maybe we should pay attention to where the heat's coming from before we buy anything. Otherwise we're just shopping on a hunch.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. I'll notice when the sun reaches the window and whether the other rooms feel as warm.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Good. A little detective work before we hire the appliance aisle.

key_facts: The living-room window faces west.
The living room reached 81°F at 5 p.m. on Sunday.
minor_details: Riley's butter was unusually soft at breakfast.
Maya had left her slippers beside the sofa.

summary: Riley discussed the apartment warming, noting 81°F in the afternoon and a west-facing window. They considered heat sources (sun vs. overall warming) and agreed to investigate before purchasing appliances. Action items: Riley will observe sun exposure and heat distribution in other rooms to identify the true heat source; Maya emphasized detective work prior to buying.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Would you be up for another game afternoon with Inez and me?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, definitely. Your apartment was a lot easier to concentrate in than the lounge.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: It was. We could play here again, if that works for you. How about July 11?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That should work. Is Inez free then?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Let me check the paper calendar hanging beside the kitchen door. I wrote down what she said.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, I can write it down too. Wait, where's my pencil?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: You've got a pencil tucked behind your ear. Very handy storage system.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh. Thanks. I was about to go looking for it.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Here it is: Inez is free July 11. It's a Saturday. Would the afternoon work?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yep, let's do July 11 in the afternoon. What should we play?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: How about Qwirkle? I can bring it out, if that works for you.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Qwirkle sounds good. I'll put it down.

key_facts: The next session is set for the afternoon of July 11.
They plan to play Qwirkle.
minor_details: Sam checks the date on a paper calendar hanging beside the kitchen door.
Riley has a pencil tucked behind one ear.

summary: Riley discussed scheduling a game afternoon with Sam and Inez at Sam's apartment. They confirmed July 11, Saturday, in the afternoon, with Inez available. They agreed to play Qwirkle, and Riley noted to record the plan and prepare the game.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Oh, wow. I just remembered the speaking exercise from Italian class. That was harder than I expected.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What did they have you do?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Pretend to buy vegetables at a market. Simple enough, until I had to say how much I wanted.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Was it the vegetable words or the numbers?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The numbers. I froze when I was asked to say the quantities out loud.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, no. Even though you knew what you wanted to say?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. I could picture the number, but getting it out of my mouth was another matter.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Your index cards didn't prepare you for the pretend market?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Apparently not. The cards are good for recognizing words, but they don't ask follow-up questions.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Rude of the pretend market to be interactive.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I know. And I kept looking at the classroom clock, which was a few minutes fast, so I thought we were closer to the end than we were.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That seems especially cruel.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I also had a pencil tucked behind 1 ear the whole time. Very prepared-looking, at least.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Maybe you need number cards too?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Maybe. Or, what if I practice by saying grocery quantities out loud at home? Like, actually say the number instead of just looking at it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So you'd point at something and say how much of it you need?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. Or say it while I'm putting groceries away. That might make the numbers feel less abstract.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And you could keep it short, like your 5-minute practice.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. Small enough that I'll actually do it, and out loud so I can't mistake recognizing a number for saying it.

key_facts: In class, Sam had to pretend to buy vegetables at a market.
Sam froze when asked to say quantities aloud.
Sam plans to practice numbers by saying grocery quantities out loud at home.
minor_details: The classroom clock was a few minutes fast.
Sam had a pencil tucked behind one ear.

summary: Riley and Sam discussed a speaking exercise from Italian class involving buying vegetables and stating quantities. The main issue was pronouncing numbers aloud, not recognizing words. Index cards helped with vocabulary but lacked follow-up questions. They considered solutions: use number cards, practice saying quantities at home, and perform short, 5-minute sessions aloud while engaging with groceries to reduce abstraction.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: You're getting through those cherries faster than I am.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It's lunch. I'm allowed to be competitive.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, I agreed to help organize the autumn ushers at the Gull House.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. That's the little cinema where you volunteer, right?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, it's a small independent cinema. The coordinator, Marisol Vale, asked me if I'd help.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And you said yes without making a spreadsheet of reasons first?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I did. I'm as surprised as you are. I did think about making one afterward.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So what does organizing the ushers involve?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: That's partly what I need to find out. I want to see how a screening actually runs before I start making plans for everyone else.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Even though you already volunteer there?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. I know bits of it, but I haven't followed an usher through a whole screening. I'm planning to shadow an experienced usher at a July screening.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That seems sensible. See what they actually do instead of guessing.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Exactly. Otherwise I'll spend 2 hours deciding where people should stand and discover there's a perfectly good reason they can't stand there.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Is there much room in the lobby?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Not a ton. There's a narrow coat rack in the lobby, which somehow makes the whole space feel narrower.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Well, you can add 'coat rack consultant' to your list of qualifications.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Right after 'person who ate fewer cherries than Riley.' Pass them over?

details_in_summary: Daniel mentions that the cinema’s lobby has a narrow coat rack.
key_facts: The Gull House is a small independent cinema where Daniel volunteers.
Cinema coordinator Marisol Vale asked Daniel to help organize the autumn ushers.
Daniel plans to shadow an experienced usher at a July screening.
minor_details: Daniel mentions that the cinema’s lobby has a narrow coat rack.
He and Riley are eating cherries as they talk.

summary: Riley and Daniel discussed Daniel helping organize Gull House autumn ushers. Daniel will shadow an experienced usher at a July screening to observe the workflow before planning staffing. He aims to understand the screening process rather than guess. They noted limited lobby space due to a coat rack. Marisol Vale asked Daniel to help; next step is the July shadowing session, with potential follow-up planning.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Oh, thank God. I think I've found a way to do the photos without making it my full-time job.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You tested something?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. Okay, so, I borrowed a flatbed scanner from a neighbor in Fremont and tried a few prints.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How'd they come out?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Pretty good. I took phone pictures of the same ones to compare, and the scans had more detail. The phone pictures were quicker, though.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Enough quicker to be tempting?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Very. But getting the light even was fiddly, and I kept catching a little glare.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And the scanner didn't have that problem?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Not on the ones I tested. I tried a couple of settings and settled on 600 dpi for the prints.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Is that the sweet spot?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: It seems good enough. More detail than the phone pictures, without each scan taking forever. I could compare settings until retirement, but I'm trying not to.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A brave departure from your usual academic method.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: The old seminar of 2 people and 40 tabs. Anyway, I ate a plum while I was waiting for the test scans.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's your unit of scanning time now? One plum?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Approximately. The scanner lid has a small blue sticker on it, which I kept looking at while it worked. That's how exciting the test was.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So the originals stay with Teresa?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, I'm keeping the original photographs with Teresa, not discarding them. She'll still have the actual prints.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And you've already got that rough inventory to work from.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Right. At least I can start with what I know, even if most of those envelope labels still don't have a year.

key_facts: Daniel borrowed a flatbed scanner from a neighbor in Fremont.
He chose 600 dpi for scanning the prints.
He will keep the original photographs with Teresa rather than discard them.
minor_details: The scanner lid has a small blue sticker on it.
Daniel ate a plum while waiting for the test scans.

summary: Riley noted Daniel tested photo capture using a flatbed scanner versus phone photos. Scans provided more detail, with 600 dpi chosen as a balance between quality and speed; phones were quicker but produced glare and lighting challenges. The originals will remain with Teresa, and a rough inventory is in place, though many envelope labels lack years. Next steps include continuing tabletop testing without full commitment to endless settings and proceeding from known items.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Oh, that's a relief. Emeka just sent me his work schedule.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh good. Does it line up with your time off?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. He expects to work October 21 through October 23, and he has October 24 and 25 free.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's nice. You'll have some days together without trying to squeeze everything in.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. And I don't have to worry about filling every weekday for both of us.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You could leave some of your daytime hours open too, while he's working.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah, I'm comfortable exploring Montreal alone. I don't need a plan for every hour.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You can see what you feel like doing when you get there.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: What if I just have a morning where I do absolutely nothing useful? A daring concept.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I support it. How did he send you the schedule?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: In a text, with a calendar screenshot. I'm trying not to turn it into a color-coded family itinerary.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: One screenshot is probably enough planning for this morning.

details_in_summary: Emeka sent his schedule in a text with a calendar screenshot.
Sam jokes that they are trying not to produce a color-coded family itinerary.

Emeka has October 24 and 25 free.
Sam is comfortable exploring alone while Emeka works.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, how do things stand with the library sign-up form?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I've started asking people at the service desk. I asked 5 patrons to talk me through signing up for an event.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did they get stuck on 'Registrant' like you'd noticed before?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: A couple hesitated there, yes. But the thing I hadn't expected was 'Contact type.' 3 patrons thought it meant they had to provide both a phone number and an email address.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, interesting. What were they looking at when they said that?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: The contact section. I tried not to explain it for them, just asked what they thought it was asking. One conversation got interrupted because the printer ran out of paper, so that was a very smooth research session.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: In my experience, even a little explanation from the person watching can change what someone does next. It's hard to keep quiet, though.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: It really is. I kept wanting to say, 'Oh, that just means—' and then stopping myself.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Were they all confused in the same way, or did they describe it differently?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: A bit differently. The common part was thinking both contact details were required. I marked the questions I wanted to follow up on with a green pen, so I can look at those again.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That makes sense. I'd want to know what they're expecting that label to tell them before changing it.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: That's where I am too. I'm also going to ask Marisol what questions come up when I'm not at the desk. 5 people is useful, but it's not everybody.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. Sounds like you've got a better picture starting to form, without having to decide what the answer is yet.

details_in_summary: Hannah used a green pen to mark questions she wanted to follow up on.
key_facts: Hannah asked five patrons to talk her through signing up for an event.
Three patrons thought 'Contact type' meant they had to provide both a phone number and an email address.
Hannah plans to ask Marisol what questions come up when Hannah isn't at the desk.
minor_details: Hannah used a green pen to mark questions she wanted to follow up on.
One conversation was interrupted by a printer running out of paper.

summary: Riley noted Hannah’s quick usability test of the library sign-up form. Findings: Patrons hesitated at Registrant; confusion centered on Contact type, with some assuming both phone and email were required. Hannah marked follow-up questions with a green pen and plans to ask Marisol about desk-less feedback. Next steps include reviewing the green-pen items, gathering broader input, and avoiding premature label changes until user expectations are clarified.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: So the new bulb didn't make any difference. The lamp still flickered.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, even with the replacement in?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yeah. I tried a new warm-white LED bulb, and it flickered too.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Well, there goes the easy explanation.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: In theory, the bulb was the easy explanation. In practice, I now have an extra bulb.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you get a pack of them?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: A 2-pack. So at least I didn't buy a whole box.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And you'd already tried another outlet, right?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Right, and it flickered there too. I've unplugged it now.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Probably best. Are you going to have someone look at it?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yeah, I'm planning to drop it off at Tacoma Lamp & Shade on July 6.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Monday, then. Do you have it ready to go?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Pretty much. I wrapped the cord around the lamp's base for the trip.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Nice and tidy.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: For once. I was trying to keep it from dragging, not win an organization award.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Still counts. It's annoying the bulb wasn't the answer, though.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yeah. I was hoping it would be that simple.

details_in_summary: Hannah wrapped the cord around the lamp's base for the trip.

The lamp still flickered with the replacement installed.

Hannah plans to take it to Tacoma Lamp & Shade on July 6 for service, with the cord tidily wrapped for transport. Preparation is nearly complete for the drop-off.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How are things going tonight, Rosa?

dialogue.speaker: Rosa
dialogue.text: Not bad. Can you read the menu on the chalkboard from out there?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Not very well. The sun's right on it.

dialogue.speaker: Rosa
dialogue.text: Yeah, the summer glare is making it hard to read. I want people passing Plover Coffee to notice the iced drinks, but the menu practically disappears.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Could I get a sparkling water, by the way?

dialogue.speaker: Rosa
dialogue.text: Sure. Oh, that delivery cyclist left a helmet on the counter.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Looks like they're still right outside. I can let them know.

dialogue.speaker: Rosa
dialogue.text: Thanks. One less thing for my lost-and-found collection.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What about putting the chalkboard under the awning? It'd be out of the glare.

dialogue.speaker: Rosa
dialogue.text: Under the awning, huh? I don't want to buy a new sign just to get through summer.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, I was thinking you could use the board you've got.

dialogue.speaker: Rosa
dialogue.text: That's worth a try. At least people might be able to see what's on it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I could hardly make out the iced drinks when I came in.

dialogue.speaker: Rosa
dialogue.text: Well, there's that. Here’s your sparkling water.

details_in_summary: Riley orders a sparkling water.
A delivery cyclist leaves a helmet on the counter.

Riley suggests moving the chalkboard under the awning.
Rosa does not want to buy a new sign.

Riley also ordered a sparkling water.

dialogue.speaker: Lucia
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. Nice evening, isn't it? Still light out.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, Lucia. Yeah, it feels like the day forgot to end.

dialogue.speaker: Lucia
dialogue.text: I was thinking about those 2 flat loaves I told you about. Do you still time your bulk fermentation?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I keep an eye on the time, but mostly I watch the dough. I use a straight-sided container so it's easier to see how much it's risen.

dialogue.speaker: Lucia
dialogue.text: That would be easier than peering into my bowl and guessing where the top was.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, I mark the starting level on the side, then I can see the change without trying to remember it.

dialogue.speaker: Lucia
dialogue.text: I have a rubber band tucked around my wrist. I could put that around the container at the starting level.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Perfect. You can move it later if you need to, but leave it there during the rise.

dialogue.speaker: Lucia
dialogue.text: And you're not waiting for it to double?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: No, especially when it's warm. I'd look for something closer to a 50% rise.

dialogue.speaker: Lucia
dialogue.text: All right. I'll try ending bulk fermentation when my dough has risen by about 50%, instead of going by the clock.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds worth trying. My kitchen scale needs a new battery, by the way, so I'm having my own little equipment problem.

dialogue.speaker: Lucia
dialogue.text: At least the rubber band doesn't need one. I'll keep the 4 hours in mind, but let the dough make the decision.

details_in_summary: Riley mentions that their kitchen scale needs a new battery.
key_facts: Riley describes using a straight-sided container to make the dough's rise easier to see.
Lucia plans to end bulk fermentation when her dough has risen by about 50%.
minor_details: Lucia has a rubber band tucked around her wrist.
Riley mentions that their kitchen scale needs a new battery.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Oh, that's surprising. The neighbor's note says the surface was damp, but the soil underneath was dry.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Really? So it looked fine until they checked below the surface.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah. Some of the chard leaves had wilted, too. The neighbor gave the bed a thorough watering, and the plants perked up afterward.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm glad they checked. That's exactly the kind of thing we would've missed just looking at the top.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but was the chard still looking better when you saw it?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, it had perked up. I checked the soil with my finger, too.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Good. So the straw helps, but we still can't just judge by the surface.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Especially at the far end, where it was drier before. I'm going to bring a small watering can to reach the far corner.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: That should make it easier to get water where it needs to go. The hose isn't exactly a precision instrument.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: No. Oh, I've still got a little dirt under one thumbnail.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I'll fold the gardener's note into a square so we can keep it. It's a useful reminder.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. Damp on top doesn't necessarily mean damp underneath.

details_in_summary: Maya folds the gardener’s note into a square.
key_facts: The neighboring gardener reported that the surface was damp but the soil underneath was dry.
Some chard leaves had wilted, but the plants perked up after a thorough watering.
Riley plans to bring a small watering can for reaching the far corner.
minor_details: Maya folds the gardener’s note into a square.
Riley has a little dirt under one thumbnail.

Riley will fold the gardener’s note into a square for reference and reminded that surface dampness doesn’t guarantee moisture below.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: The reviewed excerpts are ready, and I've got a date to put the display together. It opens on July 13.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, that's coming up. Can someone get the whole thing without using the audio?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: That's what I wanted to check. The complete written text of each audio excerpt will be available right beside it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So nobody has to listen to follow what's being said.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Right. Okay, but I also want to make sure the print is easy to find, not tucked away where it looks like an afterthought.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Could you put the text right next to the controls?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: That's what I'm thinking. I'll check the layout when I put it together.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good. You've already got enough pieces to keep track of.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Speaking of which, I'm tucking this binder clip into my work bag. Apparently the entire project depends on 1 small piece of metal.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A very important member of the team.

key_facts: The display is scheduled to open on July 13.
Complete transcripts will be available beside the audio excerpts.
minor_details: Maya tucks a binder clip into her work bag.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: You're putting it near the living-room doorway?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, I thought we'd try it there first and see if it moves some air through the apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but which way is it pointing?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Into the living room. Want to sit over here and see if you can feel it?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Oh, yeah. That's much nicer than sitting here without it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Not bad for a 12-inch floor fan. I'm glad we bought it for $35 instead of getting something huge.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: The box barely fits in the hallway recycling bin as it is. A bigger one would need its own apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What's the pencil for?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I'm marking the fan's instruction sheet with a pencil, where it explains how to take the grille off. I don't want to hunt for that later.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It's been running about 15 minutes. The room thermometer's stayed at 79°F the whole time.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: So it's making us more comfortable sitting in the living room, but it's not actually cooling the room.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. Still feels good, though. I'm going to leave it here for now.

key_facts: They buy a 12-inch floor fan for $35.
They first place the fan near the living-room doorway.
The room thermometer stays at 79°F during their first test.
minor_details: The fan's box barely fits in their hallway recycling bin.
Maya uses a pencil to mark the fan's instruction sheet.

summary: Riley discussed placing a 12-inch floor fan near the living-room doorway to move air through the apartment. Maya asked about orientation; Riley noted it would face the living room and suggested testing with Maya seated nearby. They observed the room remained 79°F after about 15 minutes, noting the fan increased comfort but did not cool the room. They documented removing the grille with a pencil and decided to leave the fan in place for now.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, I finally booked a drum lesson.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You did? After how many years of talking about it?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Enough that I was starting to think talking about it was the hobby.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: When's the lesson?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: July 11. My teacher's Marisol Ibarra.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's next Saturday. How'd you choose her?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I compared 3 lesson websites. Which is a very efficient way to make a simple decision take all afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Very on brand. Are you getting a drum kit for the apartment?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Not a full kit, no. I want to start with a quiet practice pad.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Your neighbors might appreciate that.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. I'd like to meet them without immediately becoming the guy they complain about.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Have you got the pad yet?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Not yet. I figured I'd ask Marisol what she recommends instead of comparing 3 more websites.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good call. We can drink our iced tea without opening a single product review.

key_facts: Daniel's first lesson is scheduled for July 11.
His teacher is Marisol Ibarra.
minor_details: Daniel compared three lesson websites before choosing.
He tells Riley about it over iced tea.

summary: Riley noted Daniel booked a drum lesson for July 11 with Marisol Ibarra. Daniel will start with a quiet practice pad instead of a full kit and plans to ask Marisol for a gear recommendation. Riley highlighted neighbor considerations and suggested avoiding excessive reviews. Action items: Daniel to obtain a practice pad (and seek Marisol's recommendation) before or after the lesson; maintain neighbor-friendly setup.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Oh, you've got a minute? Good. I brought another iced tea.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, I could use a Monday morning taste test. What's in this one?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Black tea again, but with peaches this time. First time I've tried them in it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. Can I have a little?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Sure. I brewed the black tea for 4 minutes, instead of the 6 I used with the lemon.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I like this direction. It's less bitter than that first one, but the peach tastes kind of cooked.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Ah. I added the peaches while the tea was still hot. That might explain it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, it's almost like canned peaches. I can actually taste them, though, unlike the strawberries in the hibiscus.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: That's something. The bottle spent the commute in an insulated lunch bag, so at least it's still cold.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It is. And the tea itself is pretty good.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I'll take that as a partial victory. The peaches have apparently been to culinary school.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Very briefly. I just rinsed my cup at the office sink, by the way. Thanks for the sample.

details_in_summary: Riley rinses their cup at the office sink afterward.
key_facts: Sam brewed the black tea for four minutes.
Sam added the peaches while the tea was still hot.
minor_details: The bottle spent the commute in an insulated lunch bag.
Riley rinses their cup at the office sink afterward.

summary: Riley discussed a new iced tea: black tea with peaches. Sam brewed 4 minutes (vs 6 with lemon); Riley noted it’s less bitter but peach flavor seems cooked, likely from adding peaches while hot. Riley compared taste to canned peaches and commented on the cold bottle after transit. Riley rinsed her cup at the office sink. No further actions explicit.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I did finish shaping the 3rd bowl, but a little crack appeared near the rim.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh no. Could you fix it?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yeah, I used some slip and a small piece of clay to repair it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Is slip just really wet clay?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Pretty much. It helped join the little piece to the bowl. Then I smoothed the repair with a damp sponge.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Can you still see where the crack was?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: A little, if you look for it. I spent longer on that rim than I intended.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Trying to make it disappear?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes, and then trying to stop fussing with it. Those are 2 separate skills, apparently.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Well, it can join the one with the thick wall. They're a family of bowls with distinguishing features.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Exactly. The mismatched set is looking more and more deliberate, in theory.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So are they all still at the studio?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: They are. The bowls are drying there before their first firing.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Are you relieved to be done shaping them?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I am. I kept thinking I'd find one more bit to smooth, especially on that 3rd one.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm glad you managed to leave the rim alone eventually.

details_in_summary: Hannah used a damp sponge to smooth the repair.
key_facts: A crack appeared near the rim of the third bowl.
Hannah repaired it with slip and a small piece of clay.
The bowls are drying at the studio before their first firing.
minor_details: Hannah used a damp sponge to smooth the repair.
She says she spent longer on the rim than she intended.

summary: Hannah completed shaping the third bowl, repairing a rim crack with slip and a small clay patch, then smoothing with a damp sponge. The repair is slightly visible. The mismatched set remains at the studio, drying before the first firing. Riley noted relief at having finished shaping, and Hannah confirmed she is glad to be done.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Becca's trying a bigger group for the next game night. She's invited 5 people.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: 5 people plus Becca?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I think so, yeah. I'm one of the 5. The invitation came through during my lunch break, and I had to count it twice.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: When is it?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: July 16, after work. The proposed game is Ticket to Ride.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Would 6 people fit in one game?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I'm not sure. I should check the player count on the box. What if we end up with someone just watching?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, that's a long time to wait for a turn. Could you split into 2 games?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Maybe, if there's another game there. I'd rather check with Becca first than arrive with a whole seating chart.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Especially since you were still getting the scoring down in Cascadia.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Right. I kept forgetting the wildlife patterns until the end of each round. Oh, and I found an old pencil in the Ticket to Ride box. At least we have a pencil.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: One problem solved. Check the player count, then see what Becca thinks.

details_in_summary: Sam found an old pencil in the game box.
key_facts: The next session is scheduled for July 16.
Becca has invited five people to that session.
The proposed game is Ticket to Ride.
minor_details: Sam found an old pencil in the game box.
The invitation went out during Sam's lunch break.

summary: Riley noted Becca is inviting 5 people to the next game night, likely making a 6-player group including Becca. The date is July 16, after work, with Ticket to Ride as the proposed game. Sam will verify the box's player count and Becca’s expectations before committing. They discussed the possibility of splitting into two games if needed and whether someone would watch. Action items: confirm the final headcount with Becca, check the player limit, and plan seating accordingly; Riley mentioned a found pencil and past Cascadia scoring issues.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. Okay, so, how's your evening going?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Pretty good. I'm winding down. How about you?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Not bad. The kiosk vendor replied just before I made dinner, so I finally have an answer about that gap.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, the 6-second silence? Was it the file?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Apparently not. The vendor traced the pause to the kiosk playlist reloading the file at each repeat.

dialogue.speaker: Me
