summary: Riley discussed progress with back and climbing. Routine extended from 45 to ~60 minutes by August; back remained comfortable, avoiding the prior 90-minute soreness. Rest between attempts averaged about 2 minutes; a full day between visits and a 5-minute warm-up are maintained. Descent is now managed without over-analysis, focusing on a safe exit. If session becomes sloppy or back hurts, stop before reaching 60 minutes. A loose shoe lace was noted and deemed easy to fix; a ferry postcard behind Jonas’s calendar was mentioned. Overall guidance: keep warm-up, breaks, easy descent, and use session feel as a guide.

dialogue.speaker: Mateo
dialogue.text: I got to the finish hold on that blue slab yesterday, Tuesday, October 6.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice! Did you get both hands on it?

dialogue.speaker: Mateo
dialogue.text: I got them there, but I couldn't control it with both hands. My feet started to slide and I came off.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Still, that's farther than the penultimate hold. How did the move onto your right foot feel?

dialogue.speaker: Mateo
dialogue.text: Better. I used the inside edge and got my hips over it before reaching. It felt a lot less like I was just hoping.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And then the finish was the tricky part.

dialogue.speaker: Mateo
dialogue.text: Yeah. New bug, same wall.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you try it right when you got there?

dialogue.speaker: Mateo
dialogue.text: No, I warmed up on 3 easier problems first. I wanted to get my feet working before I got on the slab.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds sensible.

dialogue.speaker: Mateo
dialogue.text: I'm going back after work today, Wednesday, October 7, for another session. I'd like another try while I can still remember what that position felt like.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, see if you can get settled before you bring the second hand up.

dialogue.speaker: Mateo
dialogue.text: That's what I'm thinking. I'll eat my leftover noodles before I leave the office, though. The wall can wait for lunch—or, I guess, a very early dinner.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Either way, probably better than climbing hungry.

dialogue.speaker: Mateo
dialogue.text: Right. One balance problem at a time.

details_in_summary: He warms up on three easier problems.
key_facts: Mateo climbs on Tuesday, October 6.
He reaches the finish hold but cannot control it with both hands.
He plans another session after work on Wednesday, October 7.
minor_details: He warms up on three easier problems.
He eats leftover noodles before leaving the office.

summary: Riley summarized Mateo’s progress on the blue slab, noting that Mateo reached the finish hold with both hands but feet slipped, causing a fall. The move onto the right foot felt better due to using the inside edge and hips over it. They discussed the finish as the tricky part and planned a return after work on Oct 7 to retry, with a warm-up on easier problems first and settling before bringing up the second hand. Mateo planned to eat first.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Daphne approved the revised online wording and the paper sheet for use at the branch.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, that's great! Both of them?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Both. I'm getting the final materials together now, so the staff can use the 2 options consistently.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you change the paper sheet after the craft program trial?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes, I enlarged the space for contact information. Since 2 people ran out of room, that seemed like a fairly persuasive reason.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hard to argue with that. Is the rest of it staying pretty much the same?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes. The staff checkbox is still there, so whoever enters the request can mark it. I'm also putting together the instructions for entering it while the patron is there.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That should help keep the paper and online sign-ups in the same system.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Exactly. One system, not a separate pile of reservations that we have to reconcile later. In theory, anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And where's the precious final draft?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: In a clear plastic sleeve. I'm trying not to improve it into a completely different document before I finish the instructions.

details_in_summary: Hannah kept the final draft in a clear plastic sleeve.
key_facts: Daphne approved Hannah's revised online wording and paper sheet for branch use.
Hannah enlarged the contact-information space on the paper sheet.
minor_details: Hannah kept the final draft in a clear plastic sleeve.

Hannah is finalizing materials so staff use both options consistently, including an enlarged contact-info space and a staff checkbox for requests. Instructions for in-person entry are being prepared to align paper and online sign-ups. The final draft remains in a clear plastic sleeve to avoid scope changes.

dialogue.speaker: Mateo
dialogue.text: Oh, I did it! I finished the blue slab last night.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You did? Nice! You got the finish hold?

dialogue.speaker: Mateo
dialogue.text: Yeah, with both hands. I actually held it under control this time.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's so good. Yesterday you were just getting to it and coming off.

dialogue.speaker: Mateo
dialogue.text: Right. So, October 7 is officially the day I solved the blue slab.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did the footwork feel any different?

dialogue.speaker: Mateo
dialogue.text: It felt steadier. I remembered to get my hips over that foot before reaching, instead of trying to rush the move.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's great. You stuck with it.

dialogue.speaker: Mateo
dialogue.text: I did. And then I went home and celebrated with a pear from the kitchen counter.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Very extravagant.

dialogue.speaker: Mateo
dialogue.text: I know. I also found a bit of tape stuck to the bottom of my shoe afterward. A little souvenir, I guess.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So are you going to keep climbing?

dialogue.speaker: Mateo
dialogue.text: Yeah, I think 1 weekday evening a week is realistic. It fits around the rest of my week without feeling like another thing I have to squeeze in.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's the best part. Well, that and finishing the slab.

key_facts: Mateo completes the blue slab on the evening of October 7.
He controls the finish hold with both hands.
He intends to keep climbing one weekday evening a week.
minor_details: He celebrates with a pear from the kitchen counter at home.
He finds a bit of tape stuck to the bottom of his shoe afterward.

Mateo celebrated with a pear and noted a tape souvenir on his shoe. They agreed Mateo will climb about one weekday evening per week to fit his schedule.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. Okay, so, how's your lunch?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good. I was hungrier than I thought. How's yours?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Good, yeah. I'm trying not to eat too fast for once.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Aiming for a steady tempo?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Oh, that's cruel. Actually, I've been working on 'Harbor Steps,' and I can get through most of it now.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Most of it?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, I keep losing time when it moves from single strokes to double strokes. The transition starts in bar 9.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Is it getting into the doubles, or coming out of them?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Getting into them. Here, I'll tap it on the table with my fingers. I get to that change and suddenly I'm trying to catch up.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, I can hear the little gap. Do you always start at the beginning when you practice it?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Pretty much. I marked the transition with an orange highlighter, but apparently that didn't fix it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Have you tried just practicing that section on its own? Maybe start a little before bar 9 so you still have to make the change.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: That makes sense. I keep treating the beginning as the entrance fee for getting another shot at it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And you already know you can slow things down. Like when you were counting at 65 beats per minute.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. I'll try that section slowly instead of playing the whole thing over and over. A sensible plan, which means I should probably stop comparing it to 6 other plans.

key_facts: Daniel loses time when the piece moves from single strokes to double strokes.
The troublesome transition begins in bar nine.
minor_details: He marked the transition with an orange highlighter.
He demonstrates it by tapping his fingers on the table.

summary: Riley discussed lunch with Daniel. Daniel reported progress on Harbor Steps but identified a timing gap when transitioning from single to double strokes starting at bar 9. Riley suggested isolating the problematic section, starting slightly before bar 9, and practicing it slowly. Daniel agreed to slow practice and avoid full runs, prioritizing the transition and reducing practice plan comparisons.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You're still at your desk? I thought you'd headed out.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Almost. I was checking the Montreal forecast before I shut down. It's looking a bit wet, though it's still a ways out.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, I wouldn't trust it too much yet. Are you taking a raincoat?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: A waterproof jacket, yeah. I need to put a new zipper pull on it first. The jacket's fine, the zipper's just a little too committed to staying shut.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's an easy thing to forget until you're standing in the rain.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. Emeka suggested we play a board game at his place if it rains, so there's our very elaborate backup plan.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Honestly, an afternoon inside sounds good. You wanted ordinary time together anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. It still counts as a good visit if we're at the table arguing over rules instead of walking around.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Are you bringing a game with you?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: No, I'm leaving space in my bag instead. Emeka suggested the game, so I figure we can use one at his place.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Fair. And you can still do your photo walk while he's working if the weather cooperates.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: That's the hope. I checked that my camera battery still holds a charge, at least. One thing ready to go.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: One thing down, one zipper pull to go.

Sam checked that their camera battery still holds a charge.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: It went pretty well, actually. 8 people came to the workshop.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good. How did the handout hold up?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Mostly fine, but the pale gray example was difficult to read on the library's black-and-white printouts.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Ah. Did you notice before you started?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Not until we were looking at it during the session. The gray was much lighter on paper than I expected.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's annoying. Especially when the whole point is making things easier to read.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah, an accidental demonstration. Not the kind I was aiming for.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What did people think of the tips otherwise?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Several attendees wanted to use them on notices for community groups, which was nice to hear.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's exactly the kind of thing I was hoping the examples would be useful for.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Same. And the payment deadline exercise gave us something concrete to talk about.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Are you going to change the gray before the library uses the material again?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. What if I make that example darker and check it on a black-and-white printout? Or, well, check the whole handout while I'm at it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Sounds sensible. Did you end up with many copies left?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: A few. I carried the leftover copies home in a canvas bag. I remember checking the large wall clock above the door before I packed up, mostly to make sure I hadn't kept everyone there all afternoon.

details_in_summary: The room had a large wall clock above the door.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: And they actually had the little toothed ones.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, for the lamp? Where'd you find them?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, a neighborhood hardware store in Fremont. I bought a pack.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Nice. How many came in it?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: 8 toothed washers. Which seems like a lot for 1 lamp, but that was the pack.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Have you tried one yet?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Not yet. I want to test one against the joint's metal surfaces, see how it fits.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right, since the rubber one kept slipping after you tightened it.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. It didn't hold the arm in place.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Are these about the size you were looking for?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: They look small enough. They're in a clear plastic envelope, so I could see them without opening it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And you only spent, what, 20 minutes comparing them?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I refuse to disclose that number. I also picked up a roll of masking tape.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: For the lamp?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: No, just masking tape. The washers are the part I want to try in the joint.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Well, I'm glad you found some after the first store didn't have any small enough.

details_in_summary: The washers came in a clear plastic envelope.
He also picked up a roll of masking tape.
key_facts: The second shop was a neighborhood hardware store in Fremont.
The pack contains eight toothed washers.
Daniel plans to test one against the joint's metal surfaces.
minor_details: The washers came in a clear plastic envelope.
He also picked up a roll of masking tape.

summary: Riley reported Daniel found 8 toothed washers at a Fremont hardware store and plans to test one against the joint's metal surfaces due to slipping rubber washers. Daniel noted the washers are small enough and visible in a clear envelope; he also bought masking tape (unrelated to the lamp). The first store didn’t have suitably small washers. Action item: Daniel will test the washers in the joint to assess fit.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I've got the proof open on the table here. It arrived on October 8.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good. How did it come?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: In a stiff cardboard mailer, so it didn't get bent. I've marked the troublesome pages with paper clips.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Let's see. March first?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yeah. I kept staring at that caption. It spells Spokane as 'Spokane,' doesn't it?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It does. That's right.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Okay. Apparently I can make myself doubt a word I've known my entire life.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And the other clip's on August. Oh, the ferry picture.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: The crop cuts off part of my face. On the screen I thought it was all in there, but on paper, no.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, I see it. The rest of the picture's clear, though.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: And the other pictures are readable at this printed size, I think. Even the ones I was worried would be too small.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I agree. I can make everyone out. It's really just that August crop.

details_in_summary: The proof came in a stiff cardboard mailer.
Hannah has marked the troublesome pages with paper clips.
key_facts: The printed proof arrived on October 8.
The March caption spells Spokane as “Spokane.”
The August crop cuts off part of Hannah's face.
minor_details: The proof came in a stiff cardboard mailer.
Hannah has marked the troublesome pages with paper clips.

summary: Riley discussed a proof arriving Oct 8, packed in a stiff mailer with paper clips on troublesome pages. They confirmed March 1 spelling of Spokane and noted self-doubt about a familiar word. The August crop of the ferry photo hides part of a face; printed size clarifies the rest, and other pictures are readable. Agreement that readability is good overall; action items include verifying the August crop issue on print and ensuring all images remain legible in printed form.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Oh, come on. I attached the new pocket the wrong way around.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The pocket for your brown trousers?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah. The opening doesn't line up with the opening in the trousers. I need to unpick part of it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Do you need the seam ripper?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Please. It's the one with the red handle.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Here. Is that the new pocket, the light-colored bit?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yep. I cut it from an old pillowcase. I even marked the cutting line with a pencil, so at least that part's straight.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Very precise pocket, just pointing the wrong way.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Exactly. A triumph of navigation.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Can you turn it around without taking the whole thing out?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but I have to undo this section first. Then I can turn it and sew it back in.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How's it now?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Done. The pocket's the right way around, and it's deep enough to hold my keys. I just tried them.

details_in_summary: She marks the cutting line with a pencil.
The seam ripper has a red handle.
key_facts: Maya cuts the replacement pocket from an old pillowcase.
The corrected pocket is deep enough to hold her keys.
minor_details: She marks the cutting line with a pencil.
The seam ripper has a red handle.

summary: Riley and Maya discussed a pocket attached to brown trousers being oriented incorrectly. They planned to unpick part of the seam with a red-handle seam ripper, then turn the pocket around without removing the whole unit. Maya had cut a new pocket from a pillowcase and marked the line for straight cutting. After undoing the necessary section and resewing, the pocket was positioned correctly and proven deep enough to hold keys. Action: Maya to finish any final seaming as needed.

dialogue.speaker: Andre
dialogue.text: Oh, you'll like this. Nadine recognized someone in one of the pictures.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: In the shop booklet? You gave it to her?

dialogue.speaker: Andre
dialogue.text: Yeah, I gave her the finished booklet on October 8, for her birthday.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good! How did she like it?

dialogue.speaker: Andre
dialogue.text: She spent a long time looking through it. She put on her readers before she opened it, which seemed promising.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And who did she recognize?

dialogue.speaker: Andre
dialogue.text: A customer, Mrs. Alvarez. Nadine spotted her in one of the photographs.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's wonderful. Did you know who she was when you picked the photo?

dialogue.speaker: Andre
dialogue.text: No, I didn't. I was looking at the shop, and Nadine was looking at the people.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It's nice she could tell you. How did the booklet turn out?

dialogue.speaker: Andre
dialogue.text: Well, after we discussed the proof, I made the captions larger. I'm glad I did.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good. Did you keep the space around the photos?

dialogue.speaker: Andre
dialogue.text: I did. And the finished one has a cream-colored cover. It's simple, but it looks good.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm really glad you got to give it to her.

dialogue.speaker: Andre
dialogue.text: Me too. Eighteen pictures turned out to be enough. Worth a try, anyway.

details_in_summary: The finished booklet has a cream-colored cover.
Nadine put on her reading glasses before opening it.
key_facts: After discussing the proof with Riley, Andre made the captions larger.
Andre gave Nadine the finished booklet on October 8.
Nadine recognized a customer, Mrs. Alvarez, in a photograph.
minor_details: The finished booklet has a cream-colored cover.
Nadine put on her reading glasses before opening it.

summary: Riley noted that Nadine recognized a customer, Mrs. Alvarez, in the photos; the finished booklet was given on Oct 8 for Nadine's birthday. Captions were made larger after proof, the layout preserved with space around photos, and a cream-colored cover used. Eighteen pictures were used and considered sufficient.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Are you making a list on a receipt at your desk?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. It's for the Italian conversation meetup. The next one is October 27.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. Is that the list you want to take with you?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: That's the idea. Last time I introduced myself, but I leaned pretty heavily on my notes.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And you wanted to answer a follow-up without reading a prepared sentence, right?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. So this time I plan to prepare topics rather than complete sentences. Food, where I live, that sort of thing.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds less like studying for a test.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Hopefully. The receipt's a little hard to read, though. A highlighter leaked in my bag.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Ah. Is the list still legible?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Mostly. What if you ask me a follow-up about one of the topics sometime? I can see where I get stuck.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Sure. And maybe copy the list onto something that hasn't been in your bag.

details_in_summary: Sam made the list on a receipt.
key_facts: The next meetup is scheduled for October 27.
Sam plans to prepare topics rather than complete sentences.
minor_details: Sam made the list on a receipt.
A highlighter leaked in their bag.

summary: Riley discussed Sam's plan for the Italian conversation meetup on October 27. Sam will use topic prompts (food, where Sam lives) instead of full sentences, and will be asked follow-up questions to reduce reliance on notes. A highlighter leakage affected legibility of the receipt list. Action items: transfer the list to a more durable medium and have Riley ask follow-up questions to steer Sam through topics.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I'm at the kitchen table with the calendar file open. I made those 2 changes from the proof.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good. How'd the August crop go?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I shifted the image over so it includes my whole face. A modest request, I think.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Reasonable. And the March caption?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I corrected the misspelled city name to Spokane. I checked it twice, which is apparently necessary.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Can you send me the updated preview? I can look at it over lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes, hang on. I saved the revised file with 'final-two' in the name.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a very reassuring file name.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: It is, in theory, the final one. Okay, I've sent you the digital preview.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Got it. Let's see. March says Spokane now, and your whole face is in the August picture.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Does August look all right otherwise? I didn't want to shift it so far that the rest of the picture looked odd.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, it looks good. I've checked both changes now, October 13, and they look right to me.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: That's a relief. I think the file's ready to order, then.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I think so too. Nice to have all 12 months settled.

details_in_summary: She saves the revised file with “final-two” in its name.
key_facts: Hannah corrects the misspelled city in the March caption.
She shifts the August image to include her whole face.
Riley checks the updated digital preview on October 13.
minor_details: Hannah makes the changes at her kitchen table.
She saves the revised file with “final-two” in its name.

summary: Riley discussed calendar edits with Hannah. Changes: August crop adjusted to include Hannah’s whole face; March caption corrected to Spokane. Hannah saved the revised file as 'final-two' and sent the digital preview. Riley reviewed the October 13 edits and approved. Decision: the file is ready to order; all 12 months are settled. Action: proceed with ordering the calendar.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So how do things stand with the photo boxes?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, the scanning and organizing are finished. The digital collection has 186 photographs.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. You got through all of them?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. They're in the decade folders, with the undated ones together. It feels manageable now.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And Teresa can actually find things without asking you what you meant by every folder name?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: That's the hope. The guide explains the layout, and it has the download instructions too.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right, since the browsable folders weren't quite enough on their own.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. Her niece could see the pictures, but downloading a whole folder was the tricky part.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And the compressed version worked for her.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: It did. So that part's settled. Teresa also picked some pictures she'd like to have on paper.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How many did she pick?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: 12 photographs for new prints. She marked her selections with removable paper tabs.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a nice, contained number. I was picturing you ordering 186 prints.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: No, thankfully. I ordered the 12 in a standard 4-by-6-inch size.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you spend an hour comparing print sizes first?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I did consider it. But I stopped myself. Personal growth, very moving.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm proud of you. Did you check the order?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, I checked the order on my phone while I was waiting for a bus.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And the original photos are still with Teresa?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. She's keeping those. The digital collection is the part relatives can browse without digging through boxes.

details_in_summary: Teresa marked her selections with removable paper tabs.
key_facts: The finished digital collection contains 186 photographs.
Teresa selected 12 photographs for new prints.
Daniel ordered the prints in a standard 4-by-6-inch size.
minor_details: Teresa marked her selections with removable paper tabs.
Daniel checked the order on his phone while waiting for a bus.

summary: Riley discussed the photo-box project with Daniel. Scanning and organizing are complete; the digital collection has 186 photos, sorted into decade folders with undated ones grouped together. A guide and download instructions aim to help Teresa browse, aided by a compressed version for downloads. Teresa chose 12 photos for prints (4x6), marked with removable tabs; originals remain with Teresa. Riley also confirmed the print order on her phone; relatives can browse digitally without accessing the physical boxes.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: The hallway shelf is helping with the scrolling, but the alarm situation isn't great.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, sleeping through my phone alarm from the hallway kind of defeats the point.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but we don't have to give up on the whole thing. Is there another alarm you could use?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: My wristwatch has one. I can try using that.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Do you know where it is?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I just found it in my desk drawer. I think I can set the alarm on it tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Good. And I think I need an exception for my phone sometimes.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: For what?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: When I'm waiting for a library schedule update, I'd like to keep it nearby so I can check.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That makes sense. It doesn't have to be all or nothing.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Right. Otherwise we'll need a committee to approve each phone movement.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The committee should know you're wearing mismatched socks.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: The committee has bigger problems. Let's try the watch and the schedule exception tonight.

details_in_summary: Riley finds the watch in a desk drawer.
key_facts: Riley will try using the alarm on their wristwatch.
Maya may keep her phone nearby when she is waiting for a library schedule update.
They will try the changes that night.
minor_details: Riley finds the watch in a desk drawer.
Maya is wearing mismatched socks.

summary: Riley discussed improving alarm reliability by using a wristwatch alarm after finding it in the desk. They plan to test the watch tonight and keep the watch accessible. Maya requested a temporary exception to keep the phone nearby for library schedule updates, avoids a full committee process, and both agreed to try the watch and schedule exception tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. Okay, so, this is a pretty good lunch break.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. Coffee at Low Tide was a good call.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I nearly spent the whole walk here deciding what to order. A familiar problem.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You managed, though. How's the lamp?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I tried 1 of those toothed washers from the pack. The bolt's too short with it in there.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How short?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Only 1 thread of the bolt reaches the nut with the new washer in place.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, that's barely anything.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. The nut was barely engaged, so I stopped tightening.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good. I wouldn't try to force it on.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: No. I kept looking at it like I could persuade it to be longer.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What about finding a slightly longer bolt instead?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: That's what I was thinking. Same diameter, just a little longer.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Do you have the old one to compare?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah, the old bolt's wrapped in a paper napkin in my pocket.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Convenient. And very glamorous.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I thought so. It's the 12-millimeter one, but I'd rather have it with me than just guess.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Makes sense. You can compare it at the shop.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. I'll look for a longer bolt of the same diameter.

details_in_summary: Daniel has the old bolt wrapped in a paper napkin in his pocket.
key_facts: With the new washer in place, only one thread of the bolt reaches the nut.
Daniel stopped tightening because the nut was barely engaged.
He plans to look for a longer bolt of the same diameter.
minor_details: They talk over coffee at Low Tide.
Daniel has the old bolt wrapped in a paper napkin in his pocket.

summary: Riley and Daniel discussed a lunch break and coffee choice. They reviewed a mechanical issue: a toothed washer made a bolt too short, leaving barely any thread engagement. They concluded not to force it and to seek a slightly longer bolt of the same diameter, using the old 12-mm bolt as a size reference kept in Daniel’s pocket for shop comparison.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I'm standing in the entryway looking at our new bench.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, you found one! What happened with the hook rail?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Nadiya approved fastening the rail to the wall. So we went ahead and ordered one, but it hasn't arrived yet.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Nice. And the bench fits in that little strip by the door?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: In theory, yes. It's 24 inches wide and 10 inches deep, so it's within the space I measured.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a relief after the wobbly rack.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes. I was not keen to bring home another thing that couldn't hold 2 coats and a bag.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What's the bench look like?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: It has a dark green seat. Owen assembled it with an Allen key, which looked more fiddly than the instructions suggested.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: As is tradition. Have you put it by the wall yet?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Not properly. We're waiting for the hook rail to arrive before we put everything in place.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Well, at least you've got permission and a bench. That's progress.

details_in_summary: The bench has a dark green seat.
Owen assembled it with an Allen key.
key_facts: Nadiya approved fastening the rail to the wall.
Hannah bought a bench that is 24 inches wide and 10 inches deep.
minor_details: The bench has a dark green seat.
Owen assembled it with an Allen key.

summary: Riley discussed the new bench with Hannah. Nadiya approved fastening the hook rail to the wall, and the rail has been ordered but not arrived. The bench is 24 inches wide and 10 inches deep, and should fit the space; it remains to be positioned until the rail arrives. The bench has a dark green seat, assembled by Owen with an Allen key. Next steps: wait for the hook rail, then install the bench and rail.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, Omid. I'm just coming in with a small bag of apples.

dialogue.speaker: Omid
dialogue.text: Evening, Riley. I've got my thermos of coffee, so between us we're prepared for something.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A very modest picnic. Oh, did that Cascadia tile ever arrive?

dialogue.speaker: Omid
dialogue.text: It did, actually. The replacement arrived on October 9.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The forest-and-mountain habitat tile?

dialogue.speaker: Omid
dialogue.text: That's the one. The publisher sent it at no charge, just like they said.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Nice. After you looked in the box and under the sofa, I figured the original had really disappeared.

dialogue.speaker: Omid
dialogue.text: Yes, it seems to have found a better place to live.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And are you, Farah and Dev still playing regularly?

dialogue.speaker: Omid
dialogue.text: We are. We're still meeting twice a month.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm glad. And glad your Cascadia set's complete again.

key_facts: The replacement arrived on October 9.
The group is still meeting twice a month.
minor_details: Omid has a thermos of coffee with him.
Riley is carrying a small bag of apples.

summary: Riley discussed bringing apples for a modest picnic and inquired about the Cascadia tile replacement. Omid noted the replacement tile arrived on October 9 and was provided by the publisher at no charge, and mentioned the original tile had disappeared. They confirmed Farah and Dev still meet twice a month, and Riley expressed satisfaction that the Cascadia set is complete again.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: So, how did the watch alarm go this morning?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Not great. The watch slipped under my pillow and I missed the alarm.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but was it on your wrist when you went to sleep?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: No, I took it off and put it beside the pillow. Apparently that wasn't a very good spot.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: A pillow is a pretty effective alarm muffler. I'm going to finish my peppermint tea before it gets cold.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm putting the watch on top of a book for tomorrow morning. It should be easier to hear there.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: And less likely to end up under the pillow. Want to try it there for now?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. We'll see if it wakes me up this time.

key_facts: Riley missed the alarm after the watch slipped under a pillow.
Riley puts the watch on top of a book for the next morning.
minor_details: Maya is drinking peppermint tea.

summary: Riley discussed the watch alarm missing due to it being under the pillow. They noted pillow muffling. Riley proposed placing the watch on top of a book to improve audibility and planned to try it tomorrow. Maya suggested the new spot and will observe the result.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Oh, nice, Becca just sent the game choice for tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What's she picked?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Carcassonne. Something familiar, which feels good for a Thursday after work.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And you're back at the cafe?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: No, Becca's hosting the October 15 session at her apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right. This is the first one on the third-Thursday schedule, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. It's nice not having to poll everyone about dates. A small administrative victory.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Are you still doing the rotating seat?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: That's the plan. And what if we keep those 10 minutes for questions that Tomas suggested? I think that'd be useful.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Seems like an easy way to get everyone comfortable before you start.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. Oh, and I'm bringing a container of grapes. Very complicated contribution.

details_in_summary: Sam plans to bring a container of grapes.
key_facts: Becca is hosting the October 15 session at her apartment.
The group will play Carcassonne.
minor_details: Sam plans to bring a container of grapes.

summary: Riley and Sam discussed Becca’s game choice for Thursday: Carcassonne. The October 15 session will be at Becca’s apartment, the first on the third-Thursday schedule. They plan to continue rotating seating and keep 10 minutes for questions as Tomas suggested. Riley noted this as an administrative efficiency. An action item is to implement the rotating seating and the Q&A, with Sam planning to bring grapes as a contribution.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, how do things stand with the sign-up process?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Pretty close. Marisol and I held a staff walkthrough on October 15, and the revised process is scheduled to begin at Swasey on October 21.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, that's next Wednesday. How did the walkthrough go?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Well, mostly. I used a fictional knitting program for the practice run, so nobody had to worry about accidentally signing up for a real event.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And did the paper sheet make sense to everyone?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: The sheet did, yes. But someone asked when we should check whether the event was full. I'd sort of skipped past that in the instructions.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Ah. Before taking the paper request, or before entering it?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Before entering it. The instructions now say to check event capacity before entering a paper request. That way staff can see whether there's a place or whether it's a waitlist situation.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Makes sense. And they're still entering it while the patron's there?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes, into the same registration system. That's the part I wanted everyone to practice, rather than leaving a sheet sitting around to be entered later.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Sounds like a useful question to catch before Wednesday.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: It was. Also, someone brought clementines to the walkthrough, which improved the atmosphere considerably. In theory, all procedural questions should come with citrus.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'll remember that next time I'm stuck on a form.

details_in_summary: Hannah used a fictional knitting program for the practice run.
key_facts: Hannah and Marisol held a staff walkthrough on October 15.
The instructions now say to check event capacity before entering a paper request.
The revised process is scheduled to begin at Swasey on October 21.
minor_details: Hannah used a fictional knitting program for the practice run.
Someone brought clementines to the walkthrough.

summary: Riley discussed the sign-up process update. A staff walkthrough occurred on Oct 15; the revised process starts Oct 21 at Swasey. Practice used a fictional knitting program. The paper sheet was clear, but a capacity-check step was missing; the instruction now requires checking event capacity before entering a paper request. Entries will be made in the registration system with the patron present. Action item: finalize and enforce the capacity-check workflow before Wednesday.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. Okay, so, it's properly chilly this morning.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, the gym's front windows were fogged when we arrived.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I could barely see in. Also, I brought an apple in my jacket pocket, and I think it's survived so far.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A reward for wrestling with that overhang?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. That blue problem is steeper than it looked from the floor.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You got through the start pretty smoothly, though.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: The first 3 moves, yes. The fourth, absolutely not.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I saw you almost get your hand on it that last time.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Almost is doing a lot of work there. My feet came off before I could hold it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It might help to get your hips closer to the wall before you reach.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, less dangling like an abandoned coat. I can try that after a rest.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, take your time. You got to the last hold on that green one after resting between attempts.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: That 5-minute rest helped. Today, October 17, I think the overhanging blue problem has earned me at least that.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Definitely. And there's no need to finish it today.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Speaking of taking my time, what's the difference between a punch pass and a monthly membership?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A punch pass gives you a set number of visits. With a monthly membership, you pay for the month rather than each visit. We'd have to check the desk for the current prices and terms.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Right. I need to be realistic about how often I'd actually go, not how often a very optimistic version of me would go.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah. No spreadsheet required yet, though I know you're tempted.

details_in_summary: The gym's front windows were fogged when they arrived.
key_facts: On October 17, Daniel tried an overhanging blue problem.
He could make the first three moves but not the fourth.
He asks Riley about the difference between a punch pass and a monthly membership.
minor_details: Daniel brought an apple in his jacket pocket.
The gym's front windows were fogged when they arrived.

summary: Riley and Daniel discussed gym conditions (fogged windows) and Daniel’s progress on the blue overhang, noting rest breaks and technique tips (hip position, less dangling). They referenced the green route completion after rests. They compared punch pass versus monthly membership and planned to check desk for current prices and terms, with a note to avoid overcommitting today.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You're spreading the dress across the bed?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah. I wanted to get a good look at it before I decided what to do.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Is that the tear beside the zipper?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: That's it. I was hoping I could save the dress, but the fabric around the seam is weak too.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, yeah. It looks pretty thin there.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but if I just stitch the tear closed, I think the stitches would pull at the weakened fabric.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Like the cuff did when I bent my wrist?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: A little, except this is right beside the zipper. I don't think a strip of fabric would be as simple here.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Could you put a patch behind it?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Maybe someone could. I'm not sure I could get it secure without making the zipper hard to use.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Fair enough. You've got less room to work with there.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Oh, a button just came loose while I was handling it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Here, I'll pick it up. Is that part at least fixable?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: The button, probably. But fixing that doesn't do anything for the tear.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Right. And you'd still have that weak seam.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I keep turning it over, hoping it'll look easier from the other side.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Any luck?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: No. I think this repair is beyond my skills.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Then it makes sense to let that one go. You don't have to mend everything.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah. I'm going to set the dress aside for textile recycling instead of trying to repair it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Okay. I'll put the button with it.

details_in_summary: A button comes loose while she handles it.
key_facts: The dress has a tear beside its zipper and weakened fabric around the seam.
Maya sets the dress aside for textile recycling rather than attempting the repair.
minor_details: She spreads the dress across the bed to inspect it.
A button comes loose while she handles it.

summary: Riley discussed a dress with a tear near the zipper and weak surrounding fabric. They considered stitching, patching behind the tear, and the impact on the zipper, concluding repair is unlikely. A loose button was noted, deemed fixable but not addressing the tear. Ultimately, the dress will be set aside for textile recycling, and the button will be kept with it for recycling.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You're still at your desk? I thought you might have escaped already.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Just finishing up. I'm trying not to turn tomorrow's departure into a whole new project.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How's that going?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Pretty well, actually. I've checked in for the outbound flight and set my out-of-office reply for the days I'll be away from Harborline.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Nice. And you're still working tomorrow before you leave?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah, then the flight's in the evening. My suitcase is standing by the apartment door, so I can't pretend I forgot it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you get your waterproof jacket in there?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I did. And a pair of wool socks, which feels like a very responsible thing to mention.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: You're ready for anything, as long as anything is wet feet.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. Oh, and Emeka and I agreed we'll confirm the arrival details by text. I don't need to make a separate plan for confirming the plan.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Probably not. I hope you get plenty of downtime with him.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Thanks. That's the idea. I'm going to leave the rest alone and see what the days look like when I get there.

details_in_summary: Sam packed a pair of wool socks.
key_facts: Sam has checked in for the outbound flight.
Sam has set an out-of-office reply for the days away from Harborline.
Sam and Emeka have agreed to confirm the arrival details by text.
minor_details: Sam packed a pair of wool socks.
Their suitcase is standing by the apartment door.

summary: Riley noted Sam's travel prep: finishing work, outbound flight checked in, out-of-office set, and packing reiterated (waterproof jacket and wool socks). Sam will work tomorrow, then fly in the evening, with luggage ready. He and Emeka will confirm arrival details by text and keep plans loose, letting the days unfold on arrival. Riley expressed hope for downtime during the visit and no additional planning beyond the text confirmation.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, how are we looking on a gift for Dad's birthday lunch?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I was thinking we could get him something together instead of 2 separate presents. Something practical.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, I like that. What about an insulated travel mug?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: That could work. I was comparing mugs earlier, and there are a surprising number of lids to consider.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'd vote for one that's easy to clean.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Please. My own mug lid has a stubborn coffee stain that I can't get out. In theory, the lid comes apart easily.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: In theory is doing a lot of work there.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: It really is. Anyway, an insulated travel mug sounds good for Walter. Nothing too complicated.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'll order it. How about dark green?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Dark green is good. And let's split the cost evenly.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Deal. I'll let you know the total when I order it.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Thanks. I was starting to think I'd have to make a spreadsheet about lids.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: We can put it in a plain paper gift bag, too. No elaborate wrapping required.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Perfect. A mug and a bag. That's a manageable birthday operation.

details_in_summary: Riley suggests using a plain paper gift bag.
key_facts: They choose an insulated travel mug as Walter's gift.
Riley will order the mug in dark green.
Hannah and Riley will split the cost evenly.
minor_details: Hannah's own mug lid has a stubborn coffee stain.
Riley suggests using a plain paper gift bag.

summary: Riley and Hannah discussed buying one practical gift for Dad's birthday lunch, opting for an insulated travel mug. They weighed lid options, prioritizing easy cleaning. They agreed on dark green and to split the cost. Riley will order the mug and report the total; packaging will be a plain paper gift bag to keep it simple.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: And this time I didn't have to translate every sentence before I could cook.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, what did you make?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Pasta e ceci, from an Italian recipe. Chickpeas and pasta, basically.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Nice. Was it easier than the zucchini recipe?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah, quite a bit. I could follow the sequence of cooking the chickpeas and pasta without translating every sentence.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you get through it without looking anything up?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Not quite. I checked a few words. Scolare was one of them; it means to drain. I looked that up before I started.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Probably a good one to know before the water's boiling.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. What if I figured it out while holding a hot pan? A very efficient language test.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And the verb endings didn't slow you down as much?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Not this time. I think noticing those infinitives in recipes helped. I could recognize more of the instructions as instructions.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How did the pasta e ceci turn out?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Good! I used a small saucepan, and there was enough left for lunch the next day.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a pretty good return on 5 minutes of vocabulary.

key_facts: Sam made pasta e ceci from an Italian recipe.
Sam understood the sequence of cooking the chickpeas and pasta without translating every sentence.
Sam checked the word scolare, meaning to drain, before starting.
minor_details: Sam used a small saucepan.
There was enough left for lunch the next day.

summary: Riley discussed using Italian cooking as a language-learning tool, cooking pasta e ceci with fewer translations. Sam looked up a few words like scolare (to drain) and benefited from recognizing infinitives in recipes. Riley noted improved ability to follow instructions without translating each sentence and reported a good outcome with leftovers for lunch after about five minutes of vocabulary work.

dialogue.speaker: Lucia
dialogue.text: I'm unwrapping this on your counter, if that's all right. The faded blue tea towel has been doing a respectable job of holding the crumbs.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Of course. Oh, look at that loaf. It's nice and rounded.

dialogue.speaker: Lucia
dialogue.text: It actually held its shape instead of spreading wide. I was starting to think my Dutch oven preferred pancakes.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Is this from judging the rise instead of watching the clock?

dialogue.speaker: Lucia
dialogue.text: Yes. I ended bulk fermentation when the dough had risen about 50%, like we talked about.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How long did it take to get there?

dialogue.speaker: Lucia
dialogue.text: About 5 hours and 15 minutes on this bake.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's quite a bit longer than the 4 hours you were giving it in June.

dialogue.speaker: Lucia
dialogue.text: It is. My kitchen was 66°F this morning, though, so I wasn't expecting it to move as fast.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Especially compared with that 76°F day when the second loaf came out flat.

dialogue.speaker: Lucia
dialogue.text: Exactly. And as it gets colder, I expect the rise may take longer. I'm still adjusting the timing.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: At least the dough gives you something to look at besides the clock.

dialogue.speaker: Lucia
dialogue.text: Yes. The clock is very precise about the wrong thing.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'm getting the serrated knife from the bottom drawer. Can I cut us a slice?

dialogue.speaker: Lucia
dialogue.text: Please. I didn't bring it over just to be admired.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: There we go. The crust sounds good. Here, try this piece.

dialogue.speaker: Lucia
dialogue.text: Thanks. Mm. I'm pleased with that. I'll keep watching the rise as the kitchen cools.

details_in_summary: Riley cuts a slice with the serrated knife from the bottom drawer.
key_facts: The loaf Lucia shares holds a rounded shape rather than spreading wide.
On that bake, the dough took about five hours and fifteen minutes to reach Lucia's target rise.
Lucia says her kitchen was 66°F that morning and she expects the rise may take longer as it gets colder.
minor_details: Lucia wrapped the loaf in a faded blue tea towel.
Riley cuts a slice with the serrated knife from the bottom drawer.

summary: Riley and Lucia discussed a bake where the loaf held its shape and rose about 50% during bulk fermentation. They compared timing to previous bakes, noting 5h15m at 66°F versus 4h expected, and acknowledged colder temperatures slow the rise. They plan to adjust timing as the kitchen cools and continue watching the rise rather than relying on the clock. They confirmed slicing a piece with a serrated knife and commented on the crust and loaf appearance.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Hey. Is it just me, or is it getting dark ridiculously early now?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey. Yeah, it felt like evening before I was done with work.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: It reminded me of getting back to Ballard after dark on Sunday. I was glad to be home, but I liked that weekend.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Me too. Saturday afternoon with Walter was really nice. We just talked for a while and took that short walk near his house.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I'm glad we brought the warm jackets. And that we didn't have to watch the clock the whole time.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, leaving most of the weekend open was the right call. We actually had time to hang out with him.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: And his cornbread with dinner was good. I'd happily have eaten another piece.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Same. The drive east was the part that tested my patience.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Waiting about 25 minutes for a charger to open up didn't help. The car was ready for a break, but apparently so was everyone else's.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Next time I'd leave more room in the drive for a wait like that. It wasn't terrible, just longer than I expected.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but would you still pick the same stops, or look for another option too?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I'd look for another option too, just in case. I wouldn't want to add a bunch of reservations to the weekend, though.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Agreed. And on the drive home I got that bag of apples, so at least we came back with a snack.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A pretty good souvenir for a weekend where we mostly just got to visit.

details_in_summary: Walter served cornbread with dinner.
key_facts: They spent Saturday afternoon talking with Walter and took a short walk near his house.
On the way east, they waited about 25 minutes for a charger to open up.
They got back to Ballard after dark on Sunday.
minor_details: Walter served cornbread with dinner.
Maya bought a bag of apples on the drive home.

summary: Riley discussed the early darkness and weekend plans with Maya, recounting Saturday with Walter, warm jackets, and cornbread. They noted a 25-minute charger wait on the eastbound drive and agreed to leave weekends open but consider alternative stops to reduce reservations. Riley planned to seek other options in the future and avoid overbooking. On return, they picked apples as a simple souvenir from the weekend.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How are things standing with the piece, now that the gathering's so close?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Okay, so, I did a full run-through for Marisol at my lesson. I dropped a stroke near the end, but I found the beat again and kept going.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's good, though, right? You didn't start over.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. I wanted to. There was that little moment of, well, that's ruined, let's go back to the beginning.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And then you just kept playing?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Pretty much. It felt messy, but I could hear where the beat was and got back onto it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's probably a useful thing to know you can do before Sunday.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: That's what Marisol said. She also suggested I practice the final accents after each run-through.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So even if you make a mistake, you finish the piece and then go back to those accents?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Exactly. Instead of treating the mistake like an emergency and never actually practicing the ending.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: How's that transition in bar 9 feeling now?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Still needs attention, but I got through it in the run-through. Apparently I have room in my life for more than 1 awkward section.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Very generous of you.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I know. Oh, and my music stand has 1 slightly stiff adjustment knob. I keep fiddling with it instead of getting on with the pad.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A familiar strategy. Are you feeling ready for October 25?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Ready enough to show up, I think. I'm planning to bring a bottle of water in my backpack. That's the part I've managed to decide without comparing 6 options.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's progress too. And if you drop a stroke, you know you can find your way back.

details_in_summary: Daniel's music stand has one slightly stiff adjustment knob.
He plans to bring a bottle of water in his backpack.
key_facts: Daniel dropped a stroke during his lesson run-through but found the beat again.
Marisol suggested practicing the final accents after each run-through.
minor_details: Daniel's music stand has one slightly stiff adjustment knob.
He plans to bring a bottle of water in his backpack.

summary: Riley noted Daniel completed a full run-through for Marisol, recovered from a late stroke, and kept going. Marisol advised finishing the piece and practicing final accents after each run-through. Bar 9 transition still needs work but was navigated in the run-through. Daniel mentioned a stiff music stand knob and plans to bring water for October 25. Action items: practice endings after each run-through, polish bar 9, and ensure water is packed.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I've revised the library handout since the workshop. Would you look at the new structure?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Yeah, definitely. Is that the copy there?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: It will be once I get the pages together. Oh, the stapler jammed on the first attempt.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A promising start.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The handout on making things easier to use has defeated the stapler. Here, you can just take the loose pages.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Thanks. I'll read them here beside my mug of ginger tea.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I grouped the advice under 3 action headings instead of having it all run together.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, yeah. I can see where each section starts now.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: What if you just scan it first? I'm curious what you find without reading every line.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The headings catch my eye, then the examples. It feels much easier to scan.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Good. I was worried the headings might make it feel too much like instructions.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Not really. It's not a checklist of design rules. You still explain why someone might make a change.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: That's what I was aiming for. Not 'always do this,' more 'here's what to look for.'

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And the example is much clearer. Is that the one that came out so faint?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Yeah. I changed the pale example to black text on a white background. The gray was hard to read on the library's black-and-white printouts.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That should be a lot easier to make out. The explanation next to it is short, too.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I trimmed it back a bit. And down at the bottom, I left a blank space where a library branch can add its contact information.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I see it. There's enough room without it getting in the way of the advice.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: That's the balance I was hoping for. I didn't want the contact space to look like part of the exercise.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It doesn't to me. The separation is clear.

key_facts: Sam changed the pale example to use black text on a white background.
The revised handout groups its advice under three action headings.
Sam left a blank space where a library branch can add its contact information.
minor_details: Riley reads the pages beside a mug of ginger tea.
Sam's stapler jams on the first attempt.

summary: Riley discussed Sam’s revised library handout structure, noting the pages will be combined soon. They approved grouping advice under three action headings, emphasizing why changes matter rather than a strict checklist. They favored scanning-first design, clearer black-on-white examples, and concise explanations. A blank space for each library branch’s contact info was maintained without cluttering the exercise. Action: finalize pages, confirm print readability, and preserve the separation between content and contact space.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Hi, Riley. How's your evening going?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Hey, Hannah. Pretty quiet so far. How's yours?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Not bad. I've been thinking about the Thursday swim schedule again.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The trial runs through today, right?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Right, and Daphne scheduled the decision for October 26. I checked with Marisol about whether she could keep covering the openings.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And is she up for it?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Most Thursdays, yes. She's willing to keep doing them, but there's a snag on the first Thursday of each month.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: What happens then?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: There's a recurring delivery that conflicts with Marisol's availability that morning. I noticed it when I was looking at the printed delivery calendar.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So you'd need someone else to cover that opening?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: That's what I'm thinking. I'll ask Daphne if she can cover that monthly opening, with Marisol doing most of the others.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: She did cover one during the trial, when Marisol was on leave.

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: Yes. I don't want to assume she can do it every month, though. I'll just ask.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And you've got the dates handy?

dialogue.speaker: Hannah
dialogue.text: I folded the calendar into my coat pocket to take to the meeting. In theory, that's a filing system.

key_facts: Marisol is willing to continue covering most Thursday openings.
A delivery on the first Thursday of each month conflicts with Marisol's availability.
Hannah will ask Daphne to cover that monthly opening.
minor_details: Hannah noticed the conflict while looking at a printed delivery calendar.
She folded the calendar into her coat pocket to take to the meeting.

summary: Riley discussed the Thursday swim schedule with Hannah. The trial runs through today; Daphne’s decision is scheduled for October 26. Marisol can cover most Thursdays, but the first Thursday each month conflicts with a recurring delivery. They plan for Daphne to cover that monthly opening, with Marisol handling the others. Riley noted a past coverage during Marisol’s leave. Hannah will bring the dates to the meeting and confirm details with Daphne.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Hey, Riley. Okay, so, how's your lunch?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Good. I was hungrier than I thought. How are things at the Gull House?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Busy, but manageable. The opening weeks have gone pretty well, considering we were still fiddling with the rota.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did that Saturday swap work out?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. We did have an usher arrive late to the October 16 screening, though.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, was it a scramble at the door?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: A little, but the remaining ushers covered the door until the late volunteer arrived. Nobody had to abandon it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's good. How late were they?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I'm not sure exactly. The lobby clock was running 4 minutes fast that evening, which didn't help my highly scientific timekeeping.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Did you write it down somewhere?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I kept my notes in a folded program. Anyway, I've proposed an on-call backup for future busy screenings, rather than adding another person to every shift.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That sounds sensible. You get some cover without making the rota even harder to fill.

details_in_summary: The lobby clock was running four minutes fast that evening.
Daniel kept his notes in a folded program.
key_facts: An usher arrived late to the October 16 screening.
The remaining ushers covered the door until the late volunteer arrived.
Daniel has proposed an on-call backup rather than adding another person to every shift.
minor_details: The lobby clock was running four minutes fast that evening.
Daniel kept his notes in a folded program.

summary: Riley discussed Gull House operations and schedule adjustments. Daniel reported the opening weeks were busy but manageable, with ongoing rota adjustments and a late-arriving usher on Oct 16. The team covered the door despite a minor scramble, aided by a lobby clock that ran four minutes fast. Riley noted Daniel’s folded program notes and the proposal for an on-call backup for busy screenings, rather than expanding every shift.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Oh, there's the date. The organizers are scheduling the final cleanup for November 1.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, good. That's a Sunday, right?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Yeah. Do you want to go for one more morning before winter?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: I do. Even if I have to rinse mud off a boot at home again.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: That boot did bring a little bit of the shoreline home with it.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Just the one boot, too. I don't know how I managed that.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Selective mud. Anyway, how did you feel about counting the gloves afterward?

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: It was pretty straightforward. We found 6 usable pairs, right?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: 6, yeah. Fewer than the 8 spare pairs we found in the supply box back in August.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: And one of those was already wet inside. I remember that much.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay, but for the handoff this time, I can write the remaining supply totals on the organizer's checklist.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So they know what they've got left?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Exactly. The glove count and whatever else needs to be tallied. I don't want to rely on remembering it later.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Makes sense. Do you need me to remind you?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: I've got the checklist reminder beside the fruit bowl. It's competing with the bananas for my attention.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Tough competition. I'll help with the counting, though.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Thanks. And I'll do the writing. That should make the handoff less muddled.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Sounds good. This peppermint tea is nice, by the way.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: It is. A good way to spend a Friday evening: tea and a discussion of glove totals.

details_in_summary: Maya keeps the checklist reminder beside the fruit bowl.
key_facts: The glove count found six usable pairs.
The organizers are scheduling the final cleanup for November 1.
Maya will write the remaining supply totals on the organizer’s checklist.
minor_details: Riley had to rinse mud off a boot at home.
Maya keeps the checklist reminder beside the fruit bowl.
They are drinking peppermint tea while they talk.

summary: Riley discussed a final cleanup on November 1 (Sunday) and the possibility of one more muddy morning before winter. They counted gloves: 6 usable pairs found, fewer than 8 spare pairs from August, with one spare wet. For the handoff, Maya will write remaining supply totals on the organizer’s checklist; Riley will help with counting. A reminder is kept beside the fruit bowl to track supplies.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Oh, good, it actually worked! Teresa opened the collection herself.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Oh, nice. With the private link?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. I showed her where to find it, and she opened the digital collection using the private link.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: After all that folder-download trouble, that must feel pretty good.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: It does. Okay, so, I also delivered the new prints to Teresa in Bellevue.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: The 12 she picked out?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yep, the 4-by-6s. She put them in a shallow blue tray.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: That's a nice way to keep them together. Did she like how they came out?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: She did. We looked through them, and then we had pear slices.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: A very civilized ending to the photo project.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Yeah. I was only mildly tempted to compare the thickness of each slice.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: Growth.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Enormous growth. I left Teresa a printed copy of the folder guide, too.

dialogue.speaker: Me
dialogue.text: So she can pass the link and the guide along to relatives herself now?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Exactly. They don't have to come through me every time they want to find a picture.

details_in_summary: Teresa put the prints in a shallow blue tray.
key_facts: Daniel delivered the new prints to Teresa in Bellevue.
Teresa successfully opened the digital collection using the private link.
Daniel left Teresa a printed copy of the folder guide.
minor_details: Teresa put the prints in a shallow blue tray.
They had pear slices after looking through the pictures.
